cards.q: What is the difference between .NET Framework, .NET Core and .NET 6/8/10?
cards.h: Framework = Windows house, Core = portable tent, .NET 5+ = one family where even numbers stay long.
s: .NET Framework is the original, Windows-only platform. Its last version is 4.8, and it now only gets security and bug fixes. Things like WCF and classic ASP.NET live there.

.NET Core was Microsoft's cross-platform, open-source rewrite. It runs on Linux and in containers, it's much faster, and it has dependency injection, configuration and logging built in. From .NET 5 onwards the "Core" name was dropped and it's simply called .NET, one unified platform. The even-numbered versions, like .NET 6, 8 and 10, are long-term support releases with three years of support, and the odd ones are short-term releases.

That's why in a regulated product like ours we standardise on the LTS versions. We moved from .NET 6 to 8, and in [early 2026] I upgraded [3] of our IRT services from .NET 8 to .NET 10. Mostly it was package updates and a few breaking changes, and we got about [10-15%] better p95 latency for free.
So in short: Framework is legacy, .NET is the present. I can walk through how I plan an upgrade if that helps.
cards.k: framework, core, versions, lts, runtime

cards.q: Value types vs reference types?
cards.h: Value = photocopy, Reference = shared Google Doc link.
s: A value type holds its data directly. Examples are int, bool, DateTime, enums and structs. When you assign it to another variable or pass it to a method, the value is copied, so changing the copy doesn't affect the original.

A reference type, like a class, string, array or delegate, holds a reference to an object that lives on the managed heap. When you assign it, only the reference is copied, so two variables can point to the same object, and a change through one is visible through the other. Value types usually live inline, on the stack or inside their containing object, so they avoid heap allocations. But if you put a value type into an object variable, it gets boxed, which costs an allocation.

In practice, I use structs only for small, immutable values, and classes for business objects that have identity and behaviour. For example, in our services entities like Shipment are classes, while a small Money or date-range type can be a readonly struct.
One classic trap is a mutable struct inside a list, where you end up changing a copy. I can explain boxing in more detail if you like.
cards.k: struct, class, stack, heap, boxing

cards.q: How does async/await actually work?
cards.h: Waiter takes your order and serves other tables; he does not stand at the kitchen door.
s: Async and await let a method wait for slow work, like a database call or an HTTP request, without blocking the thread.

Under the hood, the compiler rewrites an async method into a state machine. When the code hits an await on a task that isn't finished yet, it registers the rest of the method as a continuation and returns the thread to the thread pool. Importantly, no new thread is created for I/O; the operating system just notifies us when the data arrives. Then the method resumes from where it stopped, on a pool thread. Because threads aren't sitting idle while we wait, one server can handle many more requests with fewer threads.

The rules I follow are: async all the way down, never block with .Result or .Wait(), because that can cause thread starvation or deadlocks, and avoid async void except for event handlers. In our IRT APIs, every database and HTTP call is async with cancellation tokens, so threads stay free while SQL Server is working.
I can also explain ConfigureAwait or what happens with exceptions in async methods.
cards.k: state machine, thread pool, non-blocking, task, async, await, asynchronous, valuetask, configureawait

cards.q: Task vs Thread vs ValueTask?
cards.h: Thread = hiring a worker; Task = placing an order; ValueTask = order already on the shelf.
s: A Thread is an actual operating system thread. It's expensive to create, it has its own stack, and you manage its lifecycle yourself. I almost never create threads directly in modern code.

A Task represents an operation that will complete in the future. It might run on a thread-pool thread, or it might be pure I/O with no thread at all while it waits, like a database call. Tasks are what async and await are built on, they compose nicely with things like Task.WhenAll, and they carry results and exceptions.

ValueTask is a lighter alternative for methods that often complete synchronously, for example a cache lookup that usually hits. A Task is a heap object, so returning ValueTask in those cases avoids an allocation. But it has rules: you should await it only once and not store it.

In practice, in our web APIs I use Task everywhere by default, and I'd only use ValueTask in a measured hot path, like a cached configuration lookup. Threads I leave to the framework, or to a BackgroundService for long-running work. I can show where ValueTask is actually worth it.
cards.k: thread pool, valuetask, task parallel library, async, await, task, asynchronous, configureawait, thread, threading, thread-safe, concurrency, lock, race condition

cards.q: IEnumerable vs IQueryable vs List?
cards.h: IQueryable = send the shopping list to the shop; IEnumerable = bring the whole shop home, then pick.
s: All three are about collections, but they differ in where the work happens.

IEnumerable works on data in memory. When you use LINQ on it, the filters run as C# code on the application server. IQueryable is different: it builds an expression tree, and a provider like EF Core translates that into SQL, so the filtering, sorting and paging run inside the database. A List is a concrete collection that's already loaded in memory, with indexing and a Count.

The important practical point is when the query actually executes. If you call ToList too early, or pass an IQueryable as IEnumerable, EF Core pulls the whole table into memory and then filters it in C#. That's a classic performance bug.

So in our APIs I keep the query as IQueryable while I add filters, sorting and paging, then I call ToListAsync once at the end. For example, on our shipment search screen, building the filters on IQueryable meant SQL Server returned only one page of rows instead of thousands.
I can explain deferred execution too, which is closely related.
cards.k: linq, deferred execution, ef core, list, ienumerable, iqueryable

cards.q: Abstract class vs interface?
cards.h: Interface = job description; abstract class = half-built house you finish.
s: An interface is a contract. It says what a type can do, but not how, and a class can implement many interfaces. An abstract class is a partial base class. It can hold shared code, fields and constructors, but a class can inherit from only one.

So the way I decide is: if I need a capability or a dependency that I want to swap or mock, I use an interface. If several implementations share real code, I use an abstract base class. Since C# 8 interfaces can have default methods, but I still keep them mostly as pure contracts.

A real example is our SFTP integration. All three providers, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, implement one ISftpClient interface, so the business code and the unit tests depend only on the interface, and the DI container or a factory picks the provider. Then they inherit from an abstract base class that holds the shared retry, timeout and logging logic, so I didn't repeat it three times.
So it's not either-or; they work well together. I can explain how that helped with testing.
cards.k: interface, abstract, inheritance, contract

cards.q: Explain SOLID with examples from your work.
cards.h: SOLID = Single job, Open door for new rooms, Liskov swap, Interface diet, Depend on plugs not wires.
s: SOLID is a set of five design principles that keep code easy to change and test. Let me explain each with an example from my work.

S is single responsibility: a class should have one reason to change. In our CSV import, the parser, the validator and the importer are separate classes. O is open-closed: open for extension, closed for modification. When we added Rebex as a new SFTP provider, I added a new class, I didn't edit the callers. L is Liskov substitution: any ISftpClient implementation can replace another without breaking the caller, so they all behave the same for errors and timeouts. I is interface segregation: small, focused interfaces, so a class that only reads files doesn't depend on write methods. And D is dependency inversion: high-level services depend on abstractions, which ASP.NET Core injects through DI, so I can mock them in unit tests.
I treat SOLID as guidance, not rules. Too many tiny interfaces can make code harder to follow. I can go deeper into any one of them.
cards.k: single responsibility, open closed, liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion, design principles, solid

cards.q: Which design patterns have you used in production?
cards.h: My code toolbox: S-F-R-D-O = Strategy, Factory, Repository, Decorator, Observer.
s: I use patterns only when they solve a real problem, and I've used several in production.

The one I use most is Strategy, together with Adapter. In our SFTP integration, three different libraries sit behind one ISftpClient interface, and each adapter hides its library's quirks. A Factory then picks the right provider for each vendor from configuration. I've used Decorator to add retry and logging around a client without changing the client itself, which is also how Polly handlers work in HttpClient.

For messaging, I've used the transactional Outbox pattern so events aren't lost when the database save succeeds but the publish fails, and publish-subscribe with Kafka and RabbitMQ. In some services we use Repository and Unit of Work over EF Core. And for configuration and shared clients we use the Options pattern and singletons, but through dependency injection, not a static Singleton class.
So for me the value of a pattern is the shared vocabulary and a proven solution. I can walk through the SFTP design in detail if you'd like.
cards.k: design patterns, strategy, adapter, factory, decorator, outbox, singleton, repository

cards.q: How does garbage collection work in .NET?
cards.h: Nursery (Gen 0), school (Gen 1), retirement home (Gen 2); big furniture goes straight to the warehouse (LOH).
s: Garbage collection in .NET automatically frees memory for objects that nothing references any more, so we don't free memory by hand.

It's generational, based on the idea that most objects die young. New objects go into generation 0, which is collected often and cheaply. Objects that survive move to generation 1, and long-lived ones move to generation 2, which is collected less often because it's more expensive. Objects larger than about 85 KB go to the Large Object Heap, which is collected with gen 2. ASP.NET Core uses server GC by default, with a heap per core, for throughput.
One important point: the GC only handles managed memory. Things like files, sockets, database connections and SFTP sessions are unmanaged resources, so they need IDisposable and a using statement.

In practice I don't tune the GC much, but I watch for leaks. For example, I once investigated a .NET service whose memory kept growing, and the cause was event handlers that were never unsubscribed, keeping objects alive. I can walk through how I diagnosed that.
cards.k: gc, memory, generations, dispose, large object heap, garbage collection, idisposable

cards.q: Delegates, Func, Action, events and lambdas?
cards.h: Func = function with a gift back, Action = just do it.
s: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. You can store it in a variable, pass it to another method and call it later.

Func and Action are built-in generic delegates, so we rarely declare our own. Func returns a value; for example Func of int, string takes an int and returns a string. Action returns nothing. There's also Predicate, which returns a bool. A lambda is a short inline way to write the method, like x goes to x.IsActive. An event is a delegate with restricted access: other classes can subscribe and unsubscribe, but only the owning class can raise it.

One thing to be careful about is that lambdas can capture variables, which creates a closure. That's very useful, but it can keep objects alive longer than expected, and event handlers that are never unsubscribed are a common memory leak.

I use these every day: lambdas in LINQ queries, Func in minimal API endpoints, and Action delegates for options configuration, like services.AddOptions with a configure lambda. I can explain closures in more depth if useful.
cards.k: delegate, func, action, lambda, event, callback

cards.q: What is deferred execution in LINQ?
cards.h: A LINQ query is a recipe, not a cooked meal.
s: Deferred execution means a LINQ query doesn't run when you write it. It only runs when you actually enumerate it, for example in a foreach loop, or when you call ToList, Count, First or Any.

That's useful, because you can build up a query step by step, adding filters and sorting based on conditions, and with EF Core it all becomes one SQL statement at the end. But there are two risks. First, every enumeration runs the query again, so if you loop over an IQueryable twice, you hit the database twice. Second, the data can change between definition and execution, because it reads the data at the time it runs.
So my rule is: if I need the results more than once, I materialise them once with ToList or ToArray and reuse that list. Operators like ToList, Count, Sum and First run immediately.

In our search APIs we build the query conditionally on IQueryable, and only call ToListAsync after paging, so SQL Server returns just one page. I can show the double-enumeration bug in code if you like.
cards.k: linq, lazy evaluation, ienumerable, iqueryable, deferred execution

cards.q: How do you make code thread-safe?
cards.h: One key to the bathroom (lock); a bouncer counting guests (SemaphoreSlim).
s: Code is thread-safe when it behaves correctly even if many threads run it at the same time.

My first approach is to avoid shared mutable state. I keep services stateless and use immutable objects, so there's nothing to protect. When I do need shared state, I pick the right tool. For simple counters I use Interlocked. For shared caches I use ConcurrentDictionary. For a short critical section I use the lock statement, and for async code I use SemaphoreSlim, because you can't await inside a lock. SemaphoreSlim is also handy to limit concurrency, for example to deploy to only a few nodes in parallel. For lazy initialisation I use Lazy of T instead of hand-written double-checked locking.
I'm also careful with singletons in DI, because a singleton that holds mutable state is shared by every request.

And thread safety can cross processes too. In our CSV import, we used a lock row in the database so two users couldn't import into the same study at the same time. I can go into that design if helpful.
cards.k: thread safety, lock, concurrency, race condition, semaphoreslim, concurrentdictionary, thread, threading, thread-safe

cards.q: record vs class vs struct?
cards.h: Record = a receipt: two receipts with the same lines are equal.
s: All three define types, but they behave differently.

A class is a reference type with identity. Two objects with exactly the same values are still different objects, because equality compares references by default. A record is designed for data. It's still a reference type by default, but it compares by value, so two records with the same values are equal. It also gives you concise immutable syntax, a readable ToString, and with-expressions to create a modified copy. A struct is a value type, so it's copied on assignment, and it's best for small values. There's also record struct, which is a value type with value equality.

In my services I use records for DTOs, API contracts and messages we publish to Kafka or RabbitMQ, because those are pure data and should be immutable. I use classes for services and EF Core entities, because entities have identity and change over time. Structs I use rarely, only for small values.
I can explain why EF entities shouldn't be records, if that's useful.
cards.k: record, class, struct, immutable, value equality, dto

cards.q: Exception handling best practices?
cards.h: Catch the ball only if you can play it; otherwise pass it to the goalkeeper (global handler).
s: My main rule is: catch an exception only where I can actually do something about it, and let everything else bubble up to one global handler.

In practice that means a few things. I never swallow exceptions with an empty catch. When I rethrow, I use throw on its own, not throw ex, so the stack trace is kept. I log an exception once, with context like the correlation id and the study id, instead of logging it at every layer. I create specific domain exceptions for business rules, for example a StudyTransferNotAllowedException, but I don't use exceptions for normal flow like validation, because they're slow and hide intent. And I use using or finally to clean up resources.

In our ASP.NET Core APIs, one global exception handler catches anything unhandled, logs it, and returns a consistent ProblemDetails response with the right status code, without leaking stack traces to the client.
That gives us consistent errors and clean logs during an incident. I can show how we set up IExceptionHandler in .NET 8.
cards.k: exception handling, try catch, problemdetails, global error handler, logging, exception, error handling

cards.q: Generics and constraints: why use them?
cards.h: Generics = one mould, many materials.
s: Generics let me write code once and use it with many types, while keeping full type safety.

Without generics, you'd use object and cast everywhere, which is error-prone, and value types would get boxed. With List of T or Dictionary of K and V, the compiler knows the exact type, so there's no casting and no boxing. Constraints tell the compiler what a type parameter can do. For example, where T is a class, where T implements an IEntity interface, or where T has a parameterless constructor. Then I can safely call those members inside the generic code. There's also variance: IEnumerable of a derived type can be used as IEnumerable of the base type.

In my work, I wrote a generic paged result type, so every list API returns items, total count and page info in the same shape. I've also used a generic Result of T wrapper for success or error responses, and generic repository methods constrained to our entity base class.
So generics reduce duplication and catch mistakes at compile time. I can explain covariance in more detail if you want.
cards.k: generics, constraints, type safety, where t

cards.q: What did .NET 8/10 bring that matters for backend services?
cards.h: Upgrade = free horsepower plus a longer warranty.
s: For backend services, each recent release brought real, practical improvements.

.NET 8, which is an LTS, gave us a lot: keyed services in dependency injection, TimeProvider so time is testable, built-in resilience handlers on HttpClient based on Polly, IExceptionHandler for global errors, native AOT for minimal APIs, and built-in rate limiting. It also kept improving System.Text.Json, and the runtime got faster with things like dynamic PGO. .NET 10 is the next LTS, with C# 14, better OpenAPI support and more performance work, so you often get speed-ups just by upgrading.

In a regulated product, the LTS support window drives our upgrade plan. In [early 2026] I upgraded [3] of our IRT services from .NET 8 to .NET 10. It was mostly package updates and a few breaking changes, and we saw about [10-15%] lower p95 latency without touching business logic.
I can talk about how I planned and tested that upgrade.
cards.k: .net 8, .net 10, new features, keyed services, native aot, timeprovider, c# 14, net 8, net 10, upgrade

cards.q: Explain the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline.
cards.h: Airport security: each checkpoint can wave you on or stop you, and you come back through on the way out.
s: The middleware pipeline is the chain of components that every HTTP request passes through in ASP.NET Core, from the moment Kestrel receives it until the response goes back.

Each middleware gets the HttpContext and a next delegate. It can do work, call next to pass the request along, and then do more work as the response comes back through it, in reverse order. Or it can short-circuit, like the static files middleware returning a file, or authorization returning 403. The pipeline is built in Program.cs with app.Use calls, and order matters a lot. A typical order is: exception handler first, so it catches everything, then HSTS and HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, custom middleware like logging and correlation ids, and finally the endpoints.
A good mental picture is Russian dolls: each layer wraps the next.

In our services, the first custom piece is our correlation-id middleware, placed near the top so even errors from later middleware are logged with the id. That lets us trace one request across [4] services. I can explain what goes wrong when the order is wrong.
cards.k: middleware, request pipeline, request delegate, use, run, ordering, pipeline

cards.q: Explain DI lifetimes: Singleton, Scoped, Transient.
cards.h: Singleton = the office building, Scoped = your meeting room for one meeting, Transient = a paper cup.
s: Service lifetimes decide how long an object created by the DI container lives, and who shares it.

Singleton means one instance for the whole application. Everyone gets the same object, so it must be thread-safe. It's good for configuration, caches, IHttpClientFactory or a RabbitMQ connection. Scoped means one instance per scope, which in a web app is one per HTTP request. Everything in that request shares it, and it's disposed at the end. DbContext is the classic example, because it's a unit of work. Transient means a new instance every time it's requested. It's good for lightweight, stateless helpers like validators or mappers.

The most important rule is about dependencies: a service shouldn't depend on something with a shorter lifetime. If a singleton takes a scoped DbContext, that DbContext gets captured forever, shared across threads and requests. That's called a captive dependency, and ASP.NET Core's scope validation catches it in development.
In our services, DbContext is scoped, the RabbitMQ connection is a singleton, and validators are transient. Our background services create a scope per message. I can explain that pattern if useful.
cards.k: di, dependency injection, lifetimes, singleton, scoped, transient, captive dependency, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime

cards.q: Controllers vs Minimal APIs?
cards.h: Controllers = full restaurant menu; Minimal API = food truck.
s: Both build HTTP APIs on the same foundation, the same routing, DI, middleware and authentication. The difference is style and structure.

Controllers are classes that inherit ControllerBase, with actions marked by attributes like HttpGet. They give you a mature, conventional structure, the full filter pipeline, ApiController behaviours like automatic validation, and they're familiar to every .NET developer. That suits large APIs with many endpoints and teams. Minimal APIs map routes directly to lambdas or methods with MapGet and MapPost. There's less ceremony, startup is faster, performance is slightly better, and they work well with native AOT. Route groups, endpoint filters, TypedResults and, since .NET 10, built-in validation have closed most of the gaps.

So my choice is practical, not religious. For a large existing service with many controllers, I stay with controllers, for consistency. For a new small service, or a few endpoints, minimal APIs are cleaner.

In our team, the main IRT APIs use controllers, and newer small internal services use minimal APIs organised into feature-based extension methods. I can show how a minimal API is structured for a larger service.
cards.k: minimal api, controllers, mvc, endpoints, routing, minimal apis

cards.q: What happens at startup in Program.cs?
cards.h: Build the kitchen (services), lay the route (middleware), open the doors (Run).
s: Program.cs is where the application is assembled. It has two phases: building the services, and building the pipeline.

First, WebApplication.CreateBuilder sets up the basics: configuration from appsettings.json, the environment-specific appsettings file, environment variables and user secrets; logging providers; and the DI container. Then I register services on builder.Services, things like controllers, DbContext, authentication, health checks, options and my own services. Calling builder.Build creates the app and the root service provider. Second phase: I configure the middleware pipeline in order, with app.Use calls, and map the endpoints. Finally app.Run starts Kestrel, which begins listening for requests, and hosted services start too.
I also make startup fail fast. With ValidateOnStart on options and ValidateOnBuild for DI, a missing setting or registration fails the deployment, not the first user request.

In our services, configuration also comes from AWS Parameter Store and Secrets Manager, and we group registrations into extension methods like AddMessaging and AddPersistence, so Program.cs reads like a table of contents. I can walk through a real example.
cards.k: program.cs, startup, host, builder, configuration, kestrel

cards.q: Filters vs middleware?
cards.h: Middleware = building security; filters = the receptionist on your floor.
s: Middleware and filters can both run code before and after a request, but they work at different levels.

Middleware sits in the ASP.NET Core pipeline and runs for every request, including static files, health checks and requests that never reach a controller. It only knows about the HttpContext: the request, the response and the user. Filters run inside MVC, around a specific controller action. They know the action context: which controller and action is running, the bound arguments, model state and the result. They also run in a defined order: authorization, resource, then model binding, action, exception and result filters.

So my rule is simple. If the concern is about HTTP in general and applies everywhere, I use middleware, for example correlation ids, request logging, security headers or global exception handling. If it needs to know about the action, its arguments or its result, I use a filter, for example validating a model, auditing which study an action changed, or caching an action's result.

In our project, the correlation-id is middleware because it must cover every request across [4] services, while study-level audit logging is an action filter because it reads the action's arguments. I can show both in code.
cards.k: filters, middleware, action filter, mvc pipeline, cross-cutting, pipeline, request delegate, request pipeline

cards.q: How do model binding and validation work?
cards.h: Bind = unpack the parcel, validate = check nothing is broken.
s: Model binding is how ASP.NET Core turns the raw HTTP request into typed parameters for my action, and validation then checks those values before my code runs.

Binding reads values from different sources: the route, the query string, headers, form fields and the JSON body. I can be explicit with attributes like FromRoute, FromQuery and FromBody, and with ApiController, complex types come from the body by default. If a value can't be converted, like text for an integer, it's recorded as a model state error. Then validation runs, using data annotations like Required and Range, or FluentValidation for richer rules. With ApiController, an invalid model automatically returns a 400 with ValidationProblemDetails, listing each field and its error.
That checks the shape of the data. Business rules, like "this site must belong to an active depot", still belong in the service layer, because they need data and context.

For our CSV bulk import, a single request can contain [around 10,000] rows. So we validated every row and returned a per-row error report with line numbers, instead of failing on the first error. Users fixed everything in one go. I can explain that design.
cards.k: model binding, validation, data annotations, fluentvalidation, apicontroller, 400

cards.q: How do you implement global exception handling?
cards.h: One safety net at the bottom of the circus, not one per acrobat.
s: Global exception handling means one central place catches every unhandled exception and turns it into a consistent, safe error response, instead of try-catch blocks in every controller.

In ASP.NET Core, I put UseExceptionHandler at the top of the pipeline, so it wraps everything after it. Since .NET 8, I write IExceptionHandler classes that map known exceptions to the right status code. For example, a validation exception becomes 400, not found becomes 404, a concurrency conflict becomes 409, and anything unknown becomes 500. With AddProblemDetails, every error follows the standard ProblemDetails format, with a type, title, status and trace id.

Two rules matter. Log the full exception server-side, with the stack trace and correlation id. But never return internal details to the client in production, just a clear message and the id. Also, I don't use exceptions for normal flow; expected outcomes like "not found" can just return a result.

This kept our controllers clean and our errors consistent across services. When a user reports an error, they give support the correlation id from the response, and we find the exact exception in CloudWatch in seconds. I can show a sample handler.
cards.k: global exception handling, iexceptionhandler, problemdetails, useexceptionhandler, error handling, exception, exception handling

cards.q: REST principles, HTTP verbs and idempotency?
cards.h: Idempotent = pressing the lift button five times still calls one lift.
s: REST is an architectural style for APIs built on HTTP. Everything is a resource, identified by a URL, like /studies/12/shipments. Clients use standard HTTP verbs to act on them, exchange representations, usually JSON, and every request is stateless, meaning it carries everything the server needs, like the token. Responses can also be cacheable.

The verbs have clear meanings. GET reads data, and it's safe, it changes nothing. POST creates, and it's not idempotent: sending it twice creates two things. PUT replaces a resource, and it's idempotent: sending it twice gives the same result. PATCH partially updates. DELETE removes, and it's idempotent too. Idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect as doing it once, which is what makes retries safe.
Status codes complete the picture: 200, 201 with a Location header, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 and so on.

The idempotency part matters in real systems, because networks fail and clients retry. For POST operations that create important things, like a shipment, we accept an idempotency key, so a retry returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate. I can explain that pattern.
cards.k: rest, http verbs, idempotency, get, post, put, patch, delete

cards.q: How do you version an API?
cards.h: Versioning = new edition of a book; old readers keep their copy.
s: API versioning lets an API evolve without breaking existing clients.

There are four common ways to put the version in a request: in the URL, like /api/v2/shipments; in a query string, like api-version=2; in a header; or in the media type. I prefer the URL segment, because it's explicit, easy to see in logs, and easy to route at the load balancer. In .NET, the Asp.Versioning library handles this, including reporting supported and deprecated versions in response headers, and it works with OpenAPI, so each version gets its own document.

But the best strategy is to avoid needing new versions. Additive changes, like adding an optional field or a new endpoint, are not breaking. Renaming or removing fields, or changing types or meanings, are breaking, and only those need a new version. When we do release one, the old version is deprecated with a clear timeline, and we watch the logs until no one calls it.
Because external vendors integrate with our APIs, we're strict about this. We also compare OpenAPI documents in the pipeline to catch accidental breaking changes. I can explain that check.
cards.k: api versioning, v1, v2, backward compatibility, breaking change, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Configuration and the Options pattern?
cards.h: Layers of paint: the last coat (env vars) wins.
s: Configuration in ASP.NET Core comes from layered providers, and the Options pattern turns it into strongly-typed, validated classes.

The providers are layered, and later ones override earlier ones: appsettings.json, then appsettings for the environment, like Production, then user secrets in development, environment variables, and command-line arguments. In the cloud, we add AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store and Secrets Manager. With the Options pattern, I bind a section to a class, for example builder.Services.Configure of SftpOptions, and then inject IOptions of SftpOptions instead of reading strings. I add ValidateDataAnnotations and ValidateOnStart, so a missing or invalid setting stops the app at startup.
For changing values, IOptionsSnapshot re-reads per request, and IOptionsMonitor gives live updates to singletons.

In our services, vendor SFTP settings are named options, secrets like passwords and keys come from Secrets Manager, never from appsettings, and the same container image runs in every environment with different configuration. I can explain how the three options interfaces differ.

cards.q: How do you do logging and tracing in APIs?
cards.h: Every request wears a name badge (correlation id).
s: Good logging and tracing means that when something fails, I can find exactly what happened to one request across every service.

I use ILogger with structured logging, which means message templates with named placeholders, like "Shipment {ShipmentId} failed", so values are stored as searchable fields, not text. Levels matter: Debug only in development, Information for meaningful business events, Warning and Error for problems. And I never log secrets or patient data, which is critical in a clinical system. For tracing, every request gets a correlation id from middleware. It goes into a logging scope, so every log line carries it, and it's passed on to downstream HTTP calls and messages. OpenTelemetry adds distributed traces and spans for timing.
Logs go to CloudWatch as JSON, and we have dashboards and alarms in CloudWatch and Grafana on error rates and latency.

The correlation-id work I did in [2024] changed our support process. Tracing a failed shipment across [4] services used to take [about an hour]. Now one Logs Insights query shows the whole journey in [a few minutes]. I can walk through that implementation.

cards.q: How do you improve the performance of an ASP.NET Core API?
cards.h: M-A-D-C-S: Measure, Async, Database, Cache, Scale.
s: My approach to performance is always measure first, then fix the biggest bottleneck, and then measure again.

I start with data: CloudWatch and Grafana metrics for latency percentiles and error rates, traces to see where time goes, and profiling or slow query logs. Most of the time, the database is the problem. So I fix queries first: proper indexes, AsNoTracking for reads, projecting into DTOs so we only fetch needed columns, paging, and removing N+1 queries. Then the code: async I/O all the way, IHttpClientFactory for outgoing calls, avoiding unnecessary allocations in hot paths. Then caching: in-memory or Redis for reference data, and output caching for expensive responses. Response compression helps for large payloads. Only once the code is efficient do I scale horizontally behind the load balancer.

A real example: one shipment search query took [about 9 seconds]. The execution plan showed a scan with [400,000] logical reads. With a covering index and a rewritten predicate, it dropped to [under 300 ms] and [about 2,000] reads.
Upgrading the runtime also helped: moving to .NET 10 gave about [10-15%] better p95. I can go into the SQL fix in detail.
cards.k: performance, optimization, caching, async, asnotracking, paging, profiling, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: What is CORS and how do you configure it?
cards.h: CORS = guest list at the door, checked by the browser bouncer.
s: CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. Browsers enforce the same-origin policy, which blocks a page from one origin, like our front-end domain, from reading responses from a different origin, like our API domain. CORS is how the server tells the browser which other origins are allowed.

For simple requests, the browser sends the request with an Origin header and checks the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header in the response. For other requests, like ones with a JSON content type or an Authorization header, the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request, asking which origins, methods and headers are allowed, and only sends the real request if the answer allows it.

In ASP.NET Core, I call AddCors with a named policy that lists the exact allowed origins, methods and headers, and add UseCors in the pipeline after routing and before authentication, so preflight requests aren't rejected for having no token. I never combine AllowAnyOrigin with credentials, and I avoid wildcards in production.
Also, CORS isn't API security, it only affects browsers. In our services, origins come from configuration per environment. I can explain how to debug a CORS error.

cards.q: How do you make service-to-service calls resilient?
cards.h: Circuit breaker = the fuse box at home.
s: In microservices, calls to other services will fail sometimes, so resilience is about making sure a temporary problem in one service doesn't become an outage for everyone.

I use several patterns together. Timeouts on every call, because a hanging call is worse than a failed one. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, but only for transient errors, like timeouts, 503s and 429s, and only for idempotent operations. A circuit breaker: after repeated failures it opens and stops calling the failing service for a while, then tests it with a single call in the half-open state before closing again. Bulkheads to limit how many concurrent calls one dependency can use, and fallbacks, like cached data, where that makes sense. In .NET, I configure this on IHttpClientFactory with Polly, usually with AddStandardResilienceHandler.

And often the best resilience is not calling synchronously at all. For work that doesn't need an immediate answer, we publish a message to RabbitMQ, so if the other service is down, the work just waits in the queue.
Our vendor API calls use the standard resilience handler, and most short vendor outages now recover without anyone noticing. I can explain how the circuit breaker states work.
cards.k: resilience, polly, retry, circuit breaker, timeout, httpclientfactory

cards.q: REST vs SOAP (WCF) vs gRPC vs GraphQL?
cards.h: REST = postcard, SOAP = registered letter, gRPC = phone call, GraphQL = custom order.
s: These are four styles of API communication, each good at different things.

REST is resource-based HTTP with JSON. It's simple, universal, cacheable, and every client and tool understands it, so it's my default for public and front-end APIs. SOAP, which in .NET usually meant WCF, uses XML envelopes with strict contracts defined in WSDL, plus standards like WS-Security and transactions. It's heavy, but still common in older enterprise systems. gRPC uses binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2. It's very fast, strongly typed from a shared contract, and supports streaming in both directions. That makes it great for internal service-to-service calls, but browser support is limited. GraphQL exposes one endpoint where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs. That's great when many different front ends need different shapes of data, but caching and authorization per field are harder.
So the choice depends on the consumer. Public or browser APIs get REST. High-performance internal calls can use gRPC. Varied front-end needs suggest GraphQL.
In our IRT platform, the APIs are REST, and some older integrations still expose WCF SOAP endpoints, which we're gradually modernising. I can explain how I'd migrate those.
cards.k: rest, soap, wcf, grpc, graphql, protocols, service contract

cards.q: How do you run background work in ASP.NET Core?
cards.h: Background service = the night shift that keeps working after the shop closes.
s: Background work in ASP.NET Core means work that runs outside the request, either long-running, like consuming a queue, or scheduled, like a nightly cleanup.

The built-in way is a BackgroundService, which implements IHostedService. I override ExecuteAsync with a loop that runs until the stopping token is cancelled, and register it with AddHostedService. It's a singleton, so for scoped services like DbContext, I inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope for each unit of work. It must honour the stopping token for graceful shutdown, and catch and log exceptions inside the loop, so one bad message doesn't stop the service.

I'm careful not to do heavy work inside a web request, or fire-and-forget with Task.Run, because that work is lost if the instance restarts, and it uses disposed services. For heavy or important work, I put a message on a durable queue and let a separate worker process it, or use a Lambda or a scheduler.

In our platform, RabbitMQ consumers and our SFTP poller are BackgroundServices running in dedicated worker containers. That way, scaling and deployments of the API and the workers are independent. I can explain how we handle poison messages.

cards.q: How does EF Core change tracking work, and when do you use AsNoTracking?
cards.h: The DbContext is a teacher with a register: it remembers who changed.
s: Change tracking is how EF Core knows what to save. When I load entities through a DbContext, it keeps a snapshot of their original values and tracks each one's state: Added, Unchanged, Modified, Deleted or Detached.

When I call SaveChanges, EF Core detects changes by comparing the current values with the snapshot, and generates only the needed INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements, all in one transaction. That's very convenient for writes, because I just change properties and save. But tracking has a cost: memory for snapshots, and time for change detection, especially with thousands of entities.

So for read-only queries, like GET endpoints, lists and reports, I use AsNoTracking. It skips the snapshots, so queries are faster and use less memory. Even better for reads is projecting with Select into DTOs, which fetches only the needed columns and isn't tracked at all. For bulk changes, EF Core 7 added ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, which run a single SQL statement without loading entities.
In our services, reads default to no tracking, and we used ExecuteUpdate for a status update that used to load thousands of rows. I can explain how tracking interacts with concurrency.

cards.q: Eager vs lazy vs explicit loading; what is the N+1 problem?
cards.h: N+1 = going to the shop once per egg.
s: These are the three ways EF Core loads related data, and the N+1 problem is what happens when you pick the wrong one.

Eager loading uses Include, so related data comes back in the same query, for example shipments with their kits. Lazy loading loads related data automatically the first time you access a navigation property, using proxies. It's convenient but hides database calls. Explicit loading is when I deliberately load a navigation later, with Entry, Collection and Load.

The N+1 problem is one query to get a list of N parents, plus one more query for each parent's children. So listing 100 shipments and touching each one's site becomes 101 queries. It usually comes from lazy loading inside a loop, and it's slow because of the round trips. To fix it, I use Include, or better, a Select projection into a DTO that gets exactly the needed fields in one query. For several large collections, AsSplitQuery avoids a huge cartesian join.

To catch it, I watch the SQL logs in development. I once found a shipment report making hundreds of queries because of lazy loading. A projection reduced it to one query. We keep lazy loading turned off. I can explain split queries.
cards.k: eager loading, lazy loading, explicit loading, include, n+1, ef core

cards.q: How do you manage EF Core migrations in a regulated environment?
cards.h: Expand, deploy, contract: build the new bridge before closing the old one.
s: In a regulated GxP environment, database changes must be reviewed, repeatable and traceable, so we don't let the app change the schema by itself.

Developers create migrations in code with EF Core, as usual. But for deployment, we generate an idempotent SQL script with dotnet ef migrations script with the idempotent option. That script checks the migrations history table, so it's safe to run in any environment, whatever state it's in. The script is reviewed in the pull request, stored with the release, and applied by the release pipeline through each environment, FV, TechOps, UAT and then production, never automatically at app startup with Migrate. That gives us an audit trail of exactly what ran where.

The other key practice is backward-compatible changes, called expand and contract. During a rolling deployment, old and new versions of the app run at the same time. So first we add new columns or tables, deploy the code that uses them, and only remove old columns in a later release.
This approach meant our database releases were boring, which is exactly what you want. I can explain how we handle a rollback.

cards.q: How do you handle concurrency conflicts in EF Core?
cards.h: Optimistic = check the version number on the ticket before you edit.
s: Concurrency conflicts happen when two users edit the same record at the same time, and without protection, the last save silently overwrites the first. That's called a lost update.

EF Core's main approach is optimistic concurrency. I add a rowversion column, marked as a concurrency token. When EF updates the row, it includes the original rowversion in the WHERE clause. If someone else changed the row in the meantime, the rowversion no longer matches, zero rows are updated, and EF throws a DbUpdateConcurrencyException. Then I decide how to resolve it: reload and retry automatically if the change is safe to reapply, merge the values, or return 409 Conflict and let the user see the latest data and decide.
Pessimistic locking, actually locking the row with something like UPDLOCK, is only for short, critical sections where conflicts are frequent and costly.

In our IRT system, we use both. Editing shipments and sites uses optimistic concurrency, returning 409 to the UI. But allocating limited drug supply to a site uses a short pessimistic lock, because two sites must never be promised the same last kits. I can explain that allocation design.
cards.k: concurrency, optimistic concurrency, rowversion, dbupdateconcurrencyexception, 409, ef core, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: DbContext lifetime and thread safety?
cards.h: One DbContext per conversation; do not pass the phone around.
s: DbContext represents a unit of work with the database: it tracks entities, holds a connection when needed, and saves changes in one transaction. That's why it's designed to be short-lived.

In ASP.NET Core, it's registered as scoped, so each HTTP request gets its own DbContext, shared by all services in that request and disposed at the end. Crucially, DbContext is not thread-safe. If two tasks use the same instance in parallel, for example with Task.WhenAll over two queries, EF Core throws an exception about a second operation starting on this context. So for parallel work, each task needs its own context, which you get from IDbContextFactory.

In background services, which are singletons, I create a scope per unit of work, like per message, so each gets a fresh DbContext with clean change tracking. Keeping one context for a long time makes the change tracker grow and data go stale. For very high-throughput APIs, AddDbContextPool reuses context instances to reduce allocation cost.
In our RabbitMQ consumers, each message gets its own scope and DbContext. I can explain IDbContextFactory in more detail.

cards.q: How do you run raw SQL or stored procedures safely in EF Core?
cards.h: Interpolated = parameterised = injection-proof.
s: EF Core lets me run raw SQL when LINQ isn't enough, but I have to do it safely, using parameters.

For queries that return entities, I use FromSql, or FromSqlInterpolated. For commands, I use ExecuteSql or ExecuteSqlInterpolated. The important point is that with the interpolated versions, the values in the curly braces aren't pasted into the SQL text. EF Core turns them into proper SQL parameters, so they're safe from SQL injection. What I never do is build SQL by concatenating strings with user input, and I'm careful with FromSqlRaw, which needs explicit parameters. Results can map to entities, or to keyless entity types for custom shapes, and with SqlQuery I can map to unmapped types too. I can even compose LINQ on top of FromSql.
I use raw SQL for things LINQ can't express efficiently, like calling existing stored procedures, using query hints, or complex reporting queries that were tuned by hand.

In our IRT database, some older stored procedures for inventory calculations are called this way, with parameters, so we reused tested logic instead of rewriting it. I can explain how SQL injection works if useful.

cards.q: How do transactions work in EF Core?
cards.h: All or nothing, and keep the door open for as short as possible.
s: By default, each call to SaveChanges in EF Core is atomic. All the inserts, updates and deletes it generates run in one database transaction, so either all succeed or none do.

When I need several SaveChanges calls, or a mix of EF operations and raw SQL, to succeed or fail together, I start an explicit transaction with Database.BeginTransactionAsync, do the work, and call CommitAsync. If anything fails, it rolls back. With retrying execution strategies, I wrap the transaction in the strategy's ExecuteAsync, so the whole unit is retried. I keep transactions short, and never call external services inside them, because long transactions hold locks and cause blocking and deadlocks.

Across microservices, there's no shared database transaction. Distributed transactions are fragile, so we use the outbox pattern: the business change and an outbox message are saved in the same local transaction, and a separate process publishes the message afterwards. For multi-step workflows, a saga coordinates steps with compensating actions.

In our shipment flow, the shipment update and its outbox event are saved together, so we never update the database without publishing the event, or the other way round. I can explain the outbox in detail.

cards.q: What is WCF and what are its ABCs?
cards.h: ABC: Address, Binding, Contract = where, how, what.
s: WCF, Windows Communication Foundation, is the .NET Framework technology for building service-oriented applications, mostly SOAP web services, but also TCP and named-pipe communication.

Every WCF endpoint is defined by its ABCs. A is the Address, where the service lives, the URL. B is the Binding, how you talk to it: the transport and encoding, like basicHttpBinding for simple SOAP, wsHttpBinding for WS-Security and reliable messaging, or netTcpBinding for fast binary communication between .NET systems. C is the Contract, what the service offers: ServiceContract on the interface, OperationContract on each method, and DataContract on the data types. WCF also supports message-level security, transactions and reliable messaging, which made it popular in enterprises.
Modern .NET doesn't include the WCF server, only a client. For the server side, there's CoreWCF, a community project supported by Microsoft, or you move to REST or gRPC.

In our IRT platform, some older integrations still expose WCF SOAP endpoints for external partners, so I've maintained those contracts, and I've been involved in planning how to modernise them. I can explain the migration options.

cards.q: How would you migrate WCF services to modern .NET?
cards.h: Strangler fig: grow the new tree around the old one until it can stand alone.
s: Migrating WCF services is mainly about not breaking existing clients, while getting onto modern, supported .NET.

There are two main paths. The first is CoreWCF, a port of the WCF server to modern .NET. It keeps the same SOAP contracts and most bindings, so existing clients don't change at all. It's the lowest-risk path when external partners depend on the SOAP interface. The second is re-exposing the functionality as REST with ASP.NET Core, or gRPC for internal calls. That's more modern, but clients must change, so during the transition I'd keep a thin adapter that still serves the old SOAP contract.

Whichever path, I'd do it step by step. First, move business logic out of the service classes into shared libraries, so the WCF layer becomes thin. Then migrate endpoint by endpoint, using the strangler fig pattern, routing traffic gradually to the new implementation. Contract tests compare old and new responses for the same inputs, to prove behaviour is identical, which also gives validation evidence in a GxP system.
For our partner-facing SOAP integrations, CoreWCF is the pragmatic first step, and REST can come later. I can go into the testing approach.

cards.q: Do you need Repository and Unit of Work on top of EF Core?
cards.h: Do not wrap a gift that is already wrapped, unless you need a label on it.
s: Not always. EF Core already implements both patterns. DbSet behaves like a repository, a collection of entities you can query and add to, and DbContext is a unit of work, because it tracks changes and saves them in one transaction.

So wrapping EF Core in a generic repository, with methods like GetById, GetAll, Add and Update for every entity, often adds a layer without value. It either hides useful EF features, or it leaks IQueryable everywhere, which means the abstraction isn't really abstracting anything. And mocking a generic repository doesn't test your real queries anyway.

But a thin, specific repository can still help. It gives a name to complex queries, like GetActiveShipmentsForSite. It enforces rules in one place, like soft delete filters or always scoping by study, which is critical for us because data must never cross studies. And it makes the service layer easy to unit test.

So my rule is: add the layer when it removes duplication or protects an invariant, not by default. In our services, we have specific repositories for complex aggregates, while simple lookups use the DbContext directly, and query behaviour is tested against a real SQL Server in integration tests. cards.q: Clustered vs non-clustered index?
cards.h: Clustered = the dictionary itself sorted A to Z; non-clustered = the index at the back of a textbook.
s: Both are B-tree structures that help SQL Server find rows quickly, but they store data differently.

A clustered index defines the physical order of the table's rows. The leaf level of the clustered index is the actual data, so there can only be one per table, and it's usually on the primary key. A non-clustered index is a separate structure, with its own sorted key columns and a pointer back to the row, which is the clustered key. You can have many of them. When a query uses a non-clustered index but needs columns that aren't in it, SQL Server does a key lookup back into the clustered index for every row, which gets expensive for large results. A covering index solves that by adding the extra columns with INCLUDE, so the query is answered from the index alone.
The trade-off is that every index speeds up reads but slows down inserts, updates and deletes, and uses storage. So I index based on real query patterns, not guesses.

My best example is our shipment list fix. A covering index on StudyId, Status and ShipmentDate, with the displayed columns included, took the query from [about 9 seconds to under 300 ms]. I can walk through that story.

cards.q: How did you optimize a slow SQL query?
cards.h: C-P-F-M: Capture, Plan, Fix, Measure.
s: Situation: In our IRT system, the site shipment list screen started timing out for a large study with [about 300] sites. It was taking [8 to 12 seconds], and support tickets were coming in from study teams.
Task: I was asked to find the cause and fix it, without risking other screens, and with proper release evidence, because it's a GxP system.

Action: I didn't guess. I took the real query, with real parameters, from Query Store, and looked at the actual execution plan with STATISTICS IO turned on. It showed three problems: a clustered index scan over [millions] of rows, expensive key lookups, and a CONVERT to date on the ShipmentDate column, which stopped SQL Server from using any index on it. I fixed them in order, measuring after each step. First, I rewrote the date filter as a range, ShipmentDate greater than or equal to the day and less than the next day, which is free. Then I added a covering index on StudyId, Status and ShipmentDate, including the displayed columns. Then I added server-side paging. The index script was reviewed, tested for write impact, and released through FV, UAT and production.

Result: Logical reads dropped from [about 400,000 to 2,000], and the response time went from [about 9 seconds to under 300 ms]. The tickets stopped. I also added a CloudWatch latency alarm and put that query into our pre-release performance checks. I can show the before and after SQL.

cards.q: What does SARGable mean?
cards.h: Do not put the column in handcuffs (functions), or the index cannot run.
s: SARGable means Search ARGument-able. A predicate is SARGable when SQL Server can use an index seek for it, jumping straight to the matching rows in the index instead of scanning everything.

The most common way to break it is wrapping the indexed column in a function or calculation. For example, WHERE YEAR of CreatedOn equals 2024, or CONVERT to date on a datetime column, or LEFT of Code, or Column plus 1 equals 5. SQL Server has to compute that for every row before comparing, so it scans. Another hidden one is a data type mismatch, like comparing an NVARCHAR parameter to a VARCHAR column, which causes an implicit conversion on the column. Leading wildcards, like LIKE percent ABC, also prevent seeks.

The fix is to keep the column bare and move the logic to the other side. Instead of YEAR equals 2024, write CreatedOn greater than or equal to January 1st 2024 and less than January 1st 2025. Instead of LEFT, use LIKE 'ABC%'.

This exact issue was one of the causes of our slow shipment list: a CONVERT on the ShipmentDate column. Rewriting it as a date range was the first step in taking that query [from about 9 seconds to under 300 ms]. I can explain how to spot it in an execution plan.
cards.k: sargable, index seek, where clause, functions on columns, sql server

cards.q: Explain the types of joins.
cards.h: Inner = handshake, Left = left side keeps everyone.
s: Joins combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column, and the type of join decides what happens to rows that don't match.

An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables. For example, shipments with their site. A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, plus matching rows from the right, with NULLs where there's no match. So "all sites, and their shipments if any". A RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image, and in practice we just rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN. A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both sides, matched where possible, which is useful for reconciliation. A CROSS JOIN returns every combination of rows, like every site with every kit type, which is useful for generating grids but dangerous on large tables. And a SELF JOIN joins a table to itself, for example an employee table to find each person's manager.
A classic use of LEFT JOIN is finding missing data: LEFT JOIN and then WHERE the right side IS NULL.
In our IRT work, I used exactly that to find sites with no shipments in the last 30 days, for a study team's resupply review. I can explain how joins relate to performance.

cards.q: Normalization vs denormalization?
cards.h: Normalize for truth, denormalize for speed.
s: Normalisation organises a relational database to remove duplicate data, so each fact is stored in exactly one place. Denormalisation deliberately duplicates some data to make reads faster.

The normal forms build on each other. First normal form: each column holds a single, atomic value, with no repeating groups. Second normal form: every non-key column depends on the whole primary key, not part of a composite key. Third normal form: non-key columns depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns. For example, a site's country name belongs in a countries table, not repeated on every shipment row. Normalisation prevents update anomalies, where you change data in one place and forget another.

Denormalisation trades that safety for read speed: fewer joins, precomputed values. It's common in reporting databases, read models in CQRS, and NoSQL stores like DynamoDB, where you design tables around access patterns.

So the balance is: normalised for writes, denormalised for reads. In our IRT system, the transactional database is normalised, because data integrity is critical in clinical trials. But reporting views, and some read models fed by events, are denormalised for speed. I can explain how we keep them in sync.
cards.k: normalization, denormalization, normal forms, database design

cards.q: Transaction isolation levels?
cards.h: Each level adds a stronger lock on the diary.
s: Isolation levels control what one transaction can see of other transactions' uncommitted or changing data. Higher isolation means more consistency, but more locking and less concurrency.

Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads: you can see data another transaction hasn't committed yet, which might be rolled back. Read Committed, SQL Server's default, prevents dirty reads, but if you read the same row twice, it might have changed in between. Repeatable Read prevents that by holding read locks until the end, but new rows can still appear, called phantoms. Serializable prevents phantoms too, by locking ranges, so transactions behave as if they ran one after another. Then there are the row-versioning options. Snapshot isolation, and Read Committed Snapshot, or RCSI, let readers see a consistent version of the data without taking locks, so readers don't block writers.

I choose per use case. Most of our workload runs fine on read committed with RCSI enabled, which removed a lot of reader-writer blocking. For allocating the last available drug kits, correctness matters more, so that short transaction uses stricter locking.
I can explain how RCSI uses tempdb for versioning.

cards.q: What causes deadlocks and how do you handle them?
cards.h: Two cars on a one-lane bridge: someone must reverse.
s: A deadlock is when two transactions each hold a lock that the other one needs, so neither can continue. SQL Server detects the cycle, picks one transaction as the victim, rolls it back, and returns error 1205.

The common causes are: transactions accessing the same tables in a different order, transactions that are too long and hold locks while doing other work, and missing indexes, because a scan locks far more rows than a seek. Higher isolation levels make it more likely.

To fix and prevent them: access tables in a consistent order, keep transactions short with no external calls inside, add the right indexes so locks stay narrow, and consider RCSI so readers don't take shared locks. Because deadlocks can still happen occasionally, the application should retry the victim safely, which EF Core's retrying execution strategy can do for transient errors.

To investigate, I use the system_health Extended Events session, which captures the deadlock graph showing both queries and the locked resources. In our system, I traced a recurring deadlock between an inventory update and a reporting query to a missing index causing a scan. Adding the index stopped it. I can explain how to read a deadlock graph.
cards.k: deadlock, locking, sql server, retry, transactions

cards.q: Stored procedures vs inline/ORM queries; what is parameter sniffing?
cards.h: Sniffing = the plan remembers the first customer's shoe size for everyone.
s: Both have their place, and parameter sniffing is a performance issue that affects both.

Stored procedures keep logic close to the data, can be secured with execute-only permissions, and are good for complex set-based operations. But they're harder to version, review, unit test and refactor than application code. ORM queries, like EF Core LINQ, live in the codebase, are type-safe, automatically parameterised, and easy to change and test. Both get cached, reusable plans, so performance is similar for parameterised queries. I default to EF Core and use stored procedures for heavy, set-based logic or existing tuned procedures.

Parameter sniffing is when SQL Server compiles a plan using the parameter values of the first call, and reuses that plan for all later calls. If the first call was for a tiny study, it might choose a nested loop plan, which is terrible for a huge study. So the same query is fast for some values and very slow for others. Fixes include OPTION RECOMPILE for queries where values vary wildly, OPTIMIZE FOR, or separate queries for different data shapes. Query Store helps spot and force a good plan.
In our IRT data, study sizes vary a lot, so I check for this whenever a query is fast for one study and slow for another.
cards.k: stored procedures, orm, parameter sniffing, query plan, query store

cards.q: When would you choose SQL Server/RDS vs DynamoDB?
cards.h: SQL = filing cabinet with cross-references; DynamoDB = super-fast lockers by key.
s: It depends on the data and how it's accessed.

SQL Server on RDS is relational. It's the right choice when data has rich relationships, needs complex joins, strong consistency and multi-row transactions, and ad-hoc querying and reporting. That's exactly clinical trial data: studies, sites, subjects, kits and shipments, all related, with strict integrity rules. DynamoDB is a key-value and document database. It gives single-digit millisecond responses at any scale, it's serverless with pay-per-request pricing, and needs almost no operations work. But you must design the table around your access patterns up front, using partition and sort keys. It's weak at ad-hoc queries, joins and reporting, and changing access patterns later can be painful.
So my rule: if I can list the access patterns, they're simple key lookups, and scale or cost matters, DynamoDB fits. If the domain is relational, or reporting needs are unclear, I choose SQL.
In our platform, the core IRT data is in SQL Server, and DynamoDB is used for simpler, high-volume data like event or status lookups. I can explain partition key design.

cards.q: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP?
cards.h: Delete = erase lines, Truncate = tear out all pages, Drop = throw away the book.
s: All three remove data, but at very different levels.

DELETE removes rows one at a time, and can use a WHERE clause to remove only some rows. Each deleted row is fully logged, triggers fire, and it can be rolled back inside a transaction. On large tables it's slow and can escalate locks, so for big cleanups I delete in batches. TRUNCATE removes all rows from a table at once by deallocating its data pages. It's very fast and minimally logged, it resets the identity seed, and it doesn't fire DELETE triggers. It can't have a WHERE clause, and it isn't allowed if the table is referenced by a foreign key. In SQL Server it can be rolled back inside a transaction too. DROP removes the whole table: the data, the structure, indexes and permissions.

In a regulated system like ours, hard deletes of business data are rare. We usually use soft deletes, setting an IsDeleted flag or a status, with an audit trail of who did it and when, because clinical data must remain traceable. TRUNCATE is only used on staging tables, for example during data imports. I can explain how we implement soft delete with EF Core query filters.
cards.k: delete, truncate, drop, sql

cards.q: OFFSET/FETCH vs keyset pagination?
cards.h: Offset = counting from page 1 every time; keyset = keeping a bookmark.
s: Both page through large result sets, but they work very differently and perform very differently on deep pages.

OFFSET FETCH, which is Skip and Take in EF Core, says "skip the first N rows, then return the next 20". It's simple and supports jumping to any page number. But the database still has to read and discard all the skipped rows, so page 5,000 is much slower than page 1. And if rows are inserted while someone is paging, they can see duplicates or miss rows. Keyset pagination, also called seek pagination, remembers the last row's key from the previous page and asks for "the next 20 rows after this key", using a WHERE clause on an indexed column. It seeks directly to that position, so every page is equally fast, and it's stable when data changes. The downside is you can't jump to an arbitrary page, only next and previous.
So I use OFFSET for admin screens with small data and page numbers, and keyset for large tables, infinite scrolling, exports and APIs, returning a continuation token.
For our shipment history API, we switched to keyset on ShipmentDate plus Id, and deep pages became as fast as the first. I can show the query.
cards.k: pagination, offset fetch, keyset pagination, seek method, paging

cards.q: CTEs and window functions; give a use case.
cards.h: Window function = looking at your neighbours without leaving your seat.
s: A CTE, a Common Table Expression, is a named temporary result defined with WITH, at the start of a query. It makes complex queries readable, by breaking them into named steps, and recursive CTEs can walk hierarchies, like a depot and its sub-depots.

Window functions perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing them like GROUP BY does. They use the OVER clause, with PARTITION BY to define groups and ORDER BY to define order. Common ones are ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK, LAG and LEAD to look at the previous or next row, and running totals with SUM OVER.

A classic use case is "get the latest record per group". For example, the latest status for each shipment. In a CTE, I select ROW_NUMBER over PARTITION BY ShipmentId ORDER BY StatusDate descending, then filter where the row number equals 1. Another is a running total of kits dispensed per site over time.

I used exactly that pattern in IRT, to show each shipment's current status from a status history table, and LAG to calculate how long each shipment spent in each status for a delay report. I can write out the query if helpful.
cards.k: cte, window functions, row_number, rank, partition by, sql

cards.q: Unit vs integration vs end-to-end tests? What is the test pyramid?
cards.h: Pyramid: lots of bricks (unit), some floors (integration), one roof (E2E).
s: These are three levels of automated testing, and the test pyramid describes the healthy balance between them.

Unit tests check one class or function in isolation, with its dependencies mocked or faked. They run in milliseconds, so you can have thousands, and they pinpoint exactly what broke. Integration tests check that real components work together, for example the API with a real SQL Server database, or a repository with real queries. They're slower but catch wiring, configuration and query problems that mocks hide. End-to-end tests drive the whole system through the UI, like a real user, with tools like Playwright or Cucumber. They give the most confidence, but they're slow and more fragile.

The pyramid says: many unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests in the middle, and a small number of end-to-end tests at the top for critical journeys. If it's upside down, an "ice cream cone", the suite becomes slow and flaky, and people stop trusting it.

In our IRT work, we have xUnit unit tests for business rules, integration tests with WebApplicationFactory and a real database, and Playwright and Cucumber end-to-end tests for key flows like randomisation and shipment creation. I can explain how this supports GxP validation.
cards.k: unit test, integration test, end-to-end, test pyramid, testing, test, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: xUnit vs NUnit?
cards.h: xUnit = Fact/Theory; NUnit = Test/TestCase.
s: Both are mature .NET testing frameworks, and the differences are mostly style and conventions.

xUnit uses Fact for a single test and Theory with InlineData or MemberData for parameterised tests. It creates a new instance of the test class for every test, which keeps tests isolated by design. Setup goes in the constructor, cleanup in Dispose, and shared expensive setup, like a database, goes in fixtures with IClassFixture or collection fixtures. It's what Microsoft uses for .NET itself and is the default in many new projects. NUnit uses Test and TestCase attributes, has SetUp and TearDown methods, and OneTimeSetUp for shared setup. It has a rich constraint-based assertion model with Assert.That, and some built-in features like ordering and categories.
Both integrate with dotnet test, run in CI, and report coverage to SonarQube, so the choice rarely matters technically.

My practice is to use whatever the repository already uses, because consistency matters more than preference. For new projects, I prefer xUnit, because the per-test instance makes accidental shared state between tests less likely. I can show a Theory example.

cards.q: How do you use Moq, and what should you not mock?
cards.h: Mock the neighbours, not the person you are testing.
s: Moq is a library for creating fake implementations of interfaces in unit tests, so I can test a class without its real dependencies.

I create a Mock of the interface, set up behaviour, like mock.Setup for GetAsync with a given id returning a test entity, or throwing an exception to test error handling. I pass mock.Object into the class under test. After the call, I assert the outcome first, and where the interaction is the actual behaviour, I verify it, like Verify that SaveAsync was called once. I avoid verifying every internal call, because then tests break on every refactor even when behaviour is correct.

What I don't mock: things I don't own and whose behaviour is complex, like DbContext or the internals of HttpClient. Mocking DbContext doesn't test the real query translation, so I use a real database with Testcontainers instead, and for HttpClient I use a fake message handler. I also don't mock simple value objects, or the class under test itself.
For example, in our vendor exchange tests, I mock ISftpClient to fail once with a timeout and then succeed, and assert the retry worked. I can show that test.

cards.q: How do you integration-test an ASP.NET Core API?
cards.h: Spin up the whole shop in a box and buy something.
s: For integration tests of an ASP.NET Core API, I run the real application in memory and call it over HTTP, with only external dependencies replaced.

The key tool is WebApplicationFactory of Program. It boots the actual app, with the real middleware pipeline, routing, DI, filters and serialisation, on an in-memory test server, and gives me an HttpClient to call it. In ConfigureTestServices, I swap out things I can't use in tests, like a vendor API client, a message publisher, or authentication, using a test auth handler that creates a user with specific roles. For the database, I prefer a real SQL Server in Docker with Testcontainers, rather than an in-memory provider, because in-memory doesn't behave like SQL. Each test seeds its own data and cleans up, often with Respawn, so tests are independent.
Then I assert the status code, the response body, and the side effects, like the row in the database or the message published.
In our services, these tests caught things unit tests never would: wrong middleware order, missing DI registrations, and EF queries that couldn't be translated. I can show the factory setup.

cards.q: How do you write reliable Playwright end-to-end tests?
cards.h: Find buttons by name like a user, not by street address (CSS path).
s: Reliable Playwright tests are mostly about avoiding the usual causes of flakiness: brittle selectors, timing assumptions and shared state.

For locators, I use what users see: getByRole, getByLabel, getByText, or a data-testid attribute, instead of long CSS or XPath paths that break when the layout changes. For timing, I rely on Playwright's auto-waiting and web-first assertions, like expect locator toBeVisible, which retry until they pass or time out. I never use fixed sleeps. For isolation, each test gets a fresh browser context and its own seeded data, so tests can run in parallel without affecting each other. I log in once and reuse the saved storage state, which saves a lot of time.
When a test fails in CI, traces, screenshots and videos show exactly what happened, step by step. I also use the page object pattern to keep tests readable.

In our IRT suite, the biggest improvement came from replacing sleeps with web-first assertions and seeding data through the API instead of the UI. Flaky failures dropped a lot, and the suite got faster. I can explain how we run them in the pipeline.

cards.q: What is BDD with Cucumber?
cards.h: Given-When-Then = setting, action, result: a mini story.
s: BDD, Behaviour-Driven Development, is an approach where we describe how the system should behave in plain language, agreed between business, QA and developers, and then automate those descriptions as tests. Cucumber is a popular tool for it.

The scenarios are written in Gherkin, using Given, When, Then. Given sets the context, When is the action, and Then is the expected outcome. For example: Given a study with two sites and stock at the depot, When a subject is randomised at site one, Then a kit from the correct depot is assigned. Each line is connected to code through step definitions, which do the actual work, like calling the API or driving the UI with Playwright.

The big value is shared understanding. Business analysts and QA can read and review the scenarios, and the scenarios become living documentation. In a GxP product, that's especially useful, because each scenario traces back to a requirement, and the test run produces evidence for validation.
The risk is writing scenarios that are too technical or too detailed. I keep them focused on behaviour, not clicks. I can show how we structure step definitions.
