cards.q: What is a SonarQube quality gate?
cards.h: Quality gate = toll booth: no pass, no road.
s: A SonarQube quality gate is a set of pass or fail conditions that code must meet before it can be merged or released.

SonarQube analyses the code in the CI pipeline. It finds bugs, vulnerabilities, security hotspots, code smells and duplication, and it reads test coverage reports. The quality gate then checks conditions, usually focused on new code: for example, coverage on new code above 80 percent, no new bugs or vulnerabilities, all security hotspots reviewed, and duplication below a limit. If any condition fails, the gate fails, and the pipeline blocks the pull request or release.
Focusing on new code is clever, because you don't have to fix a whole legacy codebase at once. Quality improves gradually with every change, and it can never get worse.

In our regulated environment, it also gives auditors objective evidence that every release met defined quality standards. My approach is to fix issues at the source, not suppress them. If a rule genuinely doesn't apply, we mark it with a documented reason. I can explain how we keep coverage meaningful rather than just hitting a number.
cards.k: sonarqube, quality gate, static analysis, code coverage, ci

cards.q: How do you test Node.js and React code with Jest?
cards.h: Jest = xUnit for JavaScript.
s: Jest is a JavaScript testing framework. It runs tests, provides assertions and mocking, and measures coverage, all in one tool.

For Node.js code, I write tests with describe and it blocks, and expect for assertions. For dependencies, jest.fn creates mock functions, and jest.mock replaces whole modules, for example a database client or an HTTP library, so the logic is tested in isolation. Async code is easy to test with async and await. For React components, I combine Jest with React Testing Library. I render the component, query elements the way a user would, by role or label text, simulate user events like typing and clicking with user-event, and assert what appears on screen. That tests behaviour, not implementation details like internal state.
I use snapshot tests sparingly, because large snapshots get approved without anyone reading them. And for API calls in components, Mock Service Worker gives realistic network mocks.
In our React work, every new component came with Testing Library tests for its key states: loading, error, empty and data. Tests run with coverage in CI. I can show a sample component test.

cards.q: What do you look for in a code review?
cards.h: C-S-D-P: Correct, Secure, Designed, Performant.
s: In a code review, I look at the change from a few angles, roughly in order of risk.

First, correctness: does it do what the story says, and does it handle edge cases like null, empty lists, concurrency and failure paths? Second, security: input validation, authorization checks, especially study-level access in our system, no secrets in code, no injection risks, and no sensitive or patient data in logs. Third, design and readability: clear naming, single responsibility, no duplication, and code that the next person can understand. Fourth, tests: are there tests for the change, and do they test behaviour, not implementation? Fifth, performance and operability: N+1 queries, missing async, missing indexes, and whether there are useful logs and metrics if it fails in production.
Style issues are for linters and analysers, not people, so I don't spend review time on formatting.

And how I review matters too. I ask questions instead of giving orders, explain the why, mark minor points as optional, and praise good solutions. When I mentored [two graduate developers in 2024], code reviews were one of the best teaching tools. I can give an example of a bug I caught in review.

cards.q: How is testing different in a GxP regulated product?
cards.h: In GxP, if it is not documented, it did not happen.
s: In a GxP regulated product, like our clinical trial IRT system, testing isn't just about finding bugs. It's about proving, with documented evidence, that the system does what it's supposed to do, because errors can affect patient safety and trial data integrity.

That changes a few things. Every requirement must trace to tests and their results, through a traceability matrix. Validation phases, like formal verification, FV, and user acceptance, UAT, are formal, with documented test scripts, results, and sign-offs. Every change needs an impact assessment, to decide what must be retested, plus regression testing. And releases follow a quality process with audit trails, so you can show who approved what and when.

Automation helps a lot. Our Playwright and Cucumber suites make regression fast and repeatable, and they generate evidence automatically. But the evidence must still be reviewed and stored properly, and automated tools themselves may need validation.

For developers, this means writing testable code, documenting changes clearly, and never making untracked changes. I've seen how this discipline catches problems early, and I can explain how a change moves through our environments.

cards.q: How do React hooks replace lifecycle methods?
cards.h: useEffect = 'after you paint, do this; before you leave, clean up'.
s: Hooks let function components do everything class components used to do with lifecycle methods, but organised by concern instead of by lifecycle.

useState holds local state. useEffect runs side effects after render, and it covers the three main lifecycle methods. With an empty dependency array, it runs once after the first render, like componentDidMount. With dependencies, it runs again whenever they change, like componentDidUpdate for those values. And the cleanup function you return runs before the next effect and when the component unmounts, like componentWillUnmount, which is where I cancel requests or remove listeners. useRef keeps a mutable value or a DOM reference without causing re-renders, useContext reads shared context, and useMemo and useCallback help with performance.

The big advantage is custom hooks. Logic like fetching data, with loading and error state, can be extracted into a hook like useShipments, and reused across components, which was awkward with classes.

In our React screens, we have custom hooks for API calls with cancellation, so leaving a page aborts the request. A common bug I watch for is a missing dependency, which causes stale values. I can explain that.

cards.q: How does Redux Toolkit work?
cards.h: Redux loop: Click, Dispatch, Reduce, Store, Re-render.
s: Redux is a pattern for managing shared application state in one predictable place, and Redux Toolkit is the official, modern way to write it with much less boilerplate.

The core flow is: a single store holds the state. Components dispatch actions, which describe what happened. Reducers, which are pure functions, take the current state and an action and return the next state. Components subscribed to that part of the state re-render. Redux Toolkit simplifies this. createSlice defines the state, reducers and action creators together, and uses Immer, so you can write code that looks like it mutates state, while it actually produces a new immutable state. configureStore sets up the store with good defaults and dev tools. For API calls, createAsyncThunk handles async logic, and RTK Query goes further, handling fetching, caching and invalidation for you.
An important design choice is not putting everything in Redux. Server data is best handled by RTK Query or a similar data-fetching library, and local UI state stays in components.
In our React work, we used slices for things like the selected study and user preferences, and RTK Query for API data. I can explain cache invalidation with tags.

cards.q: How do you design reusable UI components?
cards.h: Lego bricks: small, typed, snap together.
s: Reusable UI components are about making something easy to use correctly in many places, without it becoming a mess of special cases.

I keep components small and focused, with clearly typed props through TypeScript interfaces, so the contract is obvious. I prefer composition over configuration: accepting children or slots instead of adding a new boolean flag for every variation, because twenty flags usually means the component is doing too much. I keep them presentational, so they get data through props, and data fetching lives in container components or custom hooks. They should be accessible by default, with proper labels, keyboard support and focus handling, and use theme tokens for colours and spacing instead of hard-coded values. Finally, they're documented, for example in Storybook, and tested with Testing Library.
A good test of reusability is whether another developer can use it correctly just by reading the props.

In our React UI, I built a reusable data table component, with sorting, paging, empty and loading states, and accessible headers. It replaced several slightly different tables across screens, and fixes now happen in one place. I can explain how I decided its API.

cards.q: How do you optimise React performance?
cards.h: Memo = do not redo homework you already did.
s: React performance work starts with measuring. I use the React DevTools Profiler to see which components re-render and how long they take, before changing anything.

The most common problem is unnecessary re-renders. When a parent re-renders, all children re-render by default. React.memo lets a component skip rendering when its props haven't changed. useMemo caches expensive calculations, and useCallback keeps function references stable, so memoised children aren't re-rendered just because a new function was created. I keep state as local as possible, because state high up the tree re-renders everything below it. For lists, I use stable unique keys, not array indexes, and for long lists or big tables, virtualisation, which only renders visible rows. For load time, I split code with React.lazy and Suspense, so each screen loads only its own code.
I don't wrap everything in memo by default, because memoisation has its own cost. I use it where the profiler shows a real problem.
In our IRT UI, a site inventory table with thousands of rows was slow. Virtualising the rows and memoising the row component made scrolling smooth again. I can explain the new React compiler too.

cards.q: Why TypeScript? interface vs type?
cards.h: TypeScript = spell-check for JavaScript.
s: TypeScript adds static types on top of JavaScript. The code compiles to normal JavaScript, but type errors are caught while you write code, instead of in production.

The benefits are real: errors like misspelled properties or passing the wrong type are caught at compile time, the editor gives accurate autocompletion, and refactoring is much safer, because renaming something shows every place it breaks. Types also document the code, especially API contracts. I always use strict mode and avoid any, which switches the checks off.

On interface versus type: both can describe object shapes, and for most cases either works. Interfaces can be extended and can be declaration-merged, meaning two declarations with the same name combine. That makes them good for object shapes and public contracts. Type aliases are more flexible: they can describe unions, like "Pending" or "Shipped", intersections, tuples, and advanced mapped and conditional types. My usual rule is interface for object shapes and props, and type for unions and compositions.
In our front end, we generate TypeScript types from our OpenAPI documents, so the front end and API stay in sync, and a backend contract change shows up as a compile error. I can show how that works.

cards.q: Angular vs React?
cards.h: Angular = furnished apartment; React = pick your own furniture.
s: Angular and React can build the same applications, but they're different kinds of tools.

Angular is a complete, opinionated framework from Google. It includes modules or standalone components, dependency injection, a router, forms, an HTTP client and RxJS for async streams, all built in, and it's TypeScript-first. Teams get one consistent way of doing things, which suits large enterprise apps. React is a UI library from Meta. It focuses on rendering components with JSX and hooks, and you choose the rest yourself, like the router, state management with Redux Toolkit, and data fetching. That gives flexibility, but needs more decisions. On rendering, Angular uses change detection, traditionally with zone.js and now with signals for fine-grained updates. React re-renders components and reconciles a virtual DOM.
My view is that either works well. Angular for large teams that want structure out of the box, React for flexibility and its huge ecosystem.
I've worked with both on IRT. I maintained Angular modules in parts of the existing UI, and built new screens in React. I can talk about how we migrated pieces between them.

cards.q: Explain the JavaScript event loop.
cards.h: One chef, one stove; finished orders wait at the pass, promises jump the line.
s: The event loop is how JavaScript handles asynchronous work, even though it runs your code on a single thread.

There's one call stack, where your code runs. When you start async work, like a timer, a network request or file I/O, it's handed off to the browser or, in Node, to libuv, which does it in the background. When it finishes, its callback is put in a queue. The event loop's job is simple: whenever the call stack is empty, take the next task and run it. There are two kinds of queues. Microtasks, which are promise callbacks and awaits, and macrotasks, like setTimeout and I/O callbacks. After each task, the loop runs all pending microtasks first, then takes the next macrotask. That's why a resolved promise's then runs before a setTimeout with zero delay.

The practical lesson: long synchronous code blocks everything, because nothing else can run while the stack is busy. In the browser the UI freezes, and in Node every request waits. So heavy CPU work goes to Web Workers or worker threads.
I can walk through a small code example that shows the ordering.

cards.q: What front-end security issues do you watch for?
cards.h: Open a new tab, but do not hand it your house keys (noopener).
s: On the front end, I watch for a few main categories of security issues.

First, cross-site scripting, XSS. React escapes values by default, which protects us, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML, or putting user input into URLs like javascript links, bypasses that, so I avoid it or sanitise with DOMPurify. A Content Security Policy adds another layer. Second, token storage. Tokens in localStorage can be stolen by any XSS, so I prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, or keeping tokens in memory. Third, reverse tabnabbing. Links with target blank used to give the new page access to window.opener, so it could redirect our original tab to a phishing page. The fix is rel noopener noreferrer. Fourth, never trusting the front end for security. Hiding a button isn't authorization; the API must check everything. And fifth, dependency vulnerabilities, checked with npm audit in the pipeline.

The tabnabbing one is a real fix I did in IRT. A security scan flagged it, and I updated [about 40] external links, added a shared link component that sets rel by default, and a lint rule so it can't come back. I can explain how CSP helps.
cards.k: frontend security, xss, csrf, csp, tabnabbing, owasp, security, sql injection, cors, cookie

cards.q: How does Node.js handle concurrency and when is it a good fit?
cards.h: Node = one very fast waiter who never waits at the kitchen.
s: Node.js runs JavaScript on a single main thread with an event loop, and uses non-blocking I/O through a library called libuv.

When a request needs a database query or an HTTP call, Node doesn't wait. It starts the operation, moves on to other requests, and runs the callback when the result arrives. So one process can handle thousands of concurrent connections with very little memory, because there's no thread per request. Things like file system operations and DNS run on a small libuv thread pool behind the scenes.

That makes Node a great fit for I/O-heavy work: APIs that mostly call databases and other services, backend-for-frontend layers, real-time apps with WebSockets, and developer tooling. Sharing TypeScript with the front end is also a productivity win. It's a weak fit for CPU-heavy work, like large calculations or image processing, because that blocks the event loop and every request waits. For those, worker threads or a different service are better. And in production, you run several processes or containers to use all CPU cores.
In my work, I've used Node and TypeScript for internal tooling and integration services, while the core domain logic stays in .NET. I can explain the event loop phases.
cards.k: node.js, concurrency, event loop, non-blocking, libuv

cards.q: How do you structure a Node.js/TypeScript microservice?
cards.h: Same layers as .NET, different accent.
s: I structure a Node.js TypeScript microservice much like a .NET one: clear layers, typed contracts, and the same operational basics.

The layers are: routes or controllers that handle HTTP, services that hold the business logic, and repositories or clients that talk to databases and other services. Request and response shapes are typed, and inputs are validated at the edge with something like zod, so the rest of the code can trust the types. I use Express for simple services, or NestJS when I want more structure, since NestJS has modules and dependency injection very similar to ASP.NET Core. Errors go through a central error-handling middleware that returns a consistent error format, and async errors are captured properly.

Operationally: configuration from environment variables, validated at startup; structured JSON logging with pino, including a correlation id; a health endpoint; and graceful shutdown on SIGTERM. Then Jest tests, ESLint, a Dockerfile with a small base image, and the same CI/CD pipeline template as our .NET services.
Keeping that consistency means any engineer can work on any service, whatever the language. I can compare NestJS with ASP.NET Core in more detail.
cards.k: node.js, typescript, microservice structure, express, layers, javascript, js, ts

cards.q: FastAPI vs Flask?
cards.h: FastAPI = Flask with a typed seatbelt and a turbo.
s: FastAPI and Flask are both popular Python web frameworks, but they're built for different eras of Python.

Flask is a minimal micro-framework, built on WSGI, and synchronous by default. It's simple, very flexible, and has a huge ecosystem, but you add things like request validation and API documentation yourself with extensions. FastAPI is newer and async-first, built on ASGI. It uses Python type hints with Pydantic models, so request bodies are validated and converted automatically, and invalid input returns a clear 422 error. It generates OpenAPI documentation and Swagger UI from the code, it has built-in dependency injection with Depends, and it's one of the fastest Python frameworks.

So for a new typed REST service, I choose FastAPI. It feels quite close to ASP.NET Core minimal APIs, with typed models and automatic docs. Flask still makes sense for very simple apps, or existing Flask codebases where there's no reason to rewrite.

I've built REST services with both. In practice, the type-driven validation in FastAPI removed a lot of hand-written checking code, and the automatic docs made integration with other teams easier. I can explain how async works in FastAPI.
cards.k: fastapi, flask, python, comparison

cards.q: How do async and validation work in FastAPI?
cards.h: Pydantic = customs officer checking every parcel.
s: FastAPI is built on ASGI, so it supports async natively, and it uses Pydantic for validation.

For async: if I declare an endpoint with async def, it runs on the event loop. That's efficient for I/O, but only if everything inside is also async, using libraries like httpx for HTTP calls and asyncpg or async SQLAlchemy for databases. If I call blocking code inside an async def, it blocks the whole event loop and every request waits. If I have to use blocking libraries, I declare the endpoint with plain def, and FastAPI runs it in a thread pool instead. That's a common mistake to watch for.

For validation, I define Pydantic models with type hints and constraints. FastAPI automatically parses and validates the request body, query and path parameters against them, and returns a 422 with detailed errors if they're invalid. Response models filter and serialise the output, so internal fields aren't leaked. Depends provides dependency injection for database sessions, authentication and configuration.
In production, I run it with uvicorn workers, behind a load balancer, in a container. It's conceptually very similar to ASP.NET Core model binding plus DI. I can show a short example.
cards.k: fastapi, async, pydantic, validation, 422, python, await, task, asynchronous, valuetask, configureawait

cards.q: How does Spring Boot compare to ASP.NET Core?
cards.h: Spring Boot is ASP.NET Core speaking Java.
s: Spring Boot and ASP.NET Core are very similar in concept, so moving between them is mostly learning new names.

Both have a built-in dependency injection container with constructor injection, use annotations or attributes to declare routes, run on an embedded web server, support configuration profiles per environment, and have a mature ORM. The mapping is quite direct. RestController in Spring is like a controller with ApiController. Constructor injection works the same way. JPA with Hibernate is like EF Core. application.yml is like appsettings.json, Spring profiles are like ASP.NET Core environments, and Maven or Gradle play the role of NuGet and the dotnet CLI. Spring filters and interceptors are similar to middleware and filters.

The differences are more about ecosystem and style. Spring has a very large ecosystem, like Spring Security, Spring Cloud and Spring Data, and relies heavily on annotations and auto-configuration, which can feel magical. ASP.NET Core is a bit more explicit, with configuration in Program.cs, and it's very fast in benchmarks.
Because the concepts transfer, I'm comfortable reading and contributing to Spring Boot services, and the design principles I use in .NET apply directly. I can compare their security models too.
cards.k: spring boot, asp.net core, java, comparison

cards.q: You work across .NET, Node.js and Python. How do you keep services consistent?
cards.h: Different languages, one dress code.
s: When a team uses several languages, consistency comes from shared contracts and conventions, not from the language.

First, contracts. Every API is designed contract-first with OpenAPI, uses the same error format, based on ProblemDetails, and follows the same versioning rules. So a consumer can't tell which language a service is written in. Second, operational conventions. Every service uses correlation ids, structured JSON logs to CloudWatch, health endpoints, and metrics to Grafana, so support works the same way everywhere. Third, the delivery pipeline. The same CI/CD template builds, tests, runs a SonarQube quality gate, builds a container image, and deploys with infrastructure as code, whatever the language. Each language has a service template with all of this ready, so a new service starts consistent.
And I choose the language by fit, not taste. .NET for core domain services, Node and TypeScript for I/O glue and tooling, and Python for data and AI scripting.

The correlation-id work is a good example. I wrote it for .NET first, then we added the same header convention in Node and Python, so one query traces a request across all of them. I can explain how we keep the templates updated.
cards.k: polyglot, consistency, standards, microservices, conventions

cards.q: How do you manage dependencies in Node and Python?
cards.h: Lock file = the exact grocery receipt, not just the shopping list.
s: In both ecosystems, the goal is the same: reproducible builds, controlled updates, and catching vulnerable packages early.

In Node, package.json declares dependencies with version ranges, and the lock file, package-lock.json, records the exact versions of everything, including transitive dependencies. The lock file is always committed. In CI, I use npm ci instead of npm install, which installs exactly what's in the lock file and fails if it's out of sync. npm audit, or a tool like Dependabot, checks for known vulnerabilities. In Python, I use a virtual environment per project, so dependencies don't clash, and pin exact versions, either in requirements.txt or with a lock file from Poetry or uv. pip-audit checks for vulnerabilities.
For both, Docker images pin versions too, including the base image, and updates happen regularly through small pull requests, so we never face one huge risky upgrade.

It's the same idea as NuGet with central package management in .NET, which I introduced during our .NET 10 upgrade after a version conflict. I can explain how we handle a vulnerable transitive dependency.
cards.k: dependency management, npm, package-lock, pip, poetry, vulnerabilities

cards.q: How do you choose the language for a new microservice?
cards.h: Pick the tool the team can carry at 2 AM.
s: I choose the language for a new microservice based on fit and on what the team can support, not on personal preference.

First, team skills and the existing ecosystem in that domain. If the team and all neighbouring services are .NET, there needs to be a strong reason to introduce something else, because every new language adds maintenance, hiring and support cost. Second, the workload. Complex domain logic or CPU-heavy work suits .NET or Java. I/O-heavy glue, backend-for-frontend layers and tooling suit Node and TypeScript. Data processing, machine learning and AI scripting suit Python. Third, libraries. Sometimes the best library decides, for example mature commercial SFTP providers in .NET, or the newest LLM SDKs often appearing first in Python and TypeScript. Fourth, operations: can we monitor, secure, test and deploy it with our existing templates and pipelines?
So in practice, our core IRT services are .NET, and other languages appear where they clearly fit better.
The decision should be written down, for example in an architecture decision record, so the next person knows why. I can give an example of a decision like that.
cards.k: language choice, technology choice, .net, node, python

cards.q: ECS vs Lambda vs EC2: when do you use each?
cards.h: EC2 = rent a house, ECS = rent furnished rooms, Lambda = hotel by the hour.
s: I use ECS with Fargate for long-running services like our APIs, because containers run all the time with no servers to manage. I use Lambda for short, event-driven tasks, like reacting to a file landing in S3, where I pay only when it runs. I use EC2 when I need full control of the machine, special software, or very steady heavy load. Our IRT services run on ECS.
cards.k: ecs, lambda, ec2, fargate, compute choice, aws, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: Explain the ECS building blocks.
cards.h: Blueprint (task def), workers (tasks), manager (service), building (cluster).
s: In ECS, a cluster is the logical group where things run. A task definition is like a blueprint: the image, CPU, memory, environment variables, secrets and IAM role. A task is one running copy of it, and a service keeps the desired number of tasks running, replaces failed ones and connects them to the load balancer. With Fargate, AWS runs the servers for us.
cards.k: ecs, cluster, task definition, task, service, fargate, aws, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: What does API Gateway do?
cards.h: API Gateway = hotel reception: checks ID, directs you, limits crowds.
s: API Gateway is the front door for APIs. It handles routing to backends like Lambda or HTTP services, authentication with JWT or IAM, throttling, request validation, usage plans and API keys. So the services behind it can focus on business logic. For containers with heavy traffic, an Application Load Balancer is often cheaper, so the choice depends on what features we need.
cards.k: api gateway, throttling, routing, authentication, aws, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: What are Lambda cold starts and how do you reduce them?
cards.h: Cold start = starting a car in winter; provisioned concurrency = engine kept running.
s: A cold start is the extra delay when Lambda has to create a new environment and load my code before the first request. For .NET it can be noticeable. I reduce it with more memory, which also gives more CPU, smaller packages, Native AOT or SnapStart, and provisioned concurrency to keep instances warm for critical functions. For steady traffic, a container on ECS avoids cold starts completely.
cards.k: lambda, cold start, provisioned concurrency, snapstart, native aot, aws, ecs, fargate, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: How do you model data in DynamoDB?
cards.h: Partition key = which drawer, sort key = order inside the drawer.
s: In DynamoDB I start from the access patterns, not from tables and joins. I choose a partition key that spreads load evenly and a sort key for ranges, like customer id and order date. Often several entity types live in one table. For other query patterns I add global secondary indexes. Getting the keys wrong is expensive to change later, so I design them carefully up front.
cards.k: dynamodb, partition key, sort key, gsi, single table design, nosql, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: What caching strategies do you know (ElastiCache)?
cards.h: Cache-aside = check the fridge, if empty go to the shop and refill.
s: The most common is cache-aside: the app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and stores the result with an expiry time. Write-through updates the cache when writing the database. I always set TTLs and invalidate on changes. We used ElastiCache Redis for reference data, and also for our token logout denylist, where lookups take about [1 millisecond].
cards.k: caching, elasticache, redis, cache-aside, write-through, ttl, cache, memory cache, hybridcache, output caching

cards.q: ALB vs NLB?
cards.h: ALB reads the letter (HTTP), NLB only reads the envelope (TCP).
s: An Application Load Balancer works at layer 7, so it understands HTTP: it can route by path or host name, terminate TLS, and do health checks on HTTP endpoints. A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 with TCP and UDP, so it is extremely fast, keeps static IPs, and suits non-HTTP traffic. For our web APIs on ECS we use an ALB.
cards.k: alb, nlb, load balancer, layer 7, layer 4, aws

cards.q: What is S3 used for, and what are presigned URLs?
cards.h: Presigned URL = a one-time visitor pass that expires.
s: S3 is object storage for files: uploads, exports, backups, logs and static websites. It is very durable and cheap. A presigned URL is a temporary link, signed with our credentials, that lets a client upload or download one specific object directly, without going through our API and without AWS credentials. It is great for large file uploads, like CSV imports.
cards.k: s3, presigned url, object storage, file upload, aws

cards.q: How do you apply IAM least privilege?
cards.h: Give a key to one room, not the master key.
s: Least privilege means every identity gets only the permissions it needs, nothing more. I give each ECS service its own task role, scope actions to specific resources like one bucket or one secret, and avoid wildcards. I use roles with temporary credentials instead of long-lived access keys. I review permissions regularly with IAM Access Analyzer and remove what isn't used.
cards.k: iam, least privilege, roles, policies, task role, security

cards.q: Describe a typical AWS network layout for microservices.
cards.h: Public lobby, private offices, guards (security groups) at each door.
s: A typical layout is one VPC across at least two availability zones. Public subnets hold only the load balancer and NAT gateway. Private subnets hold the ECS services, and separate private subnets hold databases like RDS. Security groups allow only the needed traffic, for example the database accepts only the service's security group. Outbound internet goes through NAT, and AWS services through VPC endpoints.
cards.k: vpc, subnets, network layout, security groups, nat gateway, availability zones, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: What is infrastructure as code and why use it?
cards.h: IaC = the architect's blueprint, not hand-built each time.
s: Infrastructure as code means defining servers, networks, databases and permissions in code files, like Terraform or CloudFormation, instead of clicking in the console. The benefits are that environments are repeatable and consistent, every change is reviewed in a pull request and tracked in Git, and we can rebuild an environment quickly. In a regulated product, that history is also great evidence.
cards.k: infrastructure as code, iac, terraform, cloudformation

cards.q: CloudFormation vs Terraform?
cards.h: CloudFormation = AWS's own language; Terraform = translator for every cloud.
s: CloudFormation is AWS's own service, so the state is managed by AWS, and it supports AWS features well. Terraform works with many providers, not only AWS, has a nice plan step showing exactly what will change, and a big module ecosystem, but I must manage its state file. In my work, core platform stacks were in CloudFormation and newer pieces used Terraform.
cards.k: cloudformation, terraform, iac, comparison, infrastructure as code

cards.q: What is Terraform state and how do you manage it?
cards.h: State = Terraform's memory; lock it so two people do not edit at once.
s: Terraform state is a file that maps my code to the real resources it created, so Terraform knows what to change. I store it remotely, in an S3 bucket with encryption and versioning, with locking so two people can't apply at the same time. It can contain secrets, so access is restricted. I keep separate state for each environment.
cards.k: terraform state, remote state, s3 backend, state locking, terraform, cloudformation, iac, infrastructure as code

cards.q: Describe the Terraform workflow.
cards.h: Write, Init, Plan, Apply: measure twice, cut once.
s: The workflow is: write or change the code, run terraform init to set up providers and the backend, terraform plan to see exactly what will be created, changed or destroyed, then review that plan, and terraform apply to make the changes. In a team, the plan runs in the pipeline on the pull request, and apply runs after approval.
cards.k: terraform, init, plan, apply, workflow, cloudformation, iac, infrastructure as code

cards.q: What is drift and how do you avoid it?
cards.h: Drift = someone moved the furniture without updating the floor plan.
s: Drift is when the real infrastructure no longer matches the code, usually because someone changed something manually in the console. I avoid it by making all changes through code and pipelines, limiting console write access, and running regular plans or drift detection to spot differences. When drift is found, we either update the code or revert the manual change.
cards.k: drift, drift detection, infrastructure as code, terraform, cloudformation

cards.q: Image vs container; what is a Dockerfile?
cards.h: Image = recipe card, container = the cooked dish.
s: An image is a read-only package with the app and everything it needs to run. A container is a running instance of that image, like an object created from a class. A Dockerfile is the recipe that builds the image, step by step: the base image, copying files, building, and the command to start. We build one image per service and run it everywhere.
cards.k: docker, image, container, dockerfile

cards.q: How do you write a production Dockerfile for a .NET service?
cards.h: Build in the workshop, ship only the finished product.
s: I use a multi-stage Dockerfile. The first stage uses the SDK image to restore and publish, copying the project files first so the restore layer is cached. The final stage uses the small ASP.NET runtime image, or a chiseled image, copies only the published output, runs as a non-root user and sets the entry point. The result is small, secure and fast to build.
cards.k: dockerfile, multi-stage build, .net docker, non-root, chiseled image, docker, container, image

cards.q: What is a Kubernetes pod, and what are the main Kubernetes objects?
cards.h: Pod = a room, Deployment = landlord keeping N rooms ready, Service = the building's reception.
s: A Pod is the smallest unit, one or more containers running together. A Deployment manages pods, keeps the right number running and does rolling updates. A Service gives pods a stable name and load-balances to them. An Ingress routes outside HTTP traffic to services. ConfigMaps and Secrets hold configuration, and a Namespace groups resources.
cards.k: kubernetes, pod, deployment, service, ingress, configmap, secret, namespace, k8s, helm

cards.q: What goes in a Kubernetes Deployment YAML?
cards.h: Who am I (metadata), how many (replicas), what to run (template), am I healthy (probes).
s: A Deployment YAML has the number of replicas, a selector that matches the pod labels, and a pod template. The template lists the container image and tag, ports, environment variables from ConfigMaps and Secrets, CPU and memory requests and limits, and liveness and readiness probes. It also has the rolling update strategy, like how many pods can be down at once.
cards.k: kubernetes, deployment yaml, replicas, probes, resources, rolling update, k8s, pod, deployment, service, helm

cards.q: Liveness vs readiness vs startup probes?
cards.h: Readiness = open sign on the shop; liveness = pulse check.
s: A liveness probe checks if the app is still alive, and if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container. A readiness probe checks if it can take traffic, and if it fails, the pod is removed from the service but not restarted. A startup probe gives slow-starting apps time before the other probes begin. In .NET I map these to health check endpoints.
cards.k: liveness probe, readiness probe, startup probe, health checks, kubernetes

cards.q: ConfigMap vs Secret; how do you handle configuration in containers?
cards.h: Same suitcase (image), different labels (config) per trip.
s: A ConfigMap holds normal configuration, like URLs or feature flags, and a Secret holds sensitive values like passwords, which are only base64 encoded, so they need encryption and access control. Containers get them as environment variables or files. In ECS, we pull secrets from Secrets Manager and Parameter Store into the task at startup, and the code reads them through normal .NET configuration.
cards.k: configmap, secret, configuration, environment variables, secrets manager

cards.q: How does autoscaling work in Kubernetes and ECS?
cards.h: Thermostat: keep the temperature (CPU) at the target by adding heaters (pods).
s: In Kubernetes, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds or removes pods based on CPU, memory or custom metrics, and a cluster autoscaler adds nodes when needed. In ECS, service auto scaling uses target tracking, for example keep CPU at 60 percent or a certain number of requests per target. In both cases, the app must be stateless and shut down gracefully.
cards.k: autoscaling, hpa, ecs service auto scaling, target tracking, scaling, kubernetes, k8s, pod, deployment, service, helm, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: Docker vs Kubernetes vs ECS?
cards.h: Docker = a shipping container; Kubernetes/ECS = the port that moves thousands of them.
s: Docker builds and runs containers on one machine. Kubernetes and ECS are orchestrators that run many containers across many machines, handle scaling, restarts, rolling deployments and service discovery. Kubernetes is open source, portable and very powerful but complex. ECS is AWS's simpler, managed option. Our production runs on ECS.
cards.k: docker, kubernetes, ecs, orchestration, comparison, container, dockerfile, image, k8s, pod, deployment, service, helm, aws, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: CI vs continuous delivery vs continuous deployment?
cards.h: CI = always compiles, CD = always shippable, Deploy = always shipped.
s: Continuous integration means every change is merged often and automatically built and tested. Continuous delivery means every passing build is ready to release, but a person decides when to deploy to production. Continuous deployment goes further and deploys every passing change to production automatically. In our regulated product we do continuous delivery, because production needs approvals.
cards.k: ci, continuous delivery, continuous deployment, ci/cd, pipeline

cards.q: Describe your Azure DevOps pipeline and release flow.
cards.h: Build once, promote the same box through every gate.
s: Our YAML build pipeline runs on pull requests and merges: restore, build, unit tests with coverage, SonarQube quality gate, dependency scan, then it publishes versioned artifacts and Docker images. The release pipeline promotes that same artifact through FV, TechOps, UAT and production, with approvals at each stage, using Ansible, Python and Shell scripts for multi-node installs. Every environment traces back to one tagged version.
cards.k: azure devops, pipeline, release, ci/cd, artifacts, approvals, build, deployment

cards.q: YAML pipelines vs classic release pipelines in Azure DevOps?
cards.h: YAML = recipe in the cookbook; classic = recipe on a sticky note.
s: YAML pipelines are defined in code in the repository, so they are reviewed, versioned and reusable with templates. Classic release pipelines are designed in the web UI, which is easy to start with and visual, with good approval gates, but changes are not in Git. New work should use YAML with environments and approvals. Some of our older release definitions are still classic.
cards.k: azure devops, yaml pipelines, classic release, pipeline as code, ci/cd, pipeline, build, release, deployment

cards.q: What branching and tagging strategy do you follow?
cards.h: Branches are drafts, tags are the printed edition.
s: We use a main branch that is always releasable, short-lived feature branches merged by pull request with reviews and checks, and release branches for each release so fixes can go in while new work continues. Every release build is tagged with its version, so we can always tell exactly what code is in each environment. Hotfixes are merged back to main.
cards.k: branching strategy, git, tagging, release branch, feature branch

cards.q: What role did Ansible play, and what is idempotency in it?
cards.h: Ansible = a checklist robot; running it twice does not do the job twice.
s: Ansible is an agentless automation tool that runs YAML playbooks over SSH to configure servers and install software. Our release installs ran through Ansible playbooks with Python and Shell scripts across the multi-node environments. Idempotency means running the same task again leaves the same result, so if a deployment fails halfway, we can safely run it again.
cards.k: ansible, playbook, idempotency, configuration management, automation

cards.q: Blue-green vs canary vs rolling deployments?
cards.h: Rolling = change tyres one at a time; blue-green = second car ready; canary = send one bird first.
s: Rolling deployment replaces instances a few at a time, which is simple and needs no extra servers. Blue-green runs the new version beside the old one and switches all traffic at once, so rollback is instant. Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version first and increases it if metrics look good. ECS gives us rolling updates with automatic rollback.
cards.k: blue green, canary, rolling deployment, deployment strategies, rollback

cards.q: How do you plan rollback for a release that includes database changes?
cards.h: Always leave a ladder down before you climb.
s: The key is to make database changes backward compatible, so the previous app version still works with the new schema. I use expand and contract: first add new columns or tables, deploy the app, and only remove old ones in a later release. Then rolling back the app does not need a database rollback. For risky changes we take a backup and have tested rollback scripts.
cards.k: rollback, database changes, expand contract, backward compatible, release

cards.q: How is release management different in a regulated GxP environment?
cards.h: Regulated release = a flight checklist with signatures.
s: In GxP, every release is controlled and documented. There is an approved change request, the build is validated in FV with scripted tests and evidence, users accept it in UAT, and production deployment needs approvals and a record of what was installed. The same validated artifact must be promoted, never rebuilt. That's why automation must keep audit trails and human approvals.
cards.k: gxp, release management, change control, validation, regulated, audit trail, 21 cfr part 11

cards.q: What are logs, metrics and traces?
cards.h: Metrics say something is wrong, traces say where, logs say why.
s: Logs are detailed records of events, like an error with its message and context. Metrics are numbers over time, like request rate, error rate and latency, which are cheap to store and great for alerts and dashboards. Traces follow one request as it moves through several services, showing where the time goes. Together they tell me what is wrong, where, and why.
cards.k: logs, metrics, traces, observability, three pillars

cards.q: How do you use CloudWatch and Grafana?
cards.h: CloudWatch collects, Grafana tells the story.
s: We send logs to CloudWatch Logs and use Logs Insights to query them, for example by correlation id or error type. CloudWatch metrics and alarms watch things like error rate, latency and CPU. Grafana dashboards show service health in one place, and we check them after every release to confirm everything is normal.
cards.k: cloudwatch, grafana, logs insights, dashboards, alarms, monitoring

cards.q: What are the golden signals?
cards.h: L-T-E-S: Late, Traffic, Errors, Saturation.
s: The four golden signals from Google's SRE book are latency, which is how long requests take, traffic, which is how many requests, errors, which is the rate of failures, and saturation, which is how full the system is, like CPU, memory or queue depth. If I monitor only four things for a service, it is these.
cards.k: golden signals, latency, traffic, errors, saturation, sre, monitoring

cards.q: How do you do root-cause analysis for a production issue?
cards.h: Stop the bleeding, find the wound, prevent the next one.
s: First I limit the impact, for example by rolling back. Then I collect facts: when it started, what changed, which users, and the logs, metrics and traces. I form a hypothesis and test it, and I keep asking why until I find the real cause, not just the symptom. Finally we write a blameless review with actions, like a test or alert, so it does not happen again.
cards.k: root cause analysis, rca, incident, troubleshooting, post-mortem, 5 whys

cards.q: What makes a good alert?
cards.h: If an alert wakes you up, it must need you.
s: A good alert is actionable: when it fires, someone needs to do something, and it says what is wrong and links to a runbook. It is based on user impact, like error rate or latency, rather than every CPU spike. It has sensible thresholds and durations so it doesn't flap. Too many noisy alerts make people ignore the important ones.

cards.q: Kafka vs RabbitMQ?
cards.h: RabbitMQ = post office that delivers and forgets; Kafka = a diary everyone can re-read.
s: Kafka is a distributed log: messages are kept for a retention period, many consumer groups can read the same events, and it can replay them and handle very high volume. RabbitMQ is a message broker with queues: a message is delivered to a consumer and removed once acknowledged, with flexible routing and per-message retries. We use Kafka for shipment status events and RabbitMQ for task-style work.
cards.k: kafka, rabbitmq, messaging, comparison, message broker, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, event streaming, queue, exchange, amqp, dead letter, dlq, event driven

cards.q: Explain Kafka topics, partitions and consumer groups.
cards.h: Topic = highway, partitions = lanes, consumer group = toll booths, one per lane.
s: A topic is a named stream of events, like shipment-status. Each topic is split into partitions, which allow parallel processing, and order is kept only inside a partition. A consumer group is a set of consumers sharing the work: each partition is read by one consumer in the group. So more partitions mean more parallelism, and we use the shipment id as the key to keep its events in order.
cards.k: kafka, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, ordering, event streaming, messaging, message broker, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: RabbitMQ exchange types?
cards.h: Direct = named letter, Topic = postcode pattern, Fanout = flyer to every house.
s: RabbitMQ has four exchange types. Direct sends a message to queues whose binding key exactly matches the routing key. Topic matches patterns with wildcards, like shipment dot star. Fanout sends to all bound queues, ignoring the key. Headers routes based on message headers. We mostly use topic exchanges, with dead-letter queues for failures.
cards.k: rabbitmq, exchange, direct, topic, fanout, headers, routing key, queue, amqp, dead letter, dlq, messaging, message broker, kafka, event driven

cards.q: What are publisher confirms and how did they fix the RabbitMQ outage?
cards.h: Publisher confirm = registered post with a delivery receipt.
s: In [mid-2024], RabbitMQ hit a memory alarm, blocked publishers and dropped connections. Because we published without confirms, shipment status updates were lost silently for [about 40 minutes]. I recovered by replaying the vendor files, which was safe because consumers upsert. Then I fixed it properly with publisher confirms, so RabbitMQ acknowledges each message once stored, plus retries, alerts and memory tuning. Since then we haven't lost a message.
cards.k: publisher confirms, rabbitmq outage, message loss, story, reliability, rabbitmq, queue, exchange, amqp, dead letter, dlq, messaging, message broker, kafka, event driven

cards.q: At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once delivery?
cards.h: Better to get the letter twice and ignore one than never get it.
s: At-most-once means a message is delivered zero or one time, so it can be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once means it is never lost but can arrive more than once, which is the most common choice. Exactly-once is hard across systems, so in practice we use at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers, which gives exactly-once effect.
cards.k: delivery guarantees, at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once, messaging

cards.q: How do you make a consumer idempotent?
cards.h: Stamp each letter 'done' so you never act on it twice.
s: An idempotent consumer gives the same result even if it gets the same message twice. I do it by giving each message a unique id and storing processed ids in a table with a unique key, in the same transaction as the business change, so a duplicate is simply skipped. Another way is using upserts or checking the current state, for example ignore a status update older than what we already have.
cards.k: idempotent consumer, deduplication, message id, upsert, at-least-once

cards.q: What is a dead-letter queue?
cards.h: DLQ = the lost-and-found box.
s: A dead-letter queue is where messages go when they can't be processed, for example after several retries or if the message is invalid. This keeps one bad message from blocking the queue or being retried forever. We monitor the dead-letter queue with alerts, look at why the message failed, fix the issue and then replay it.
cards.k: dead letter queue, dlq, poison message, retries, rabbitmq, kafka, queue, exchange, amqp, dead letter

cards.q: What is the transactional outbox pattern?
cards.h: Write the letter in the same notebook as the change; a postman collects it later.
s: The outbox pattern solves the problem of saving to the database and publishing an event reliably. In the same transaction as the business change, I insert the event into an outbox table. A background process then reads the outbox and publishes to the broker, marking rows as sent. So if the broker is down, events wait safely in the database and nothing is lost.
cards.k: outbox pattern, transactional outbox, reliable messaging, events, dual write

cards.q: Authentication vs authorization?
cards.h: Authentication = passport check, authorization = boarding pass for a specific seat.
s: Authentication answers who you are, for example by validating a login or a token. Authorization answers what you are allowed to do, like checking roles, policies or whether you have access to a specific study. Authentication always comes first. In ASP.NET Core they are separate middleware, and a failed authentication returns 401, while a failed authorization returns 403.
cards.k: authentication, authorization, 401, 403, identity, roles, policies

cards.q: What is a JWT and how is it validated?
cards.h: JWT = a sealed wristband: anyone can read it, nobody can forge it.
s: A JWT is a signed token with three parts: a header, a payload with claims like user id, roles and expiry, and a signature. It is only encoded, not encrypted, so no secrets go inside. The API validates the signature with the identity provider's public key, then checks the issuer, audience and expiry. If all are good, it trusts the claims without calling the server.
cards.k: jwt, json web token, claims, signature, token validation, bearer, token, access token, refresh token

cards.q: Explain the OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect authorization code flow with PKCE.
cards.h: Code is a cloakroom ticket; only the person with the matching stub (verifier) gets the coat.
s: The app redirects the user to the identity provider with a code challenge, which is a hash of a random secret. The user logs in there, and the provider redirects back with a short-lived authorization code. The app exchanges the code plus the original secret for tokens. PKCE makes sure a stolen code is useless. OpenID Connect adds an ID token that tells the app who the user is.
cards.k: oauth, openid connect, oidc, authorization code flow, pkce, sso, auth, authentication, authorization, login

cards.q: Why is logout hard with tokens, and how did you fix token-based logout?
cards.h: Logout must take the wristband back, not just say goodbye.
s: JWTs are checked without calling a server, so a token keeps working after logout until it expires. In [2024] a security review found tokens in one module still working [60 minutes] after logout. I reduced access tokens to [15 minutes], revoked refresh tokens on the server, and added a denylist of token ids in ElastiCache that is checked on every request, which costs about [1 millisecond]. Old tokens were rejected immediately.
cards.k: jwt logout, token revocation, denylist, jti, elasticache, story

cards.q: What causes 'request header too long' with SSO cookies, and how did you fix it?
cards.h: Do not carry your whole wardrobe in your pocket; carry the locker key.
s: Browsers send all cookies with every request, and servers limit header size, about [16 KB] in our setup. Our SSO cookie had many group and role claims, so users in many groups got a 400 "request header too long" error. I moved the auth ticket to the server side with ITicketStore, so the cookie only holds a key, and loaded study permissions per request with caching. The cookie went from about [13 KB to under 1 KB].
cards.k: sso cookie, request header too long, iticketstore, cookie size, story, auth, authentication, authorization, login, oauth, oidc, sso

cards.q: What is reverse tabnabbing?
cards.h: Never let the new tab hold the remote control of the old tab.
s: Reverse tabnabbing happens when a link opens a new tab with target blank, and the new page uses window.opener to change the original tab to a fake login page. The fix is adding rel noopener noreferrer to those links, which modern browsers also do by default now. I fixed this on about [40] links in our application after a security scan.

cards.q: Which OWASP Top 10 risks matter most for APIs and how do you prevent them?
cards.h: A-I-C-M: Access, Injection, Crypto, Misconfig.
s: For APIs, the biggest one is broken object-level authorization, where a user changes an id and sees someone else's data, so I check access to each object, not just the endpoint. Then broken authentication, injection, excessive data exposure and missing rate limits. I prevent them with per-resource checks, parameterized queries, response DTOs instead of entities, rate limiting and security tests.

cards.q: XSS vs CSRF?
cards.h: XSS = intruder inside the house; CSRF = forged letter signed with your name.
s: XSS is when an attacker gets their script to run in our page, for example through unescaped user input, so it can steal data from the user's session. CSRF is when another site tricks the user's browser into sending a request to our site with their cookies. For XSS, I encode output and use a Content Security Policy. For CSRF, I use SameSite cookies and anti-forgery tokens.

cards.q: How do you manage secrets?
cards.h: Secrets live in a vault, not under the doormat.
s: Secrets never go in code, config files in Git or logs. We store them in AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, encrypted with KMS, and services read them at runtime using their IAM role, so no keys are hard-coded. Access is limited to the services that need each secret, and we rotate them. Locally, developers use user secrets.

cards.q: What makes a good tool definition for an AI agent?
cards.h: Tools are written for a new colleague who reads nothing but the label.

cards.q: What prompt engineering techniques do you use?
cards.h: R-C-G-F: Role, Context, Goal, Format.
s: I give clear context and a role, describe the exact task and the output format I want, and include examples when format matters. For complex work I ask it to plan first and go step by step. cards.q: Explain RAG (retrieval-augmented generation).
cards.h: RAG = open-book exam: find the right page, then answer.

Instead of relying only on what the model learned, we first search our own documents for the relevant parts, using embeddings and a vector search, and give those parts to the model with the question. So answers are based on current, private information, and can cite their sources. We built a [runbook assistant] this way.

Claude Code and Cursor agents do this with coding tools, and AutoGen lets several agents work together. Our deployment agent does this with our MCP tools, with humans approving controlled steps.

cards.q: Monolith vs microservices?
cards.h: Monolith = one big ship; microservices = a fleet of boats that need radios.

Microservices split the system into small services that own their data and deploy independently, which helps big teams and scaling, but adds network failures, data consistency and operations work. I'd start with a well-structured modular monolith and split only where there's a clear need.

I'd build a service that takes a randomization request with an idempotency key, uses a pre-generated, blinded randomization list per study, and assigns the next slot in a strongly consistent transaction. cards.q: Design drug supply and shipment tracking.
cards.h: Stock drops, rule fires, shipment travels, vendor confirms.

A shipment service creates shipments and sends them to depots and couriers through APIs or SFTP files. cards.q: Design a scalable CSV bulk import for clinical study data.
cards.h: Upload, Queue, Parse, Validate, Write, Report.
s: The client uploads the file to S3 with a presigned URL, and the API creates an import job and returns 202 with a job id. A worker streams the rows, validates format and business rules, and collects errors per row. Valid data is written in batches inside a transaction, all or nothing. The user sees progress and an error report, every import is audited, and a file hash stops duplicate imports.

cards.q: What is the API gateway pattern and backend-for-frontend?
cards.h: Gateway = front desk; BFF = a personal assistant for each client.
s: An API gateway is a single entry point in front of many services. It handles routing, authentication, rate limiting and logging, so each service doesn't repeat that. Backend-for-frontend means a separate small gateway for each type of client, like web or mobile, shaped exactly for what that client needs, so the front end makes fewer calls.

cards.q: Explain the CAP theorem.
cards.h: When the phone line is cut: wait for confirmation (C) or answer anyway (A).
s: The CAP theorem says that when the network splits, a distributed system has to choose between consistency, meaning everyone sees the latest data, and availability, meaning every request gets an answer. You can't have both during a partition. So for things like randomization I choose consistency, and for things like notifications or reports I accept eventual consistency to stay available.

cards.q: What is the saga pattern?
cards.h: Saga = travel booking: if the hotel fails, cancel the flight.
s: A saga handles a business process that spans several services, where one database transaction isn't possible. It is a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event that triggers the next step. If a step fails, compensating actions undo the earlier steps, like cancelling a reservation. It can be choreographed through events, or orchestrated by one coordinator service.
cards.k: saga pattern, distributed transactions, compensation, orchestration, choreography

cards.q: Design an audit trail for a GxP system.
cards.h: Audit trail = CCTV for data: always on, never edited.
s: In GxP, the audit trail must record who did what, when and why, with old and new values, for every change to regulated data. I'd write audit records in the same transaction as the change, make them append-only so nobody can edit or delete them, use server time in UTC, and record the reason for change. It must be easy to report on for auditors.

cards.q: How would you design rate limiting?
cards.h: Token bucket: coins refill steadily; each request spends one.
s: I'd first decide the key, like per user, per API key or per IP, and the limit for each. Then pick an algorithm: token bucket allows short bursts, sliding window is smoother. For one server, ASP.NET Core's built-in rate limiter is enough. Across many servers I'd keep counters in Redis or use the API gateway. Rejected calls return 429 with a Retry-After header.

cards.q: Explain IQVIA IRT to someone non-technical.
cards.h: IRT = fair dealer + pharmacy stock manager for clinical trials.
s: Let me explain it with a simple picture. When a new medicine is tested, thousands of patients in hospitals around the world take part. Each patient is randomly given either the new medicine or a comparison treatment, and nobody, not the doctor and not the patient, should know which one. That's what keeps the trial fair.

IRT is the system that makes that random choice fairly and secretly. When a site enrols a patient, IRT decides the treatment group and tells the site which numbered drug kit to give, so the kit number hides what's inside. It also acts like an automatic stock manager: it watches the stock at every hospital, sends shipments from depots before they run out, and tracks those shipments. It also supports electronic consent.

Because mistakes here can affect patient safety and the trial results, it's a regulated, GxP system. Every change we make is tested, validated and approved, and every action is recorded in an audit trail.

cards.q: Memory keeps growing in a .NET service until it restarts. How do you investigate?

s: One of our ECS workers grew [about 150 MB a day] and was killed every [three days] or so. I took memory snapshots with dotnet-gcdump a few hours apart and compared them. The cause was a static dictionary caching study configuration for every version, with nothing ever removed. I replaced it with IMemoryCache with a size limit and a [30-minute] sliding expiry, and load tested overnight. Memory has stayed flat since.

cards.q: What was the most challenging project you worked on?

cards.q: Tell me about a technical decision you made.
cards.h: Preview first, then all or nothing.
s: A decision I'm proud of was the design of our CSV bulk import for clinical study data.

The situation was that study teams wanted to upload large CSV files instead of entering data one record at a time. The key choice was: if some rows are bad, do we save the good rows, a partial import, or nothing at all?

I owned the design, so I weighed both options. Partial imports feel friendlier, but in a GxP system they leave a study half-configured, they make rollback and the audit trail messy, and users have to work out what got saved. All-or-nothing is safer, but frustrating if users only find errors at the end.

So I proposed a two-step design: first a validate-only preview that checks every row and shows all errors with row numbers, and then an all-or-nothing save in one transaction, but only once the file is clean. I walked the BA and the QA lead through the trade-off and we agreed on it.

The result: it's live in production, users fix every error before saving, and we've never had a half-imported study. I learned that the best decision often combines both options. I can go into the technical design too.

cards.q: Tell me about a time you improved an existing system.
cards.h: Swap the plug, not the wiring.
s: A good example is our SFTP integration for vendor file exchange.

The situation was that all our vendor file transfers were tied to one SFTP library, ComponentPro. In [2024] a depot vendor hardened their server security, and our connection broke. Because the library calls were spread across the code, switching libraries was risky.
My task was to fix it, and to make sure a library change would never touch business code again.

I introduced a common ISftpClient interface for connect, upload, download and list, with a factory that picks the provider for each vendor from configuration. I added a base class for the shared parts like retries, timeouts and logging. Then I implemented three providers behind it, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, and moved vendors over one at a time by configuration, verifying each one in UAT first.
The result was that Rebex went to production with [no failed transfers caused by the switch], no business code changed, and a future library change is now one class plus a config entry.
It's a nice real example of the open-closed principle and the strategy pattern. I'm happy to explain how I tested it.

cards.q: What are the main OOP principles?
cards.h: A PIE: Abstraction, Polymorphism, Inheritance, Encapsulation.
s: The four main OOP principles are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.

Encapsulation means an object keeps its data private and changes it only through its own methods, so it protects its rules. Abstraction means exposing what something does and hiding how it does it, usually through an interface. Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend the behaviour of a base class. And polymorphism means one interface, many implementations, where the right method is chosen at runtime.

They work best together. In my SFTP integration component, business code depends on an ISftpClient interface, which is abstraction. Three providers, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, implement it, which is polymorphism, since the caller just calls UploadAsync and configuration decides which one runs. They inherit shared retry and logging logic from a base class, which is inheritance. And each provider keeps its connection details private, which is encapsulation.
In practice I prefer composition over deep inheritance trees. I can go deeper into any of the four.
cards.k: oop, object oriented programming, four pillars, principles, object oriented, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction

cards.q: Explain encapsulation.
cards.h: Capsule: only the pill's surface is visible.
s: Encapsulation means bundling an object's data with the methods that change it, and hiding the internal state, so the object can protect its own rules.

In C# that means private fields, properties with private setters where needed, and public methods that enforce business rules. The outside world can only ask the object to do something; it can't put it into an invalid state directly. The benefit is that the rules live in one place, so the data stays valid and the code is safer to change later, because callers don't depend on the internals.

A real example is a shipment in our system. Instead of a public Status property anyone can set, the Shipment class has methods like MarkDispatched and MarkDelivered. MarkDelivered checks that the shipment was actually dispatched first, and records the time. If someone tries to deliver a cancelled shipment, it throws a clear domain exception. In a GxP system that's important, because every state change must be valid and auditable.
I can explain how this relates to rich versus anaemic domain models if that helps.
cards.k: encapsulation, oop, private fields, data hiding, object oriented, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction

cards.q: Explain inheritance.
cards.h: The child gets the parent's toolbox.
s: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend the behaviour of another class, called the base class. It models an "is-a" relationship; for example, a Rebex SFTP client is an SFTP client.

In C#, a class can inherit from only one base class, but it can implement many interfaces. The derived class gets the base members, can add its own, and can override virtual methods to change behaviour. It's powerful for sharing real code, but it creates tight coupling, because changes in the base class ripple into every child. Deep hierarchies also become hard to understand.

So I use it carefully. In our SFTP component, an abstract SftpClientBase class holds the common retry, timeout and logging logic, and each provider class inherits it and only implements the library-specific connect, upload and download. That removed a lot of duplication.
But when the relationship is really "has-a", or behaviour varies a lot, I prefer composition, injecting a collaborator instead of inheriting. I can talk about when I'd avoid inheritance if you like.
cards.k: inheritance, oop, base class, derived class

cards.q: Explain polymorphism.
cards.h: Same remote, different TVs.
s: Polymorphism means "one interface, many forms". The same method call behaves differently depending on the actual object behind it.

In C# there are two kinds. Runtime polymorphism happens through virtual and override methods, or through interfaces: the method that runs is decided at runtime based on the real type of the object. Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading, where the compiler picks a method by its parameters. Runtime polymorphism is the important one for design, because it lets code depend on an abstraction and lets new behaviour plug in without changing the caller.

My real example is the SFTP integration. The business code calls UploadAsync on an ISftpClient. Depending on the vendor's configuration, the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro implementation runs, and the calling code has no idea which one. When we added Rebex, nothing in the callers changed.
It also makes testing easy, because in unit tests I just pass a mock that implements the same interface. I can explain how dependency injection uses this too.
cards.k: polymorphism, oop, virtual, override, interfaces, object oriented, encapsulation, inheritance, abstraction

cards.q: Explain abstraction.
cards.h: Steering wheel, not engine internals.
s: Abstraction means showing only what the user of a class needs to know, and hiding the complex details of how it works.

In C#, we usually express abstraction with interfaces and abstract classes. They describe the essential contract, the operations and their meaning, while the implementation details stay inside. It's slightly different from encapsulation: encapsulation is about protecting an object's data, while abstraction is about modelling a simple concept that hides complexity. Good abstractions make code easier to use, easier to test and easier to change.

For example, our ISftpClient interface only exposes a few things: connect, upload, download and list files. Behind it, each library deals with its own complexity, like different authentication APIs, key formats, timeouts and error types. Business code just thinks "send this file to the vendor", and doesn't care about any of that.

The trap is creating abstractions too early, or leaking details, like exposing library-specific exceptions through the interface. I mapped all provider errors to our own exception types to avoid that. I can show the interface design if useful.
cards.k: abstraction, oop, interface, hiding complexity

cards.q: Class vs object?
cards.h: Cookie cutter vs cookie.
s: A class is the blueprint, and an object is an actual instance created from that blueprint.

The class defines the type: what data it holds through fields and properties, and what it can do through methods. It's written once in code. An object is created at runtime with new, it has its own copy of the data in memory, and you can create as many objects from one class as you need. Changing one object's data doesn't affect the others, unless they share static members, which belong to the class itself rather than to any one object.

For example, Shipment is a class in our code. It defines properties like ShipmentId, Status and Destination, and methods like MarkDispatched. When EF Core loads ten shipments from the database, it creates ten Shipment objects, each with its own id and status.
A simple analogy is the plan of a house versus actual houses built from that plan. I can also explain how classes differ from records and structs.
cards.k: class, object, instance, oop

cards.q: Method overloading vs overriding?
cards.h: Overload = more options; override = replace.
s: Both let one method name have multiple versions, but they work at different times.

Overloading means having several methods with the same name but different parameters in the same class, for example a Log method that takes a string, and another that takes a string and an exception. The compiler picks the right one at compile time based on the arguments, so it's compile-time polymorphism. The return type alone isn't enough to overload.

Overriding means a derived class provides its own version of a virtual or abstract method from the base class, with the same signature. The decision is made at runtime, based on the actual object, even if you call it through a base-class reference. That's runtime polymorphism.

A real example: in our SFTP providers, the base class has a virtual method for building connection settings, and the Rebex provider overrides it to add its own key handling. Separately, we have overloaded upload methods, one taking a file path and one taking a stream.
I can also explain new versus override, which is a related trap.
cards.k: overloading, overriding, polymorphism, compile time, runtime

cards.q: virtual vs override?
cards.h: Virtual = may be replaced; override = replaced.
s: The virtual keyword is used on a base-class method to say derived classes are allowed to replace it. The override keyword is used in the derived class to actually replace it.

When you call a virtual method, the runtime looks at the actual type of the object, not the type of the variable. So even if I hold the object through a base-class reference, the derived override runs. Without virtual, a method can't be overridden at all; C# methods are non-virtual by default, which is a deliberate design choice for performance and safety. An override can call the base version with base dot method name, and it can be marked sealed to stop further overriding.

In our SFTP component, the base class has a virtual method that builds connection options with sensible defaults. The Rebex provider overrides it, calls the base version first, and then adds its specific settings. That way the shared defaults live in one place.
Abstract methods are similar but have no body, so derived classes must override them. I can explain the difference between override and new as well.
cards.k: virtual, override, polymorphism, inheritance

cards.q: new vs override, and what is method hiding?
cards.h: Override = real replacement; new = a disguise.
s: Override and new both put a method with the same name in a derived class, but they behave very differently.

Override replaces a virtual method. Whichever reference you use, base type or derived type, the derived version runs, because it's decided at runtime by the actual object. That's normal polymorphism. The new keyword hides the base method instead, which is called method hiding. Then the version that runs depends on the declared type of the variable: through a base-class reference the base version runs, and through a derived reference the new version runs. So the same object can behave differently depending on how you hold it.
That's confusing and a common source of bugs, so I avoid it. If you forget both keywords, the compiler warns you that you're hiding a member, and in our projects we treat warnings as errors in CI.
The only legitimate use I've seen is when a base class you don't control adds a member with the same name as yours. I can show a small code example if you like.
cards.k: new keyword, method hiding, override, inheritance

cards.q: What is a sealed class, and a sealed method?
cards.h: Sealed = end of the family line.
s: A sealed class is a class that can't be inherited from. A sealed method is an override that can't be overridden again by classes further down the hierarchy.

Sealing communicates design intent: this class wasn't designed for extension, so nobody should depend on its internals by subclassing it. It also prevents subtle bugs where a subclass breaks the class's assumptions. There's a small performance benefit too, because the JIT can devirtualise calls on sealed types. The string class is a well-known example of a sealed class. A sealed method is useful when you've overridden something carefully and want to lock that behaviour down.

In our code, we seal classes by default when they aren't meant to be inherited, which is most service classes, handlers and DTOs, and some analyzers even suggest it. If later we really need extension, we usually add an interface rather than unsealing.
For example, our concrete SFTP providers are sealed, while the shared base class is abstract, so the hierarchy is exactly one level deep. I can explain how that keeps the design simple.
cards.k: sealed class, sealed method, inheritance

cards.q: Stack vs heap?
cards.h: Stack = sticky notes on your desk; heap = warehouse with a cleaner.
s: The stack and the heap are two areas of memory that .NET uses in different ways.

The stack is per thread. It stores method call frames: parameters, local variables and return addresses. It works last-in, first-out, so it's extremely fast, and the memory is freed automatically when a method returns. The heap is shared memory where objects created with new live, mostly reference types. Objects on the heap stay until the garbage collector finds nothing references them.
