A common misconception is that value types always live on the stack. Actually, a value type lives where it's declared. A local int is on the stack, but an int field inside a class object is on the heap, as part of that object. And boxing moves a value type onto the heap.

In practice this matters for performance. Fewer heap allocations means less GC work. For example, when tuning CSV parsing, using Span of T to slice strings without allocating new ones reduced GC pressure noticeably. I can explain how the GC cleans up the heap if useful.
cards.k: stack, heap, memory, value types, reference types

cards.q: What is boxing and unboxing?
cards.h: Boxing = putting a coin in a gift box.
s: Boxing is when a value type, like an int or a struct, is wrapped inside an object on the heap. Unboxing is extracting the value back out with an explicit cast.

Boxing happens implicitly, for example when you assign an int to an object variable, put it in an old non-generic collection like ArrayList, or call an interface method on a struct through the interface. Each box is a new heap allocation, and it creates extra work for the garbage collector. Unboxing needs a cast to the exact type, or you get an InvalidCastException.

In normal business code it rarely matters, but in hot paths, like processing thousands of CSV rows or logging in a tight loop, it adds up. The fix is generics: List of int instead of ArrayList, generic methods instead of object parameters, and structured logging templates, which avoid boxing in newer .NET versions.
So my rule is simply: use generic collections and APIs, and watch allocations in a profiler when performance matters. I can talk about how I measure allocations if helpful.
cards.k: boxing, unboxing, value types, performance, generics

cards.q: What is IDisposable, the using statement and the using declaration?
cards.h: using = auto-close the tap.
s: IDisposable is the interface for objects that hold resources the garbage collector doesn't manage, like file handles, database connections, network streams or SFTP sessions. Its Dispose method releases them deterministically, right away, instead of waiting for the GC.

The using statement is the safe way to call Dispose. You write using, create the object, and put the code in a block; Dispose is called automatically at the end of the block, even if an exception is thrown, because it compiles into try-finally. The newer using declaration, from C# 8, is just using var x equals something, without braces, and it disposes at the end of the current scope, which means less nesting. For async cleanup there's IAsyncDisposable with await using.

In our SFTP component, every connection is wrapped in a using, so sessions are always closed, even when a transfer fails halfway. With dependency injection, the container disposes scoped and transient services at the end of the request, so I don't dispose injected services myself.
I can explain the full dispose pattern with finalisers if needed.
cards.k: idisposable, using statement, using declaration, dispose, resources, garbage collection, gc, memory

cards.q: const vs readonly vs static readonly?
cards.h: const = carved in stone; readonly = set at birth.
s: All three make a value unchangeable, but at different times and in different ways.

A const is a compile-time constant. It's implicitly static, and its value is copied into every assembly that uses it. So it must be a simple literal, like a number or string, and if you change it, every calling assembly needs recompiling, otherwise they keep the old value. A readonly field can be set only in its declaration or in the constructor, so each object can have a different value, decided at runtime. A static readonly field is set once for the whole type at runtime, and it can hold any object, like a TimeSpan, a Regex or a list.

My rule is: const only for values that are truly fixed forever, like a header name. Static readonly for shared defaults and objects, like a compiled Regex for validating study codes. Readonly for injected dependencies in constructors, which is the most common use in our services.
And for configuration that can change between environments, I use the Options pattern, not constants at all. Happy to explain that further.
cards.k: const, readonly, static readonly, constants

cards.q: What are ref, out and in?
cards.h: ref = two-way, out = return slot, in = look but don't touch.
s: ref, out and in are all ways to pass an argument by reference, instead of passing a copy.

With ref, the variable must be initialised before the call, and the method can read and change it, and the caller sees the change. With out, the method must assign a value before it returns, and the caller doesn't need to initialise it. The classic example is int.TryParse, which returns a bool for success and gives the parsed number through an out parameter. With in, you pass a read-only reference: the method can't change it, and the point is to avoid copying a large struct.

In everyday code I use out mostly for Try-pattern methods. For example, our CSV validator has a TryParseRow method that returns true or false and gives the parsed row as an out parameter, so we avoid exceptions for normal validation failures.
I use ref and in rarely, mostly in performance-sensitive code. Usually returning a result object or a tuple is clearer. I can show an example if useful.
cards.k: ref, out, in, parameters, by reference

cards.q: What are nullable reference types?
cards.h: Null gets a warning label.
s: Nullable reference types are a C# 8 feature that makes null-safety part of the type system.

Once you enable it in the project, a normal reference type like string means "should never be null", and you mark something that can be null with a question mark, like string question mark. The compiler then does flow analysis and warns you if you might dereference something that could be null without checking, or if you assign null to a non-nullable reference. It doesn't change runtime behaviour, but it moves a whole class of NullReferenceException bugs to compile time.

All our newer IRT projects have it enabled, and we treat the warnings seriously in code review. It also makes APIs self-documenting: if a method returns Shipment question mark, callers know they must handle the not-found case.
When enabling it on an older project, I do it file by file, so the team isn't hit with hundreds of warnings at once. I can talk about how we rolled it out.
cards.k: nullable reference types, null safety, null reference exception

cards.q: What is pattern matching?
cards.h: Ask the shape, then act.
s: Pattern matching lets me test the shape or type of a value and extract data from it in a single, readable step.

In C# there are several forms. The is keyword with type patterns, like if x is Shipment s. Switch expressions, which return a value. Property patterns, which check properties, like a status equal to Dispatched. Relational patterns like greater than 10, logical patterns with and, or and not, and list patterns. It replaces long if-else chains and casting code, and the compiler can warn you if a switch doesn't cover every case.

In our code, for example, I use a switch expression on shipment status to decide the next allowed status, and a property pattern to calculate shipping priority, like express shipments first, then heavy ones, then the rest. It also helps when handling messages: a switch on the message type routes each event to the right handler.
It makes business rules much easier to read and review. I can write a small example if you like.
cards.k: pattern matching, switch expression, is, c#

cards.q: What are extension methods?
cards.h: Bolt-on methods without touching the class.
s: An extension method is a static method that you can call as if it were an instance method on an existing type, without modifying that type.

You write it in a static class, and you put the this keyword before the first parameter, which is the type you're extending. Then it appears in IntelliSense on that type. It's resolved at compile time, so it can't access private members, and a real instance method with the same signature always wins. All of LINQ, like Where and Select, is built as extension methods on IEnumerable and IQueryable.

I use them for small, focused helpers. For example, a ToPagedResultAsync method on IQueryable, so every list API pages in the same way. And for clean dependency injection registration, like services.AddSftpProviders and app.UseCorrelationId, so Program.cs reads like a story instead of fifty lines of setup.
The rule I follow is not to overuse them for business logic, because it hides where behaviour lives. I can show how we organise registration extensions.
cards.k: extension methods, static, linq, helpers

cards.q: What is an enum?
cards.h: Enum = named numbers.
s: An enum is a set of named constants backed by an integer type. For example, ShipmentStatus with Created, Dispatched, Delivered and Cancelled.

It makes code readable and type-safe compared with magic numbers or strings. The compiler stops you passing a random int where a ShipmentStatus is expected, and switch expressions can warn about missing cases. With the Flags attribute, values can be combined bitwise, like permissions. One thing to remember is that any integer can be cast to an enum, even if it isn't defined, so values coming from APIs or files must be validated, for example with Enum.IsDefined.

We also decide deliberately how to store them. EF Core stores enums as int by default, but for audit-friendly tables we sometimes store them as strings, so the data is readable, and so reordering the enum can't silently change meaning. In APIs we serialise them as strings with JsonStringEnumConverter.
I can talk about when I'd replace an enum with a proper class instead.
cards.k: enum, constants, flags

cards.q: What is deadlock in async code?
cards.h: Holding the door while waiting for someone who needs that door.
s: An async deadlock happens when code blocks on async work, for example by calling .Result or .Wait() on a task, in an environment that has a synchronization context.

In classic ASP.NET or desktop UI apps, the synchronization context means the continuation after an await must resume on the original thread. If that same thread is blocked waiting on .Result, the task can never finish, because it needs the thread that's waiting for it. So both wait forever. ASP.NET Core doesn't have that synchronization context, so you don't get this exact deadlock, but blocking still causes thread-pool starvation under load, where requests pile up and the API slows to a crawl.
The fix is async all the way: await instead of blocking, and make callers async too. In library code we use ConfigureAwait(false) so it's safe in any environment.
I've seen the starvation version in practice: an old helper that called .Result on an HTTP call caused timeouts under load, and making it async fixed it. I can explain how I spotted it.
cards.k: async deadlock, result, wait, synchronization context, async all the way, async, await, task, asynchronous, valuetask, configureawait

cards.q: What is ConfigureAwait?
cards.h: false = any thread will do.
s: ConfigureAwait controls where the code after an await continues running. ConfigureAwait(false) says "I don't need to come back to the original synchronization context; any thread-pool thread is fine."

This matters in environments that have a synchronization context, like WinForms, WPF or classic ASP.NET. There, by default, the continuation is posted back to the original UI or request thread. That costs a context switch, and if someone blocks on the task with .Result, it can deadlock, because the thread the continuation needs is the one that's blocked. With ConfigureAwait(false), the continuation runs on the pool, so it's a bit faster and avoids that deadlock.

ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so in application code like controllers and services it makes no practical difference, and we don't clutter our code with it. But in reusable libraries, which might be used from any kind of app, I still add ConfigureAwait(false) to every await. For example, our shared SFTP library does that.
The real fix for deadlocks is still async all the way. I can explain that in more detail if useful.
cards.k: configureawait, async, synchronization context, libraries, await, task, asynchronous, valuetask

cards.q: What is LINQ?
cards.h: SQL-like questions in C#.
s: LINQ stands for Language Integrated Query. It's a set of query operators built into C#, like Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy, Join, Any and Sum, that work the same way on many data sources.

Over in-memory collections, which are IEnumerable, LINQ runs as normal C# code using delegates. Over IQueryable, like an EF Core DbSet, it builds an expression tree that the provider translates into SQL, so the work happens in the database. You can write it with method syntax, which is most common, or query syntax that looks like SQL. Most operators use deferred execution, so the query only runs when you enumerate it or call ToList.

I use LINQ every day. The important skill is knowing where each part runs. For example, on our shipment search I make sure the filters and paging are translated to SQL, and I check the generated SQL in logs, so we don't accidentally pull thousands of rows into memory or trigger client-side evaluation.
LINQ makes data code short and readable. I can explain IEnumerable versus IQueryable in more detail.
cards.k: linq, query, where, select, ef core, ienumerable, iqueryable, deferred execution

cards.q: IEnumerable vs ICollection vs IList?
cards.h: Walk, count, index.
s: These three collection interfaces build on each other, each one adding more abilities.

IEnumerable is the simplest. It only lets you loop over items, forward only, and it supports deferred execution. ICollection adds Count, Add, Remove, Contains and Clear, so you know the size and can change the contents. IList adds access by index, like getting item number five, plus Insert and RemoveAt. There are also read-only versions, IReadOnlyCollection and IReadOnlyList, which give Count and indexing without allowing changes.

My rule for API design is: accept the smallest interface you need, and return the most useful read-only type. If a method only loops over items, it takes IEnumerable, so callers can pass a list, an array or a query. If it needs the count up front, it takes IReadOnlyCollection. And methods usually return IReadOnlyList, so callers can index but can't modify our internal list.
One caution: accepting IEnumerable and enumerating it twice can run an expensive query twice. I can explain that trap if useful.
cards.k: ienumerable, icollection, ilist, collections, interfaces, linq, iqueryable, deferred execution

cards.q: First vs FirstOrDefault, Single vs SingleOrDefault?
cards.h: Single = there can be only one.
s: These four LINQ methods all return one element, but they behave differently when there are zero or multiple matches.

First returns the first matching element and throws if there's none. FirstOrDefault returns the first match, or the default value, which is null for reference types, if there's none. Single expects exactly one match: it throws if there are none, and also throws if there's more than one. SingleOrDefault allows zero, returning default, but still throws if there's more than one. In SQL terms, Single fetches up to two rows to check for duplicates, while First fetches one.

So the choice expresses intent. I use Single or SingleOrDefault when looking up by something that must be unique, like a study code or a kit number, because if duplicates exist, that's a data bug and I want to know about it immediately rather than silently picking one. I use FirstOrDefault when "not found" is normal, usually with an OrderBy so "first" is well-defined.
Using First without an order is a subtle bug, because the database can return rows in any order. I can give more examples if helpful.
cards.k: first, firstordefault, single, singleordefault, linq

cards.q: Any() vs Count()?
cards.h: Any = is anybody home? Count = take a census.
s: Any and Count can both tell you whether there are items, but Any is the right tool for checking existence.

Any stops as soon as it finds one matching item, so it's cheap no matter how big the data is. Count has to go through every item to count them, unless the collection already knows its size. In EF Core, Any translates into an EXISTS query, which SQL Server can stop at the first row, while Count translates to SELECT COUNT, which has to count every matching row. On a big table that difference is huge.
Note that the Count property on a List or an array is different, it's already stored, so reading it is free. The issue is the Count method on queries and lazy sequences.

So in our code, a check like "does this study already have an active import" is written with AnyAsync, never CountAsync greater than zero. Code analyzers even flag that pattern now. I can explain how to verify the generated SQL if useful.
cards.k: any, count, linq, exists, performance

cards.q: What is a closure in C#?
cards.h: The lambda packs a lunchbox from home.
s: A closure is a lambda or local function that captures variables from the code around it, and keeps using them even after that outer method has finished.

Under the hood, the C# compiler moves captured variables into a hidden class, and both the outer method and the lambda share that object. That's why the lambda sees the latest value of the variable, not a copy from when it was created. This is very useful, for example in LINQ filters that use a method parameter, or in callbacks.

There are two classic pitfalls. First, capturing a loop variable: in old C# a foreach loop shared one variable, so all the lambdas saw the last value. Modern C# fixed foreach, but a for loop index can still surprise you. Second, a closure can keep a large object alive longer than expected, for example an event handler lambda that captures a big service, which becomes a memory leak if it's never unsubscribed.
In performance-sensitive code, I also watch for closures allocating on every call, and use static lambdas where possible. I can show the loop-variable bug in code if you like.
cards.k: closure, lambda, captured variables

cards.q: Explain the Liskov Substitution Principle with an example.
cards.h: Swap the battery brand; the torch still works.
s: The Liskov Substitution Principle says that objects of a derived type must work anywhere the base type is expected, without the caller getting surprises. A subtype can add behaviour, but it must keep the base type's promises.

The textbook violation is Square inheriting from Rectangle. If code sets the width of a rectangle and expects the height to stay the same, a Square breaks that expectation. A more realistic violation is a read-only repository that inherits a Save method and throws NotSupportedException. The fix there is to split the interface, not to throw.

In my SFTP component, Liskov was a real design goal. All three providers implement ISftpClient, and they must behave the same way for the caller: same behaviour when a file already exists, same timeout handling, and every failure surfaces as our own SftpTransferException, never a silent failure or a library-specific exception. I enforced that with a shared set of contract tests that every provider must pass.
That's why we could switch a vendor from ComponentPro to Rebex with only a configuration change. I can explain the contract tests if useful.
cards.k: liskov substitution principle, lsp, solid, single responsibility, open closed, liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion

cards.q: Explain Interface Segregation with an example.
cards.h: Small menus, not one giant menu.
s: The Interface Segregation Principle says clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't use. So it's better to have several small, focused interfaces than one big "fat" interface.

When an interface is too large, every implementer must implement methods it doesn't need, often by throwing, and every consumer gets access to more than it should. Changes to unrelated methods also force recompiles and test changes everywhere. Microsoft follows this principle with IReadOnlyList being separate from IList.

A practical example from our code: instead of one big IShipmentRepository with read, update and delete, we can split it into an IShipmentReader for queries and an IShipmentWriter for commands. A reporting service only takes the reader, so it physically can't modify shipments, which is nice in a GxP system, and its unit tests only need to mock two or three methods. Similarly, in the MCP server, tools are grouped by capability, so read-only tools don't get access to deployment operations.
The balance is not to go too far, with one-method interfaces everywhere. I can talk about how I find the right size.
cards.k: interface segregation principle, isp, solid, single responsibility, open closed, liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion

cards.q: Explain Dependency Inversion with an example.
cards.h: Plug into the socket, not the power plant.
s: The Dependency Inversion Principle says high-level business code should depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level classes. Both sides depend on the interface, so the dependency direction is inverted.

Without it, a business service creates its infrastructure directly, like new-ing up a specific SFTP library. Then the business logic is tied to that library, changing it means editing business code, and you can't unit test the service without a real server.

In our vendor file exchange, the VendorExchangeService depends only on ISftpClient, which is defined alongside the business logic. The infrastructure layer contains the Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro implementations, and Program.cs registers them in the ASP.NET Core DI container. So the business code never references Rebex at all. When a vendor needed a different library, it was a configuration change, and in unit tests I simply inject a mock ISftpClient with Moq.
Dependency injection is the mechanism, and dependency inversion is the design principle behind it. I can explain how this shapes our project structure, if useful.
cards.k: dependency inversion principle, dip, solid, abstractions, single responsibility, open closed, liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion

cards.q: Why did you choose an interface?
cards.h: Interface = contract; base class = shared code.
s: I chose an interface for our SFTP integration for three concrete reasons.

First, I needed several interchangeable implementations behind one contract. We had three libraries, Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro, and different vendors needed different ones. An interface let business code depend on ISftpClient and stay completely unaware of which library ran. Second, testability. With an interface I can inject a mock with Moq in unit tests, so testing the file-exchange logic doesn't need a real SFTP server. Third, extensibility. Interfaces let me add decorators, like retry and logging wrappers, around any provider without touching the providers, and adding a new library is just a new class.

I also used an abstract base class, because the providers shared real code like retry policies, timeouts and logging. So the interface is the contract, and the base class is shared implementation. Callers only see the interface.
The result was that switching a vendor to Rebex was a configuration change with no business code edits. I can explain how the factory chooses the provider.
cards.k: interface, design decision, abstraction, testing

cards.q: When would you avoid inheritance?
cards.h: Has-a beats is-a when in doubt.
s: I avoid inheritance in a few situations.

First, when the relationship isn't truly "is-a". If I just want to reuse a few methods, inheritance is the wrong tool, and composition, having a collaborator, is better. Second, when behaviour varies in several independent ways. For example, transfer method and retry policy are separate concerns, and subclasses for every combination explode, so strategies or decorators work better. Third, when hierarchies get deep. A change in a base class ripples to every child, which is called the fragile base class problem. And fourth, across module or team boundaries, where others would inherit from my class and depend on its internals.

A real example: we needed retry and logging around SFTP clients. Instead of creating a RetryingRebexClient, a RetryingSshNetClient and so on, I wrote one retry decorator that wraps any ISftpClient. That's one class instead of three.
I still use inheritance where it's natural and shallow, like one abstract base class for shared provider code. I can explain composition over inheritance further if useful.
cards.k: composition over inheritance, inheritance, design

cards.q: How does garbage collection affect performance?
cards.h: Less garbage, fewer pickups.
s: Garbage collection affects performance because, while the GC runs, it has to pause or slow down application threads to find and free unused objects.

Gen 0 collections are very quick, but if the app allocates a lot of objects, they happen very often. The expensive ones are gen 2 and Large Object Heap collections, which can cause noticeable pauses and push up tail latency, like p99. So the main lever is allocation rate: the less garbage you create, the less the GC has to do. ASP.NET Core uses server GC by default, tuned for throughput, with background collection to reduce pauses.

In hot paths I reduce allocations with a few techniques: Span of T and Memory of T to slice data without copying, ArrayPool to reuse buffers, avoiding boxing, avoiding big temporary strings and LINQ chains in tight loops, and streaming large data instead of loading it whole. I measure with dotnet-counters and a profiler before and after.
For example, for our CSV import I streamed the file row by row instead of loading it all, which kept memory flat even for large files. I can explain how I'd investigate a GC problem in production.
cards.k: garbage collection, gc, performance, allocations, latency, memory, dispose, idisposable

cards.q: What happens if an exception occurs inside an async method?
cards.h: The error waits inside the Task until you await it.
s: When an exception happens inside an async method, it doesn't crash straight away. It's captured and stored inside the Task that the method returns.

When you await that task, the exception is rethrown at the await, with its original stack trace, so a normal try-catch around the await works exactly as you'd expect. But if nobody awaits the task, for example a fire-and-forget call, the exception is unobserved and effectively lost, which hides bugs. With async void methods it's worse: there's no task to hold the exception, so it's raised on the synchronization context or thread pool and can crash the whole process. That's why I only use async void for event handlers.
With Task.WhenAll, await throws the first exception, but the task's Exception property holds all of them, so I check that when I need every failure.

In our services, every async call is awaited, background work runs in a BackgroundService with its own try-catch and logging, and unhandled request exceptions go to our global exception handler. I can show how I test async exceptions with xUnit.
cards.k: async exception, task, await, async void, error handling, async, asynchronous, valuetask, configureawait, exception, problemdetails, exception handling

cards.q: What is Dependency Injection and why do we use it?
cards.h: Don't build your tools; get them handed to you.
s: Dependency injection means a class receives the objects it needs, its dependencies, from outside, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them itself with new.

In ASP.NET Core there's a built-in DI container. In Program.cs I register services with a lifetime, singleton, scoped or transient, and when a controller or service is created, the container builds it and passes in everything it needs, then disposes things at the right time.

We use it for four reasons. Loose coupling, because classes depend on interfaces, not concrete types. Testability, because in unit tests I can pass mocks instead of real databases or servers. Flexibility, because I can swap implementations through configuration. And central lifetime management, so things like DbContext are created per request and disposed automatically.

A real example: our VendorExchangeService gets an SFTP client factory, a logger and its options injected. In production the factory returns the right library for each vendor, and in unit tests I inject a mock, so I can test the retry and error logic without a real SFTP server.
I can explain the three lifetimes next if that's useful.
cards.k: dependency injection, di, ioc, constructor injection, loose coupling, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes

cards.q: What is a dependency?
cards.h: What you cannot work without.
s: A dependency is anything a class needs in order to do its job.

Typical dependencies are a repository or DbContext for data, an HttpClient for calling another service, a logger, configuration options, a message publisher, or an SFTP client. Less obvious ones are the current time and random numbers, because code that calls DateTime.Now directly is hard to test. If a class creates its dependencies itself, with new or static calls, it's tightly coupled to them: you can't swap them, and you can't test the class in isolation.
With dependency injection, those dependencies are passed in through the constructor, so the class just declares what it needs and the container provides it.

For example, our study-transfer safety guard depends on a repository to read study state, a logger, and TimeProvider for the current time. Because time is injected, in unit tests I use a fake time provider to test rules like "block transfers after the cut-off date" without waiting for real time to pass.
A good sign of too many dependencies is a long constructor, which usually means the class does too much. I can say more about that.
cards.k: dependency, di, coupling

cards.q: What is Inversion of Control, and what is an IoC container?
cards.h: The container is the factory manager.
s: Inversion of Control is a design idea where the framework controls the flow of the program and calls your code, rather than your code controlling everything. It's often summed up as "don't call us, we'll call you".

In ASP.NET Core, I don't write a main loop that reads requests. The framework receives the request, runs the middleware pipeline, creates my controller and calls the action. Object creation is also inverted: instead of my classes creating their dependencies, something else creates and supplies them. Dependency injection is the most common form of IoC.

An IoC container is the component that does that work. You register types and their lifetimes, and it builds the whole object graph, injects constructor parameters, manages singleton, scoped and transient lifetimes, and disposes objects at the right time. In .NET the built-in one is IServiceCollection for registration and IServiceProvider for resolution. Third-party ones like Autofac add features like property injection or modules.
In our services the built-in container is enough. I can explain lifetimes or how scopes work next.
cards.k: inversion of control, ioc, ioc container, di, dependency injection, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes

cards.q: Constructor injection vs property injection?
cards.h: Constructor = must-haves; property = nice-to-haves.
s: Both are ways of giving a class its dependencies, but constructor injection is the one I use almost always.

With constructor injection, dependencies are parameters of the constructor. That makes required dependencies explicit; you can't create the object without them, so it's always fully ready. The fields can be readonly, so they can't be swapped later, and it's easy to see in tests what to mock. With property injection, dependencies are set through public properties after the object is created. That hides what's required, allows half-initialised objects, and makes the dependency mutable. It's only reasonable for truly optional dependencies.
The built-in .NET container supports only constructor injection; property injection needs something like Autofac. With C# 12 primary constructors, constructor injection is also very concise.

One useful side effect: if a constructor grows to seven or eight parameters, it's a clear signal the class has too many responsibilities. I've split services for exactly that reason, for example separating CSV parsing from validation. I can talk about that refactoring if useful.
cards.k: constructor injection, property injection, di

cards.q: What is IServiceProvider?
cards.h: The vending machine for services.
s: IServiceProvider is the interface of the built-in .NET DI container. It's the object that actually resolves services, through GetService or GetRequiredService.

You register services on an IServiceCollection in Program.cs, and when the host is built, that becomes the root IServiceProvider, which holds the singletons. For each HTTP request, ASP.NET Core creates a scope, a child provider, which holds that request's scoped services like DbContext, and HttpContext.RequestServices points to it. When the request ends, the scope is disposed, along with its scoped and transient disposables.

In normal code I don't use IServiceProvider directly. I use constructor injection, because calling the provider all over the code is the service locator anti-pattern and hides dependencies. I use it in a few specific places: inside factories that pick an implementation at runtime, and in singletons or background services where I create a scope with IServiceScopeFactory to get scoped services. For example, our background message consumer creates a scope per message to get a fresh DbContext.
I can explain scope validation and captive dependencies, which relate to this.
cards.k: iserviceprovider, di container, getservice, resolve

cards.q: Which lifetimes can depend on which (Singleton, Scoped, Transient)?
cards.h: Depend only on things that live at least as long as you.
s: The rule is that a service should only depend on services that live at least as long as it does.

A singleton lives for the whole application, so it should depend only on other singletons. A scoped service lives for one request, so it can depend on scoped and singleton services. A transient is created every time, so it can depend on anything, as long as it's resolved inside a scope when it needs scoped services. A singleton can technically take a transient, but that transient then effectively becomes a singleton, which can surprise you.

The dangerous case is a singleton depending on a scoped service, like DbContext. That's called a captive dependency: the singleton holds the first request's DbContext forever, which isn't thread-safe and serves stale data. ASP.NET Core catches this in development with scope validation, which throws at startup.
When a singleton genuinely needs scoped work, like our background consumer, it injects IServiceScopeFactory and creates a scope per unit of work. I can show that pattern in code.
cards.k: di lifetimes, captive dependency, singleton, scoped, transient

cards.q: GetService() vs GetRequiredService()?
cards.h: Required = fail loudly.
s: Both resolve a service from the DI container, but they behave differently when the service isn't registered.

GetService returns null if the service isn't registered. So it's meant for optional services, where the caller handles the null case. GetRequiredService throws an InvalidOperationException with a clear message naming the missing type. So it's for services that must exist. GetRequiredService is an extension method on IServiceProvider, and there's a generic version of each.

I prefer GetRequiredService, because failing fast with a clear message is much easier to diagnose than a NullReferenceException somewhere later. With GetService, a forgotten registration can turn into a confusing null error in a completely different place. ASP.NET Core also validates the whole container at startup in development, which catches missing registrations early.

But honestly, I rarely call either one. In normal code I use constructor injection. I only call GetRequiredService in factories or after creating a scope in a background service, for example to get a fresh DbContext for each message in our consumer. I can explain why the service locator pattern is considered an anti-pattern.
cards.k: getservice, getrequiredservice, di, iserviceprovider

cards.q: How does constructor injection work in ASP.NET Core, and how are controller dependencies resolved?
cards.h: Per request: new scope, new controller, wired graph.
s: In ASP.NET Core, a controller simply declares what it needs as constructor parameters, and the framework supplies them for every request.

When a request arrives, ASP.NET Core creates a DI scope for it, available as HttpContext.RequestServices. The controller activator then creates the controller from that scope. The container looks at the constructor, chooses the one with the most parameters it can satisfy, and resolves each dependency, and their dependencies, recursively, building the whole object graph. Scoped services, like DbContext, are shared by everything in that one request. When the request ends, the scope is disposed, along with the scoped and transient disposables.
Minimal APIs work the same way but inject straight into the handler's parameters, and in controllers I can use the FromServices attribute to inject into a single action.

For example, our shipments controller takes an IShipmentService and a logger. The service takes the DbContext and a publisher. One request, one DbContext, shared by both, and disposed at the end. I can explain the lifetime rules that make this safe.
cards.k: constructor injection, controller dependencies, di, request scope

cards.q: How do you register and resolve multiple implementations of an interface?
cards.h: Many plugs: take the whole strip or ask by name.
s: The DI container lets you register several implementations of the same interface, and there are three main ways to resolve them.

First, if I inject IEnumerable of the interface, I get all registrations in the order they were added. That's perfect for a pipeline of validators or notifiers, where every one should run. Second, if I inject the interface on its own, I get the last one registered, which is how you override a default. Third, when I need one specific implementation, .NET 8 added keyed services: I register with AddKeyedScoped and a key, and inject with the FromKeyedServices attribute or resolve with GetRequiredKeyedService. Before .NET 8, I used a small factory that picks by configuration.

In our vendor exchange, each vendor's configuration names its SFTP library. Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro are registered as keyed services, and the factory resolves the right one by key. For our CSV import, a list of validators is injected as IEnumerable and each one checks a different rule.
I can show the registration code if helpful.
cards.k: multiple implementations, keyed services, ienumerable, di

cards.q: Can you manually create a scope, and when would you use IServiceScopeFactory?
cards.h: Open a meeting room when you need one.
s: Yes. You inject IServiceScopeFactory, call CreateScope, resolve the services you need from scope.ServiceProvider, and dispose the scope when the unit of work is done, usually with a using statement. There's also CreateAsyncScope for services that need async disposal.

You need this wherever there's no request scope but you need scoped services. The classic case is a BackgroundService or hosted service, which is a singleton. If it injected DbContext directly, that would be a captive dependency, one DbContext forever, which isn't thread-safe and fills up its change tracker. So instead it creates a new scope per unit of work.

In our system, the SFTP poller is a BackgroundService. On each polling run, it creates a scope, resolves the vendor exchange service and a fresh DbContext, processes the files, and disposes the scope. Our RabbitMQ consumer does the same per message. That keeps every run isolated, with clean change tracking and connections returned to the pool.
I can show the code pattern, it's only a few lines.
cards.k: iservicescopefactory, createscope, background service, scoped

cards.q: What is the service locator anti-pattern?
cards.h: Hidden dependencies are surprise bills.
s: The service locator anti-pattern is when a class pulls its dependencies from the container itself, typically by injecting IServiceProvider and calling GetService inside its methods, instead of declaring them in the constructor.

It's called an anti-pattern because it hides the real dependencies. Looking at the constructor, you can't tell what the class needs, so the API lies. Missing registrations only fail at runtime when that line runs, not at startup. And tests get harder, because you have to build or mock a whole service provider instead of just passing two mocks. It also makes it easy to resolve the wrong lifetime by accident.

There are legitimate places for it: the composition root in Program.cs, factories that pick an implementation at runtime, middleware, and background services creating scopes. Those are infrastructure code.

In business classes, I always use constructor injection. In code reviews, if I see IServiceProvider injected into a service, I ask what it needs and move that to the constructor. I can explain how this relates to testability.
cards.k: service locator, anti-pattern, di, iserviceprovider

cards.q: How would you unit test a DI-based service?
cards.h: Unit tests use new, not the container.
s: Because a DI-based service receives everything through its constructor, unit testing it is straightforward. I don't use the container at all in unit tests.

I create the class directly with new, passing mocks or fakes for its interfaces, usually with Moq, plus simple fakes like FakeTimeProvider for time or NullLogger for logging. Then I call the method and assert the outcome, like the return value or the state change, and verify only the key interactions, like "upload was called once with this file name". I avoid verifying every call, because that makes tests brittle.

For example, for the vendor exchange service, I mock ISftpClient to throw a timeout on the first call and succeed on the second, then assert that the retry worked and the transfer was logged as successful. No real SFTP server is needed.

Separately, I test the wiring. Integration tests with WebApplicationFactory replace only external services, and building the provider with ValidateOnBuild and ValidateScopes catches missing registrations and captive dependencies. I can explain the integration test setup if useful.
cards.k: unit testing, di, mocking, moq, testing, dependency injection, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes, test, unit test, integration test, xunit, mock

cards.q: Give a real DI example from your application.
cards.h: Factory picks the plug; DI hands it over.
s: A good real example is our vendor file exchange service.

The VendorExchangeService takes three things through its constructor: an ISftpClientFactory, an IOptions of SftpOptions with vendor settings, and an ILogger. It has no idea which SFTP library is actually used. The factory reads each vendor's configuration and returns the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro implementation. In Program.cs, the factory is registered as a singleton because it's stateless, the exchange service is scoped, and each SFTP client is created per transfer and disposed afterwards, so connections are never shared across threads.

Across the system we use all three lifetimes deliberately. DbContext is scoped, one per request. The RabbitMQ connection is a singleton, because connections are expensive and thread-safe, while channels are per consumer. Validators are transient, because they're light and stateless.
The benefit was real: when a vendor needed a different library, it was a configuration change, and every piece is unit tested with mocks. I can show how the factory chooses the provider.
cards.k: di example, real example, sftp, story, di, dependency injection, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes

cards.q: Why shouldn't everything be Singleton, or everything Transient?
cards.h: Right lifetime for the right job.
s: Choosing lifetimes is a trade-off, and both extremes cause problems.

Not everything can be a singleton, because one instance is shared by every thread and every request. So it must be thread-safe, and it must never hold per-request data, or one user could see another user's data. A singleton also can't safely hold scoped things like DbContext, which leads to captive dependency bugs, stale data and concurrency exceptions.

Not everything should be transient either. Creating new objects for every injection wastes allocations, expensive objects get rebuilt constantly, and you lose per-request sharing. For example, if two services in one request need the same unit of work, they need the same DbContext, which scoped gives you. Disposable transients resolved from the root also pile up until shutdown.

So my rule: singleton for stateless or thread-safe shared things, like configuration, caches, HttpClient factories and the RabbitMQ connection. Scoped for per-request state, like DbContext and the current user. Transient for light, stateless helpers, like validators. I can go through the lifetime dependency rules too.
cards.k: di lifetimes, singleton, transient, scoped, choosing lifetime

cards.q: What happens when a request ends?
cards.h: Meeting over: lights off, room cleaned.
s: When a request finishes, several things happen in a clean order.

First, the endpoint returns, and the response flows back out through the middleware pipeline in reverse order, so middleware can add headers or log the result. Then the response is completed and flushed to the client. After that, ASP.NET Core disposes the request's DI scope. That disposes every scoped service and every transient disposable created in that scope. For example, the DbContext is disposed, which returns its database connection to the pool. Finally, the HttpContext is released, and its objects can be reused for the next request.

There's also the early-end case. If the client disconnects before we finish, HttpContext.RequestAborted, the request's cancellation token, is triggered. Code that passes that token down to EF Core and HttpClient stops working instead of finishing a response nobody will read.

That's why I never keep references to scoped services, like DbContext, beyond the request, for example in a fire-and-forget task. That would use an already disposed object. I can explain how to do background work correctly instead.
cards.k: request end, dispose, scope, request lifecycle

cards.q: Who disposes Scoped and Singleton services, and how does DI handle IDisposable dependencies?
cards.h: Whoever creates it, cleans it.
s: The rule is simple: the container disposes what it creates.

Scoped services, and transient services resolved inside a scope, are disposed when that scope ends. For web requests, that's at the end of the request. Singletons the container created are disposed when the root provider is disposed, which happens at application shutdown. The container calls Dispose, or DisposeAsync for IAsyncDisposable, in reverse order of creation.

There are two gotchas. First, if I create an instance myself and register it, like AddSingleton with new MyService, the container did not create it, so it won't dispose it. I'm responsible for that. Second, if a disposable transient is resolved from the root provider, not a scope, the container keeps a reference so it can dispose it at shutdown. That means every resolution stays in memory, which is a slow memory leak.
In our background services, that's exactly why we create a scope per unit of work, so disposables like DbContext are cleaned up each time. I can explain how scope validation catches lifetime issues.
cards.k: dispose, idisposable, di, scoped, singleton, dependency injection, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes, garbage collection, gc, memory

cards.q: What is ASP.NET Core?
cards.h: Modern .NET for the web, anywhere.
s: ASP.NET Core is Microsoft's modern, open-source and cross-platform framework for building web applications, mainly web APIs, but also MVC sites, Razor Pages, real-time apps with SignalR, and gRPC services.

It's built around a few core pieces. A middleware pipeline that every request passes through. Built-in dependency injection. A flexible configuration system, from appsettings files, environment variables and secret stores. Built-in logging, and the Kestrel web server. It runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, and in containers, and it's consistently one of the fastest mainstream web frameworks in benchmarks.
Compared with the old .NET Framework ASP.NET, it's modular, you only add what you need, it isn't tied to IIS, and it gets a new version every year.

In my work, all our IRT APIs are ASP.NET Core Web APIs, running in Docker containers on AWS ECS behind an Application Load Balancer. We recently upgraded them to [.NET 10 in early 2026], which gave a [10 to 15 percent] improvement in p95 latency on [3] services. I can go into the request pipeline or hosting model next.
cards.k: asp.net core, web framework, .net

cards.q: What is Kestrel?
cards.h: Kestrel = the engine inside every ASP.NET Core app.
s: Kestrel is the web server built into ASP.NET Core. It's cross-platform, fully asynchronous, and very fast, and it supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, as well as HTTPS and WebSockets.

When an ASP.NET Core app starts, Kestrel listens on the configured ports, accepts connections, parses the HTTP request, and hands it to the middleware pipeline. It can be exposed directly to the internet, but in most production setups it sits behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, like IIS, Nginx or an AWS Application Load Balancer. The proxy handles TLS termination, routing, and protection, and Kestrel focuses on running the app. In that setup, you need the forwarded headers middleware so the app knows the original scheme and client IP.

In our case, each service runs Kestrel inside a Docker container on ECS. The ALB terminates TLS with an ACM certificate and forwards to Kestrel on port 8080. We configure request limits, like maximum body size, on Kestrel for endpoints like the CSV import. I can explain IIS in-process hosting as well, if needed.
cards.k: kestrel, web server, reverse proxy, asp.net core

cards.q: What happens if middleware is registered in the wrong order?
cards.h: Wrong order = guard checks tickets before checking ID.
s: Middleware runs in exactly the order it's registered, so a wrong order doesn't usually crash the app. It quietly breaks behaviour, which is worse.

Some common examples. If UseAuthorization comes before UseAuthentication, the user isn't identified yet when authorization runs, so every protected endpoint returns 401 or 403. If UseCors is placed after the endpoints, or after authentication, preflight requests don't get CORS headers and the browser blocks the call, even though Postman works fine. If the exception handler is added late, exceptions thrown by earlier middleware aren't caught, and the client gets a raw 500. And if static files come after authentication, even public files need a login.
A typical correct order is: exception handling and HSTS, HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, then the endpoints.

I actually hit one of these. When adding our correlation-id middleware in [2024], we placed it after the exception handler, so error logs had no correlation id. Moving it earlier fixed that. I can walk through the full order if useful.
cards.k: middleware order, pipeline order, bugs, cors, authentication, middleware, pipeline, request delegate, request pipeline

cards.q: Use vs Run vs Map?
cards.h: Use = pass along, Run = stop here, Map = fork.
s: Use, Run and Map are the three basic ways to build the middleware pipeline.

Use adds middleware that receives the context and a next delegate. It can do work before calling next, call next to pass the request on, and then do more work as the response comes back. It can also choose not to call next and short-circuit. Run adds terminal middleware: it doesn't get a next delegate, so it always ends the pipeline, and anything registered after it never runs. Map branches the pipeline by path. For example, Map of "/health" creates a separate mini-pipeline for that path. MapWhen branches on any condition, and UseWhen branches but rejoins the main pipeline.

In practice, for normal application routes I use endpoint routing, MapControllers, MapGet and so on, not raw Map. Use is what I use for custom middleware, like our correlation-id middleware, which sets the id, calls next, and adds the id to the response.
A common mistake is putting Run in the middle and wondering why later middleware never executes. I can sketch it if helpful.
cards.k: use, run, map, middleware, pipeline branching

cards.q: What is endpoint routing?
cards.h: Pick the destination first, check the ticket, then travel.
s: Endpoint routing is the routing system in ASP.NET Core that separates matching a route from executing it.

UseRouting runs early in the pipeline. It matches the request to an endpoint, like a controller action or a minimal API handler, and stores that endpoint on the HttpContext. The endpoint carries metadata, such as the Authorize attribute, a CORS policy, a rate limiting policy or AllowAnonymous. So middleware that runs between routing and the endpoint, like CORS, authentication, authorization and rate limiting, can read that metadata and make decisions. Finally, the endpoint itself executes at the end of the pipeline.

The big benefit is one consistent routing system for controllers, minimal APIs, gRPC, SignalR and health checks, and policy-aware middleware. Before it, in old MVC, routing happened inside MVC, so middleware couldn't know which action would run.

I've used it directly. Our correlation-id and audit middleware calls GetEndpoint to read a custom attribute, so certain endpoints, like health checks, skip auditing. I can explain how authorization uses the endpoint metadata.
cards.k: endpoint routing, userouting, endpoints, metadata

cards.q: What happened to Startup.cs?
cards.h: Two files became one.
s: Since .NET 6, Startup.cs is no longer part of the default template. Microsoft introduced the minimal hosting model, which merges Program.cs and Startup.cs into one file.

Previously, Program.cs built the host, and the Startup class had two methods: ConfigureServices for registering services, and Configure for building the middleware pipeline. Now, you create a WebApplicationBuilder. The service registrations that were in ConfigureServices go on builder.Services. Then you call builder.Build to get the app, and the pipeline that was in Configure goes on the app object, with app.Use and app.Map calls. Top-level statements remove the boilerplate.
Nothing is lost. Startup still works if you prefer it, and large apps often keep things organised with extension methods, like AddPersistence or AddMessaging, so Program.cs stays readable.

When we upgraded our services from older versions, we moved to the minimal hosting model step by step. We grouped registrations into extension methods per area, which made Program.cs much shorter and easier to review. I can show what a typical Program.cs looks like.
cards.k: startup.cs, program.cs, minimal hosting, .net 6

cards.q: Does CORS provide security?
cards.h: CORS is a browser courtesy, not a lock.
s: CORS does not protect your API. It's a browser rule, not a server security feature.

Browsers follow the same-origin policy, which stops a script on one site from reading responses from another origin. CORS, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, is a way for the server to relax that rule, by telling the browser which other origins are allowed to read its responses. For non-simple requests, the browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request first and checks the headers.

But only browsers enforce it. Postman, curl, a script or another server can call the API regardless of the CORS settings. So CORS protects users in the browser from malicious sites reading data with their cookies. It doesn't stop anyone from calling your API directly.

Real API security comes from authentication, authorization, input validation and rate limiting. In our services, CORS only allows our own front-end origins explicitly, never a wildcard with credentials, and every endpoint still requires a valid token with the right roles. I can explain how a preflight request works step by step.
cards.k: cors, security, same-origin policy, browser, owasp, xss, csrf, sql injection, cookie

cards.q: How do you configure HTTPS?
cards.h: Encrypt every hop that matters.
s: HTTPS has two parts: where TLS is terminated, and how the app enforces it.

In development, ASP.NET Core uses a local dev certificate, trusted with dotnet dev-certs. In production you can configure a certificate on Kestrel directly, but more commonly TLS is terminated at a load balancer or API gateway. In the app, I add UseHttpsRedirection, so plain HTTP requests are redirected, and UseHsts in production, which tells browsers to always use HTTPS for that domain. When behind a proxy, I configure the forwarded headers middleware, so the app knows the original request was HTTPS and redirects and links are correct.

In our AWS setup, the Application Load Balancer terminates TLS using a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager, which renews automatically. HTTP on port 80 is redirected to 443 at the ALB. Traffic between components is also encrypted where our policy requires it, and the database connections use TLS.
For a regulated system, we also enforce modern TLS versions with a TLS security policy on the ALB. I can explain how HSTS works in more detail.
cards.k: https, tls, certificates, hsts, ssl

cards.q: What is health checking?
cards.h: A pulse and a ready sign.
s: Health checks are endpoints that report whether the app and its dependencies are healthy, so infrastructure can make routing and restart decisions automatically.

In ASP.NET Core, I call AddHealthChecks and add checks for important dependencies, like the database, RabbitMQ or Redis, either from community packages or custom IHealthCheck classes. Then I map them with MapHealthChecks. I usually expose two. A liveness endpoint that only says the process is running, and a readiness endpoint that checks dependencies, so the instance only receives traffic when it can actually serve it. Each check returns Healthy, Degraded or Unhealthy.

In our setup, the Application Load Balancer target group calls the health endpoint, and only healthy containers get traffic. ECS replaces tasks that keep failing. We keep liveness cheap, because if it checked the database, a database blip would make ECS restart every container at once, which makes things worse.
The health endpoints are excluded from authentication and audit logging. I can explain how we monitor them with CloudWatch alarms.
cards.k: health checks, liveness, readiness, monitoring, load balancer

cards.q: How do you implement graceful shutdown?
cards.h: Finish the plates on the table, take no new orders.
s: Graceful shutdown means that when an instance is stopped, it finishes or safely hands back its current work, instead of dropping requests or messages halfway.

When a container is stopped, for example during a deployment, it receives a SIGTERM signal. The ASP.NET Core host then stops accepting new requests, lets in-flight requests finish within the shutdown timeout, which is 30 seconds by default, fires the ApplicationStopping event, and cancels the stopping token for every BackgroundService. After that, it disposes services and exits.

My job is to make the code cooperate. Background loops check the stopping token. Our RabbitMQ consumers stop taking new messages, finish and acknowledge the current message, and then close the channel. Anything not acknowledged goes back to the queue for another instance, so nothing is lost. On AWS, the ALB deregistration delay drains connections first, and the ECS stop timeout gives the container time before it's killed.
This is a big reason we use manual acks. I can explain how we test it during deployments.
cards.k: graceful shutdown, sigterm, shutdown timeout, stopping token

cards.q: How do you handle cancellation tokens?
cards.h: If the caller hangs up, stop cooking.
s: A CancellationToken is how .NET tells asynchronous work to stop early, and I treat it as a normal part of every async method signature.

In an API action, I accept a CancellationToken parameter. ASP.NET Core binds it to HttpContext.RequestAborted, which is cancelled if the client disconnects. I pass that token all the way down, to EF Core queries, HttpClient calls and Task.Delay, so an abandoned request stops using the database. For timeouts, I create a linked CancellationTokenSource with CancelAfter. In background services I use the stopping token.

When cancellation happens, an OperationCanceledException is thrown. I treat that as normal, not as an error, so it isn't logged as a failure or returned as a 500. And I'm careful where I stop: I don't cancel halfway through a database transaction without rolling back.

A concrete benefit: on a heavy shipment report endpoint, users often navigated away. Passing the token to the EF Core query meant SQL Server stopped running those abandoned queries. I can show how to test cancellation.
cards.k: cancellation token, cancellation, async, requestaborted

cards.q: PUT vs PATCH?
cards.h: PUT = replace the form; PATCH = correct one box.
s: PUT and PATCH both update a resource, but PUT replaces it completely, while PATCH changes only part of it.

With PUT, the client sends the full representation of the resource, and the server replaces what it has. Any field the client leaves out is cleared or set to its default. PUT is idempotent, so sending the same request twice gives the same final state, which makes it safe to retry. PATCH sends only the changes. There are two common formats: JSON Merge Patch, where you send just the fields to change, and JSON Patch, a list of operations like replace or remove. PATCH isn't guaranteed to be idempotent, for example an "add item" operation.
The risk with PUT is a client that sends an old or partial object and accidentally wipes fields. That's why, for small updates, PATCH is safer.

In our APIs, we use PATCH for things like updating only a shipment's status or a site's contact details, combined with a row version, so if someone else changed the record in the meantime, we return 409 instead of silently overwriting it. I can explain the concurrency check if useful.
cards.k: put, patch, http verbs, rest, partial update

cards.h: 201 = born.
s: Both are success codes, but they mean different things to the client.

200 OK is the general success response. The request worked and the result is in the body, for example a GET returning a shipment, or a PUT returning the updated resource. 201 Created specifically means the request created a new resource. By convention, a 201 response includes a Location header with the URL of the new resource, and usually the created resource in the body, including server-generated values like its id. There's also 202 Accepted, when work has been queued but not finished yet, and 204 No Content, when it succeeded with nothing to return, like a DELETE.
Using the right code helps clients and tools behave correctly without reading the body, and it makes the API self-documenting in OpenAPI.

In ASP.NET Core, I return CreatedAtAction or TypedResults.Created. For example, when a POST creates a shipment, we return 201 with a Location pointing to the GET endpoint for that shipment. And our CSV import returns 202 Accepted with a link to check the import status, because processing runs in the background. I can explain the other status codes as well.
cards.k: 200, 201, status codes, created, rest

cards.h: 400 = bad form, 401 = who are you, 403 = not you.
s: These three are the most commonly confused client errors.

400 Bad Request means the request itself is wrong: invalid JSON, a missing required field, or a failed validation rule. The client needs to fix the request. 401 Unauthorized, despite its name, actually means unauthenticated. We don't know who you are, because the token is missing, invalid or expired, so the client should log in or refresh its token. 403 Forbidden means we know exactly who you are, but you're not allowed to do this. Logging in again won't help.

The distinction matters for the client's behaviour. On 401, our front end tries a token refresh once and then redirects to login. On 403, it shows an "access denied" message. If we returned 401 for permission problems, users would get stuck in a login loop.

A real example: in our IRT system, a user logged in with valid access to one study who tries to open another study's shipments gets a 403 from our resource-based authorization check. Some teams return 404 there to avoid revealing that the record exists. I can explain that trade-off.
cards.k: 400, 401, 403, status codes, unauthorized, forbidden

cards.h: 404 = wrong address; 405 = right address, wrong door.
s: Both mean the request couldn't be matched, but at different levels.

404 Not Found means the thing doesn't exist. Either there's no route for that URL at all, or the route exists but the specific resource doesn't, like GET on a shipment id that isn't in the database. 405 Method Not Allowed means the URL does exist, but not for that HTTP method. For example, sending DELETE to an endpoint that only supports GET and POST. The response should include an Allow header listing the supported methods, and ASP.NET Core endpoint routing returns 405 for you automatically.

This distinction really helps debugging. A 404 makes me check the URL, the route template or the data. A 405 tells me the URL is right, but the client is using the wrong verb, often a typo in the front end or a missing HttpPut attribute.

A small but important point: some teams intentionally return 404 instead of 403 for records the user isn't allowed to see, so we don't leak that the record exists. I can talk about that security choice.
cards.k: 404, 405, status codes, not found, method not allowed

cards.h: 409 = clash with reality; 422 = makes no sense.
s: 409 and 422 are both about valid-looking requests that we still can't accept, but for different reasons.

409 Conflict means the request clashes with the current state of the resource. Typical cases are creating something that already exists, like a duplicate site number, or an optimistic concurrency conflict, where the client is updating an old version of a record that someone else has already changed. The client usually needs to reload and try again. 422 Unprocessable Entity means the request is well-formed, the JSON is valid and the fields are the right types, but it breaks a business rule. For example, requesting more kits than the depot has, or a ship date in the past.
Some teams use 400 for all validation errors, which is also fine, as long as it's consistent and the ProblemDetails body explains the problem.

In our APIs, the EF Core row-version check maps DbUpdateConcurrencyException to 409, and our business rule validation returns 422 with a ProblemDetails listing each failed rule. That gives the front end a clear way to react. I can show what that error body looks like.
cards.k: 409, 422, status codes, conflict, validation

cards.h: 500 = I broke, 502 = my supplier broke, 503 = closed for now.
s: These are server-side errors, and each one points to a different layer, which is very useful when troubleshooting.

500 Internal Server Error means something failed inside our own service, usually an unhandled exception. The fix is in our code or data, so I go to the logs with the correlation id. 502 Bad Gateway means a proxy or load balancer, like our ALB or API gateway, got an invalid response from the service behind it. Often the container crashed, closed the connection, or isn't listening on the right port. 503 Service Unavailable means the service is temporarily unable to handle requests, for example overloaded, in maintenance, or the load balancer has no healthy targets. Ideally it includes a Retry-After header. And 504 Gateway Timeout means the upstream took too long.
So when I see these, I know where to look. 500, our application logs. 502 or 503, the ALB target health and ECS task events. 504, slow queries or downstream calls.
During a deployment issue, a spike of 503s told us that new tasks were failing health checks, not that the code was throwing. I can walk through how I'd debug each.
cards.k: 500, 502, 503, status codes, server error

cards.q: What are DTOs and why use them?
cards.h: DTO = the envelope, not the whole filing cabinet.
s: A DTO, or Data Transfer Object, is a simple class or record that defines exactly what data crosses a boundary, like what an API accepts in a request or returns in a response. It holds data only, with no business behaviour.

The main reason to use DTOs is to separate the API contract from the internal model. Database entities change for internal reasons, and if they were the contract, every schema change could break clients. DTOs also let us hide internal or sensitive fields, prevent over-posting, because input DTOs only contain fields the client may set, put validation attributes on inputs, and shape data per use case, like a short list item versus a full detail view.

In our services, DTOs are C# records, which are concise and immutable. For reads, we project directly into DTOs with a Select in EF Core, so SQL only fetches the needed columns. For writes, we map request DTOs to entities in the service layer.
In a clinical system this separation is important, because we must never accidentally expose something like treatment assignment data. I can explain mapping options like Mapster or manual mapping.
cards.k: dto, data transfer object, api contract, records

cards.q: Why shouldn't you expose EF entities directly?
cards.h: Show the menu, not the kitchen.
s: Exposing EF entities directly from an API looks quick, but it causes several real problems.

First, coupling. The database schema becomes the public contract, so renaming a column or splitting a table breaks clients. Second, data leakage. Entities often have internal or sensitive fields, and adding a new column could silently expose it. Third, over-posting. If you bind input directly to an entity, a client can set fields it shouldn't, like a status or an approval flag. Fourth, serialization problems. Navigation properties cause circular references, and with lazy loading, serializing can trigger many extra queries. And fifth, performance: you usually load full entities, and their relationships, instead of only the columns needed.
In a clinical trial system, the leakage risk is serious. Accidentally exposing a blinding-related field would be a major compliance issue, not just a bug.

So in our services, every endpoint uses DTOs. Reads use Select projections into DTOs, and writes map request DTOs to entities in the service layer, with tests that check responses contain only expected fields. I can explain how we keep the mapping code manageable.
cards.k: ef entities, dto, security, over-posting, api design

cards.q: DTO vs ViewModel?
cards.h: DTO travels; ViewModel is displayed.
s: A DTO and a ViewModel are both simple data classes, but they serve different purposes.

A DTO, Data Transfer Object, carries data across a boundary, like between an API and its clients, or between services. It's a transport contract, shaped for the use case and kept stable, with no behaviour. A ViewModel is shaped for one specific screen, usually in server-rendered MVC or Razor Pages. It contains exactly what that view needs, and can include display-only data, like formatted dates, dropdown lists or flags that control what's shown.
In an API-first architecture with a separate front end, like React, the server mostly deals with DTOs. The front end builds its own view state from them, so the ViewModel concept moves to the client.

In our system, the APIs return DTOs, for example a ShipmentSummaryDto for lists and a ShipmentDetailDto for one shipment. The React front end then combines them into what each screen needs. In older MVC parts of the system, we had ViewModels with select lists for forms. I can talk about how we design DTOs for list versus detail endpoints.
cards.k: dto, viewmodel, mvc, api

cards.q: What is [ApiController]?
cards.h: One attribute, API manners included.
s: ApiController is an attribute I put on API controllers, and it switches on a set of behaviours that make building Web APIs simpler and more consistent.

First, automatic validation responses. If the model is invalid, it returns a 400 with a ValidationProblemDetails body before the action runs, so I don't need "if not ModelState IsValid" in every action. Second, binding source inference. Complex types come from the body, route values from the route, and simple types from the query string, so fewer FromBody attributes. Third, attribute routing is required, so routes are explicit. Fourth, error status codes are returned as ProblemDetails, the standard error format.
It's usually applied on a base controller, or at assembly level, so every API controller gets it.

In our services, we put it on a shared base controller and customised InvalidModelStateResponseFactory, so validation errors also include our correlation id. That way, every 400 from every service has the same shape, and support can trace it in the logs. I can explain how it compares with minimal APIs, which handle this differently.
cards.k: apicontroller, attribute, model validation, problemdetails

cards.q: What is routing, and attribute routing vs conventional routing?
cards.h: Attribute = address on each door; conventional = one street map.
s: Routing is how ASP.NET Core maps an incoming URL and HTTP method to the code that handles it, like a controller action or a minimal API handler.

There are two styles. Attribute routing puts the route template directly on the controller and actions, for example Route "api/studies/{studyId}/shipments" on the controller, and HttpGet "{id}" on an action. It's explicit, supports route constraints like int, and matches REST resource design well, so it's the standard for APIs and is required with ApiController. Conventional routing defines one central pattern in Program.cs, like "controller/action/id", and all controllers follow it. It's common in traditional MVC websites, where URLs follow a predictable pattern.
Minimal APIs use their own MapGet and MapPost calls, which are essentially attribute routing in code, and route groups help share prefixes and policies.

In our services, we use attribute routing with versioned, resource-based routes, like api/v1/studies/{studyId}/shipments. That makes the URL design visible right in the code and in the OpenAPI document. I can explain route constraints or versioning next.
cards.k: routing, attribute routing, conventional routing, endpoints

cards.q: How do you implement filtering and sorting?
cards.h: Filter, sort, then page, all in SQL.
s: Filtering and sorting in an API is about giving clients flexibility while keeping the queries safe and fast.

I accept parameters in the query string, like status equals Shipped, siteId equals 12, sortBy equals shipDate and descending equals true, usually bound to a query object. Then I build the query step by step on IQueryable. For each filter that's present, I add a Where clause. For sorting, I map the sortBy value to a known expression from an allow-list, never to a raw column name or SQL string, which prevents injection and stops clients from sorting by unindexed columns. Then I apply paging with Skip and Take, or keyset paging for large tables, and return the total count or a next link.
Because everything stays on IQueryable until the end, EF Core translates it all into one SQL query, so the database does the work.

On our shipment search, I made sure the most common filter combinations, study, status and ship date, were covered by an index, and checked the execution plans. That kept the search fast as the data grew. I can explain keyset versus offset paging.
cards.k: filtering, sorting, paging, iqueryable, query parameters

cards.q: How do you document APIs, and what is Swagger/OpenAPI?
cards.h: OpenAPI = the API's manual.
s: OpenAPI is a standard, machine-readable way to describe a REST API, in JSON or YAML. It lists every endpoint, its parameters, request and response models, status codes and security requirements. Swagger is the original name and now the name of the tooling around it, like Swagger UI, which renders the document as an interactive page where you can try the calls.

In .NET, the document is generated from the code. Historically we used Swashbuckle, and since .NET 9, there's built-in support with Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi. To make it genuinely useful, I add XML comments, ProducesResponseType for every status code, examples, and the authentication scheme so you can test with a token.

The real value is that the contract is shared. Front-end and vendor teams read it, and they can generate typed clients from it, so they don't hand-code requests. We also publish it per version, and in our pipeline, a check compares the new document with the previous one to catch breaking changes.
For security, Swagger UI is enabled only in non-production environments. I can explain how we handle breaking changes with versioning.
cards.k: swagger, openapi, api documentation, swagger ui

cards.q: How do you secure an API?
cards.h: Lock, ID check, permission, limits, logs.
s: I secure an API in layers, so that if one control fails, the others still protect it.

First, transport: HTTPS only, with HSTS. Second, authentication: every request needs a valid JWT from our identity provider, and we validate the issuer, audience, signature and expiry. Third, authorization: role and policy checks, plus resource-level checks, like "does this user have access to this specific study", which is critical in multi-tenant clinical data. Fourth, input: DTOs, validation, parameterised queries through EF Core, and size limits. Fifth, abuse protection: rate limiting and restricted CORS. And sixth, operations: secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, no sensitive data in logs, least-privilege IAM and database roles, dependency scanning in the pipeline, and audit logs for every change.
Security also covers logout and token lifetime. We use short [15-minute] access tokens, and for immediate logout, we added a token-id denylist in ElastiCache that the API checks in about [1 ms].
Every new endpoint goes through a security checklist in code review. I can go deeper into any of these layers.
cards.k: api security, authentication, authorization, jwt, owasp, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Access token vs refresh token?
cards.h: Access = day pass; refresh = membership card at reception.
s: An access token and a refresh token work together, but they have very different jobs and lifetimes.
