The access token is short-lived, in our case [15 minutes]. It's sent with every API call, usually as a bearer JWT, and the API validates it to know who the user is and what they can do. Because it's short-lived, if it leaks, the damage window is small. The refresh token lives much longer, hours or days. It's never sent to the APIs, only to the identity provider's token endpoint, to get a new access token when the old one expires, so the user doesn't have to log in again. It must be stored securely, and it can be revoked on the server, and with rotation, each use issues a new one.

We used this in a real fix. Users reported that after logging out, their old token still worked until it expired. We revoked the refresh token on logout, and added a denylist of token ids in ElastiCache, which every API checks in about [1 ms]. So logout became immediate.
I can explain how token rotation detects stolen refresh tokens.
cards.k: access token, refresh token, jwt, oauth, token lifetime, token, bearer

cards.q: Role-based vs policy-based authorization, and how do you implement policies?
cards.h: Roles = job title; policies = specific rules.
s: Both control what an authenticated user can do, but policies are more flexible.

Role-based authorization checks whether the user is in a role, like Authorize with Roles equals StudyManager. It's simple, but coarse. You end up with many roles and checks scattered across code. Policy-based authorization defines a named policy, made of one or more requirements. A requirement can check a claim, a role, or run custom logic in an authorization handler. I register policies in AddAuthorization in Program.cs, then use Authorize with Policy, or RequireAuthorization on minimal API endpoints. Roles are really just one kind of policy underneath.
For checks that depend on the actual data, there's resource-based authorization. I inject IAuthorizationService, and call AuthorizeAsync with the user, the resource and a requirement.

That's essential in our clinical system. Being a study manager isn't enough, you must be assigned to that specific study. So we have a StudyAccess requirement and handler that checks the user's study assignments, and returns 403 if they're not on the study. I can show that handler.
cards.k: role-based authorization, policy-based authorization, policies, authorization handler

cards.q: How do you prevent over-posting?
cards.h: Only accept what is on the form.
s: Over-posting, also called mass assignment, is when a client sends extra fields that the server didn't intend to accept, and they get saved because the API binds directly to an entity.

For example, a user updates their profile, but adds "isAdmin: true" or "status: Approved" to the JSON. If the action takes the EF entity as its parameter and saves it, those fields are written to the database. It's a well-known security issue in the OWASP API Top 10.

The main prevention is input DTOs. Each endpoint has a request DTO containing only the fields that the client is allowed to set. Then the service layer loads the entity and maps only those fields onto it. Server-controlled values, like status, created-by and approval flags, are set by the server logic, never by the client. The Bind attribute is an older alternative, but DTOs are cleaner.

We also have tests that send extra fields, like a different study id or an approval flag, and assert they're ignored. In a GxP system, an unauthorised status change would be an audit finding, so we take it seriously. I can talk about how this relates to authorization checks.
cards.k: over-posting, mass assignment, dto, security

cards.q: How do you handle large request payloads?
cards.h: Big things go by freight, not in the envelope.
s: Large payloads can exhaust memory and threads, so I handle them in several ways.

First, limits. Kestrel has a default maximum body size of about 30 MB, and I set tighter limits per endpoint with the RequestSizeLimit attribute, so oversized requests are rejected early, before we read them. Second, streaming. Instead of buffering the whole body into memory, or into a big model object, I read the request stream directly and process it incrementally. Third, for really large files, I don't send them through the API at all. The client uploads directly to S3 using a presigned URL, and the API only gets the object key. Fourth, for heavy processing, the API accepts the request, returns 202 Accepted, and a background worker does the work. And on the response side, pagination and response compression.

Our CSV import follows this. Files are limited to [5 MB, roughly 10,000 rows], the parser streams rows instead of loading everything, and processing runs in the background with a status endpoint. Each user can have at most [2] imports running at once.
I can explain the presigned URL flow in more detail.
cards.k: large payloads, request size limit, streaming, s3, upload

cards.q: How do you handle file uploads?
cards.h: Check it, store it safely, process it later.
s: For file uploads, I think about three things: size, safety and where the file ends up.

For small files, I accept an IFormFile with a request size limit. For larger ones, I stream the multipart body with MultipartReader, so the file isn't buffered in memory, or I use presigned S3 uploads, where the client uploads straight to S3. Then validation. I check the size, the extension against an allow-list, and the actual content, like magic bytes, because the extension and content type can be faked. I never trust the original file name, I generate a random one. Files are stored outside the web root, usually in S3 with encryption, and scanned for malware when required. Processing happens asynchronously.

Our CSV import is a good example. The upload is limited to [5 MB]. We check it's really a CSV, then a streaming parser validates the header and each row, collecting all row errors with their line numbers, before anything is saved. Users get a clear error report instead of a partial import.
I can explain how we avoided importing the same file twice.
cards.k: file upload, iformfile, multipart, s3, validation

cards.q: How do you design a production-ready API?
cards.h: Contract, Security, Resilience, Observability, Performance.
s: For me, production-ready means the API is not only correct, but also safe, observable and easy to operate at 2 a.m.

I think in six areas. Contract: DTOs, OpenAPI documentation, versioning, validation, and consistent ProblemDetails errors. Security: HTTPS, JWT authentication, policy and resource-level authorization, rate limiting, restricted CORS, and secrets in a secret store. Resilience: timeouts and retries with Polly for downstream calls, idempotency keys for creates, health checks and graceful shutdown. Observability: structured logs with correlation ids, metrics, tracing and CloudWatch alarms. Performance: async all the way, paging, caching and efficient queries. And quality: automated tests, and a CI/CD pipeline with quality gates and security scans.
A detail people often skip is validating configuration at startup, with ValidateOnStart, so a missing setting fails the deployment instead of the first request.
When I joined new work, I turned this into a checklist that every new service in our team follows. That's how our correlation-id middleware ended up in [4] services. I can go deeper into any area.
cards.k: production ready api, api design, best practices, checklist, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Where should validation happen?
cards.h: Door, desk, and vault each check.
s: Validation should happen at every boundary, but each layer validates for a different purpose.

At the API layer, I validate the shape and format of the request: required fields, lengths, ranges, formats, using data annotations or FluentValidation. ApiController returns a 400 automatically when that fails, so bad input is stopped as early and cheaply as possible. In the service or domain layer, I validate business rules, which need context or data, like "a site must belong to an active depot", or "you can't ship more kits than are available". Those return a 422 with a clear message. And in the database, constraints are the final safety net: primary and foreign keys, unique indexes and check constraints. They catch anything that slips through, including race conditions between two concurrent requests.
UI validation is useful for user experience, but it's never trusted, because anyone can call the API directly.

In our system, for example, the unique site number is checked in the service for a friendly message, and enforced by a unique index for correctness. I can explain how we report multiple validation errors at once.
cards.k: validation, layers, business rules, constraints

cards.q: How do you prevent duplicate requests?
cards.h: Same key, same answer, done once.
s: Duplicate requests happen all the time: users double-click, clients retry after a timeout, and message brokers redeliver. So I design for it on purpose.

The main technique for creates is an idempotency key. The client sends a unique key, often in an Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the key with the result of the first request. If the same key comes again, it returns the stored result instead of executing again. I back that with database protection: natural keys with unique constraints, so even a race between two requests can't create two rows, and optimistic concurrency for updates. On the client side, disabling the button after submit helps, but it's never enough.
For messaging, consumers are idempotent too. We store processed message ids, so redelivered messages are skipped.

A real example is our CSV import. We store a hash of each uploaded file per study. If the same file is uploaded again, we reject it with a clear message instead of importing the rows twice. I can explain how idempotency keys expire.
cards.k: duplicate requests, idempotency key, idempotency, unique constraint

cards.q: What is Entity Framework Core?
cards.h: Objects in, SQL out.
s: Entity Framework Core is Microsoft's open-source ORM, an object-relational mapper, for .NET. It lets me work with the database using C# classes and LINQ, instead of writing SQL and mapping rows by hand.

It maps entity classes to tables and properties to columns, using conventions plus configuration in OnModelCreating. When I write a LINQ query over a DbSet, EF Core translates it into SQL, runs it, and turns the rows back into objects. When I change objects and call SaveChanges, its change tracker works out the INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements and runs them in one transaction. Migrations keep the database schema in step with the model. It supports many databases through providers, like SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite and Cosmos DB.
The trade-off is a little overhead and the risk of inefficient queries if you don't watch the generated SQL. So I always check the SQL for important queries.

In our IRT services, EF Core with SQL Server is the main data access layer. We use AsNoTracking and projections for reads, ExecuteUpdate for bulk changes, and reviewed idempotent migration scripts for releases. I can go into any of those.
cards.k: ef core, entity framework, orm, database, ef, dbcontext, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: EF Core vs ADO.NET?
cards.h: ADO.NET = manual gearbox; EF Core = automatic.
s: ADO.NET and EF Core both talk to the database, but at very different levels of abstraction.

ADO.NET is the low-level foundation: you open a connection, create a command with SQL text and parameters, execute it, and read rows with a data reader, mapping each column to your objects by hand. It's the fastest option and gives full control, but it's a lot of repetitive code and easy to get wrong. EF Core sits on top of ADO.NET. You write LINQ, and it generates the SQL, maps the results, tracks changes, handles relationships, and manages migrations. That's much more productive and safer for everyday work, with a small performance overhead that rarely matters.
There's also a middle ground, Dapper, a micro-ORM: you write the SQL yourself, and it maps the results to objects very quickly.

My rule: EF Core for most CRUD and business operations, and Dapper or raw ADO.NET for hot paths or complex reporting SQL that's been tuned by hand. In our services, almost everything is EF Core, with a few heavy reports using Dapper. I can explain when EF Core's overhead actually matters.
cards.k: ef core, ado.net, dapper, orm, comparison, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: What is DbContext, and what is DbSet?
cards.h: DbContext = the session; DbSet = a table inside it.
s: DbContext and DbSet are the two central types in EF Core.

DbContext represents a session with the database. It combines several responsibilities: it's a unit of work, because it collects changes and saves them together in one transaction; it holds the change tracker, which knows the state of every loaded entity; and it manages the database connection, opening it only when needed. The model, meaning table names, keys, relationships and indexes, is configured in OnModelCreating, usually with separate configuration classes per entity. In ASP.NET Core, a DbContext is registered as scoped, one per request, and it's not thread-safe.

A DbSet of T represents a table, or more precisely the collection of entities of that type. I use it to query, with LINQ, which starts as an IQueryable that's translated into SQL, and to add or remove entities, which are saved on SaveChanges.

In our IRT services, each bounded context has its own DbContext, for example inventory and shipments, with only the DbSets it needs, rather than one giant context for the whole database. That keeps the models smaller and clearer. I can explain how we configure entities.
cards.k: dbcontext, dbset, ef core, entity framework, ef, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: Include() vs ThenInclude()?
cards.h: Include = children; ThenInclude = grandchildren.
s: Both are used for eager loading related data, but at different levels of the object graph.

Include loads a navigation property of the root entity you're querying. ThenInclude continues from that navigation to load the next level down. For example, querying studies, Include sites, then ThenInclude shipments, loads each study with its sites, and each site with its shipments, all in one query. You can chain multiple Includes for different branches, and since EF Core 5 you can filter inside Include too, like only active sites.

The thing to watch is that deep or multiple collection includes can create a huge result set, because SQL joins multiply the rows, which is called cartesian explosion. If a study has 300 sites and each has 50 shipments, the parent data is repeated for every row. AsSplitQuery fixes this by running a separate query for each collection. Often the better option is a Select projection into a DTO with just the fields needed.
In our IRT services, I prefer projections for read endpoints and use Include mainly when loading an aggregate to update it. I can show an example of split queries.
cards.k: include, theninclude, eager loading, ef core

cards.q: How do you create EF migrations?
cards.h: Add, review, script, release.
s: EF Core migrations are how the database schema evolves in step with the C# model.

When I change the model, for example adding a property or an index, I run dotnet ef migrations add with a descriptive name, like AddShipmentStatusIndex. EF Core compares the current model with the last snapshot and generates a migration class with an Up method, to apply the change, and a Down method, to reverse it. I review that code like any other code, because generated migrations can do surprising things, like dropping and recreating a column on a rename, which loses data. If needed, I edit it, for example to add a data migration step.

For deployment, I don't run migrations automatically at application startup. I generate an idempotent SQL script with dotnet ef migrations script with the idempotent option. That script checks the migrations history table, so it can safely run against any environment. It's reviewed and applied by the release pipeline.
In our regulated environment, that script is part of the release evidence for FV, UAT and production. I can explain how we keep migrations backward-compatible during rolling deployments.
cards.k: ef core migrations, dotnet ef, schema changes, database

cards.q: Code First vs Database First?
cards.h: Code drives DB, or DB drives code.
s: These are two approaches to deciding what's the source of truth: the C# model or the database.

In Code First, the C# entity classes and their configuration are the source of truth. You design the model in code, and migrations create and evolve the database schema. It works well when the development team owns the database, because the schema is versioned with the code, reviewed in pull requests, and reproducible in every environment. In Database First, the database already exists, often designed and owned by DBAs, or it's a legacy schema. You use dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold to generate the entity classes and DbContext from the existing tables, and you re-scaffold when the schema changes. It's the practical choice when you can't control the schema.
EF Core removed the old EDMX designer, so both approaches now produce plain code. You can also mix them: scaffold once from an existing database, then continue with migrations.

In our IRT services, newer services are Code First with migrations, while some older shared databases were scaffolded Database First, because other systems depend on that schema. I can explain how we handle schema changes there.
cards.k: code first, database first, scaffolding, ef core

cards.q: What is LINQ-to-Entities?
cards.h: LINQ that speaks SQL.
s: LINQ-to-Entities means writing LINQ queries against EF Core's DbSet, which is an IQueryable, and having EF Core translate them into SQL that runs in the database.

When I write something like Shipments where status is Pending, order by date, take 20, nothing runs yet. EF Core builds an expression tree describing the query. When I enumerate it, for example with ToListAsync, the provider translates the whole expression tree into one SQL statement, sends it to SQL Server, and maps the rows back into objects. So filtering, sorting, paging and aggregates all happen in the database, which is efficient.

The key restriction is that only translatable operations can be used. Standard operators, comparisons, many string and date functions, work fine. But a custom C# method inside a Where can't be translated, and EF Core will throw an exception rather than silently loading everything.

That's different from LINQ-to-Objects, which runs on in-memory collections using delegates. Knowing which one you're in, IQueryable or IEnumerable, is one of the most important things in EF Core performance. I can explain how to check the generated SQL.
cards.k: linq to entities, ef core, iqueryable, sql translation, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq, ienumerable, deferred execution

cards.q: What causes client-side evaluation?
cards.h: If SQL can't say it, EF won't run it in the DB.
s: Client-side evaluation is when part of a query runs in .NET memory instead of in the database, which can mean loading far more data than needed.

It happens when the query uses something EF Core can't translate into SQL, like calling a custom C# method inside a Where clause, or certain complex string operations. In old EF Core 2, it silently switched to client evaluation: it pulled every row into memory and then filtered, which was a hidden performance disaster. Since EF Core 3, it throws an exception instead, except in the final Select projection, where running C# on the results is harmless.
The other cause is our own code: calling AsEnumerable, ToList or ToArray too early in the chain. Everything after that point runs in memory. So filtering after ToList loads the whole table first.

To avoid it, I keep the query on IQueryable until the end, rewrite custom logic into translatable expressions, and check the generated SQL with ToQueryString or logging. In a code review on our team, I once caught a ToList before a Where on a large shipment table. Moving it to the end cut the data loaded from the whole table to a few rows. I can show the difference.
cards.k: client-side evaluation, ef core, query translation, performance

cards.q: How do you optimize EF Core queries and performance?
cards.h: Track less, select less, round-trip less.
s: For EF Core performance, I start by looking at the generated SQL and the execution plan, because most problems are in the query, not in EF itself.

Then I apply a set of habits. For read-only queries, AsNoTracking, so no change-tracking overhead. Project with Select into DTOs, so SQL fetches only the needed columns. Filter and page in the database, keeping everything on IQueryable. Avoid N+1 queries by using projections or Include, and use AsSplitQuery when several collections are included. Make sure the right indexes exist for the filters and sort order. For bulk changes, use ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, which run one SQL statement without loading entities. For very hot paths, compiled queries and DbContext pooling reduce overhead. And always pass cancellation tokens, so abandoned requests stop querying.
I log the generated SQL in development, and in production, Query Store and CloudWatch latency metrics show which queries need attention.
A concrete example: our shipment list screen went from [about 9 seconds to under 300 ms] mainly through a SARGable rewrite, a covering index, and server-side paging. I can walk through that.
cards.k: ef core performance, optimization, asnotracking, projection, n+1, ef core, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: What is SaveChanges(), and SaveChanges() vs SaveChangesAsync()?
cards.h: One commit for all changes; async frees the thread.
s: SaveChanges is the method that writes all pending changes tracked by the DbContext to the database.

When I call it, EF Core first runs change detection, comparing tracked entities with their original snapshots to find what's added, modified and deleted. Then it generates the INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements, batching them where possible, and runs them all inside one transaction. So either all of the changes are saved, or none are. After success, it updates the entities, for example with generated identity values and new concurrency tokens, and marks them as unchanged. It returns the number of rows affected.

SaveChangesAsync does exactly the same, but asynchronously. While the database is doing the work, the thread is released back to the thread pool, instead of sitting idle. In ASP.NET Core, that's what you want, because it lets the server handle more requests under load. So in web APIs and services, I always use SaveChangesAsync, passing the cancellation token.

One more point: I call it once per unit of work, at the end of the operation, not after every small change. That keeps the operation atomic and reduces round trips. I can explain how concurrency tokens work with it.
cards.k: savechanges, savechangesasync, ef core, transactions

cards.q: How do you handle bulk operations?
cards.h: Bulk = set-based, not row by row.
s: Bulk operations are where the default EF Core approach, loading entities, changing them, and saving, becomes too slow.

For updates and deletes, EF Core 7 added ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete. They translate directly into a single set-based UPDATE or DELETE statement, without loading any rows into memory or using the change tracker. For example, marking all expired kits at a depot as unusable becomes one SQL statement instead of thousands of tracked updates. For inserts, AddRange plus SaveChanges already batches statements, which is fine for hundreds or a few thousand rows. For very large loads, like tens or hundreds of thousands of rows, I use SqlBulkCopy, or a bulk extensions library, which uses SQL Server's bulk insert path and is much faster. I usually process in chunks, so transactions and memory stay manageable.
One caution: ExecuteUpdate bypasses the change tracker, so audit logic in SaveChanges interceptors doesn't run. In a GxP system, we make sure auditing still happens for those operations.
Our CSV import of [about 10,000] rows uses batched inserts in chunks inside a transaction, after validation. I can explain why we chose that over SqlBulkCopy.
cards.k: bulk operations, executeupdate, executedelete, sqlbulkcopy, ef core

cards.q: What are compiled queries?
cards.h: Translate once, run many.
s: Compiled queries are a way to skip the cost of translating a LINQ query into SQL every time it runs.

Normally, when EF Core executes a LINQ query, it has to process the expression tree and produce SQL. It caches that work internally, keyed by the shape of the query, so repeated queries are already fairly cheap. But there's still some overhead in computing the cache key from the expression tree on every call. With EF.CompileAsyncQuery, or EF.CompileQuery, I define the query once, as a static delegate with parameters. EF Core translates it once, and every call reuses it directly, so the overhead disappears.

The gain is real but small, usually noticeable only on very hot paths with simple queries, executed thousands of times per second. Compiled queries are also less flexible, because the query shape is fixed.

So my rule is to use them only after measuring shows translation overhead matters. In our services, I've used a compiled query for a frequently called lookup, getting a kit by its number, which sits on a hot path during dispensing. For most queries, indexes and projections matter far more. I can explain other EF hot-path optimisations.
cards.k: compiled queries, ef core, performance

cards.q: How do you log generated SQL?
cards.h: See the SQL before you trust it.
s: Seeing the SQL that EF Core generates is essential, because that's where most performance problems show up.

There are a few ways. The simplest in development is LogTo on the DbContext options, for example LogTo Console.WriteLine, filtered to Information level. In an ASP.NET Core app, I can enable the log category Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command at Information level in configuration, and the SQL appears in the normal logs, with execution times. For a single query, ToQueryString returns the SQL without executing it, which is handy in tests and debugging. And for parameter values, EnableSensitiveDataLogging shows them, but only in development, because in production it could log personal or clinical data.
Outside the application, SQL Server tools help too: Query Store shows the heaviest queries over time, and Extended Events can capture specific ones.

In our team, during code reviews of data-heavy changes, we look at the generated SQL for new queries. That's how we've caught N+1 queries and accidental client-side evaluation before they reached production. I can explain how to read the execution plan next.
cards.k: log sql, ef core logging, toquerystring, debugging, sql, sql server, query, index, t-sql, database

cards.q: How do you handle relationships: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many?
cards.h: 1:1 pair, 1:N parent, N:N join table.
s: EF Core supports all three relationship types, configured by convention or with the Fluent API.

One-to-many is the most common. A principal has a collection navigation, and the dependent has a reference navigation and a foreign key. For example, a Site has many Shipments, and each Shipment has a SiteId. In Fluent API, that's HasMany Shipments WithOne Site HasForeignKey SiteId, and I choose the delete behaviour explicitly. One-to-one uses reference navigations on both sides, and the dependent holds the foreign key, for example a Subject and their ConsentRecord, configured with HasOne WithOne. Many-to-many, since EF Core 5, can be configured with collections on both sides, and EF creates the join table automatically.
But when the link itself has data, like a role or an assigned date, I model an explicit join entity instead.

That's our case for users and studies. A user can be on many studies, and a study has many users, but each assignment has a role and an assigned date, which our authorization checks use. So we have an explicit StudyAssignment entity. I can explain how we configure cascade deletes safely.
cards.k: relationships, one-to-many, many-to-many, one-to-one, ef core, fluent api

cards.q: What are shadow properties?
cards.h: Columns the class never sees.
s: Shadow properties are properties that exist in the EF Core model and in the database table, but not in the C# entity class.

You configure them in OnModelCreating with Property of type and a name, and EF Core tracks them like normal properties. To read or filter by them in queries, you use EF.Property with the entity and the property name. To set them, you go through the change tracker, for example entry.Property of "LastModifiedBy" CurrentValue. EF Core also creates shadow properties automatically, for example a foreign key column when the class only has a navigation property.

They're useful when a column matters to the database but shouldn't clutter the domain model. The classic use is audit columns, like CreatedBy, CreatedAt, LastModifiedBy and LastModifiedAt. Instead of adding these to every entity class, I define them as shadow properties on all entities, and set them centrally in a SaveChanges interceptor, using the current user and TimeProvider.
In our services, that's how audit columns are populated consistently, so no developer can forget to set them, which matters for GxP audit trails. I can show the interceptor code.
cards.k: shadow properties, ef core, audit columns

cards.q: What is owned entity mapping?
cards.h: Owned = lives inside its owner.
s: Owned entities are how EF Core maps value objects, types that don't have their own identity and only exist as part of another entity.

You configure them with OwnsOne for a single value object, or OwnsMany for a collection. For example, a Site has an Address, with street, city, postcode and country. Address isn't an entity on its own, it has no id, and it only makes sense as part of a site. With OwnsOne, EF Core stores the address fields as columns in the Site table, like Address_City, and loads them automatically whenever the site is loaded. OwnsMany stores the collection in a separate table, but it's still owned and loaded with its owner. Since EF Core 8, complex types offer a similar option for value objects.

The benefit is a richer domain model. Instead of loose string properties on Site, I have a proper Address type, with its own validation, which can be reused in other entities like Depot, while the database stays simple.
In our IRT model, addresses and some quantity-with-unit values are owned types. That made validation consistent across sites and depots. I can explain how this relates to domain-driven design.
cards.k: owned entity, value object, ef core, complex types

cards.q: How do you configure indexes in EF Core?
cards.h: Index in code, built by migration.
s: In EF Core, indexes are part of the model, so they're defined in code and created through migrations, which keeps them versioned and reviewed.

With the Fluent API, in the entity configuration, I call HasIndex with the columns. For example, HasIndex of StudyId and Status creates a composite index, and column order matters. I can add IsUnique for a unique index, like a kit number. HasFilter creates a filtered index, for example only active rows. And with SQL Server, IncludeProperties adds included columns, to make a covering index. HasDatabaseName gives it a clear name. Alternatively, the Index attribute on the entity class works for simple cases. Then I add a migration, and the index is created through our normal release scripts.
The important part is choosing indexes from real query patterns, using the execution plan, rather than adding them everywhere, because every index slows down writes.

The covering index from our shipment list fix, on StudyId, Status and ShipmentDate including the displayed columns, was added exactly this way, through a reviewed migration script. I can show the configuration code.
cards.k: indexes, hasindex, ef core, unique index, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: What is a primary key, and what is a foreign key?
cards.h: PK = my ID; FK = my parent's ID.
s: Primary and foreign keys are the basic tools for identity and integrity in a relational database.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. It can't be null, and there's only one per table, though it can span multiple columns. In SQL Server, the primary key creates a clustered index by default, so it often also defines the physical order of the data. A good primary key is small, stable and never changes, like an integer identity or a GUID. A foreign key is a column, or columns, in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. It enforces referential integrity: you can't create a shipment for a site that doesn't exist, and you can't delete a site that still has shipments, unless you've defined cascade rules, like cascade delete or set null.
In practice, I always index foreign key columns, because SQL Server doesn't do it automatically, and joins and deletes depend on them.
In a clinical system, foreign keys are a cheap but very strong guarantee of data integrity, so we never skip them for convenience. I can explain how to choose between integer and GUID keys.
cards.k: primary key, foreign key, relational database, constraints

cards.q: What is a unique constraint, and primary key vs unique key?
cards.h: One PK, many uniques.
s: A unique constraint guarantees that no two rows have the same value in a column, or a combination of columns. SQL Server enforces it with a unique index behind the scenes.

A primary key is also unique, but there are differences. A table has only one primary key, but can have many unique constraints. A primary key can't contain nulls, while a unique constraint in SQL Server allows one null, or with a filtered unique index you can allow many. The primary key is the row's main identity, used by foreign keys, while unique constraints protect alternate keys, which are natural business identifiers. And by default, the primary key is clustered, while unique constraints are non-clustered.
A typical design is a surrogate primary key, like an integer Id, plus unique constraints on natural keys that must never duplicate.

In our IRT database, kits have an integer Id as the primary key, but KitNumber has a unique constraint, because two physical kits with the same number would be a serious problem in a trial. The database enforces it even if two requests race each other. I can explain how we surface that as a 409 in the API.
cards.k: unique constraint, unique key, primary key, constraints

cards.q: What is a composite index?
cards.h: Phone book: last name, then first name.
s: A composite index is an index on more than one column, for example StudyId, Status and ShipmentDate together.

The order of columns matters a lot. The index is sorted by the first column, then by the second within that, and so on, like a phone book sorted by surname then first name. So it can support seeks on the leading columns: StudyId alone, or StudyId and Status, or all three. But it can't efficiently seek on Status alone, because Status isn't the leading column. That's called the leftmost prefix rule.

My rule for column order is: put equality columns first, the ones compared with equals, and range columns last, like dates with greater than or less than, because once you hit a range, the following columns can't be used for seeking. Then add INCLUDE columns for anything the query selects, to avoid key lookups.

Our shipment list index followed exactly that: StudyId and Status for equality, then ShipmentDate for the range, with the displayed columns included. That's what let the query seek directly to a study's pending shipments in a date range. I can show the execution plan difference.
cards.k: composite index, multi-column index, column order, sql server, index, indexes, clustered, non-clustered, filtered index

cards.q: What is a filtered index?
cards.h: Index only the rows you search.
s: A filtered index is a non-clustered index with a WHERE clause, so it only contains a subset of the table's rows.

For example, an index on ShipmentDate, WHERE Status equals Pending. If only a small percentage of shipments are pending at any time, this index is much smaller than a full one. That means less storage, faster seeks, cheaper maintenance on writes, and more accurate statistics for that subset. It's ideal for queries that always target a "hot" subset of the data. Another classic use is a filtered unique index, like enforcing that a kit number is unique only where it's not null, or only among active records.

The catch is that the query's predicate has to match the filter, so SQL Server knows the index covers it. Parameterised queries can make that tricky, because the optimizer can't always prove a parameter matches the filter. It works best with literal values, like Status equals Pending in the query text.

In our IRT system, dashboards repeatedly query pending and in-transit shipments, which are a small fraction of all shipments. A filtered index on those statuses made those dashboard queries much faster. I can explain how to check whether the index is used.
cards.k: filtered index, partial index, sql server, index, indexes, clustered, non-clustered, composite index

cards.q: How do indexes improve performance, and when can they hurt?
cards.h: Fast reads, taxed writes.
s: Indexes improve performance by letting SQL Server find rows without reading the whole table.

An index is a B-tree, sorted by its key. Instead of scanning millions of rows, SQL Server navigates the tree in a few page reads, which is logarithmic, and seeks straight to the matching rows. A covering index, with included columns, can answer the whole query without touching the table. Indexes also help with sorting and joins, because data is already ordered.

But they have costs. Every insert, update and delete must also update every relevant index, so write-heavy tables slow down with too many indexes. They use disk and memory. Random keys can cause page splits and fragmentation. And indexes on low-selectivity columns, like a true or false flag, or indexes no query uses, are pure cost with no benefit.

So I add indexes based on real queries and execution plans, and periodically check the index usage DMVs to find unused or duplicate indexes to remove. When we added the covering index for our shipment list, we also tested the write impact in validation, because shipments are updated frequently. I can explain how to find missing index suggestions.
cards.k: indexes, performance, write overhead, sql server

cards.q: What is an execution plan?
cards.h: The plan is the query's GPS route.
s: An execution plan is the optimizer's recipe for running a query: which indexes to use, in what order to access tables, which join algorithms to use, and where to sort or aggregate.

SQL Server's optimizer creates the plan based on statistics about the data, and then caches it for reuse. The plan is a tree of operators, like index seeks and scans, key lookups, nested loops, hash and merge joins, and sorts. Each shows estimated rows and cost, and in the actual plan, the actual rows too. There are two versions: the estimated plan, which doesn't run the query, and the actual plan, which runs it and shows what really happened.

When I read a plan, I look for a few red flags: scans on large tables where I expected a seek, expensive key lookups, sorts or hash operations spilling to tempdb, and big differences between estimated and actual rows, which point to stale statistics or parameter sniffing. I use SSMS for single queries, and Query Store to see plans over time and spot regressions.
In our shipment list fix, the plan showed a clustered index scan and key lookups, and that directly told me what to fix. I can walk through that plan.
cards.k: execution plan, query plan, sql server, tuning

cards.q: Table scan vs index scan vs index seek?
cards.h: Scan = read the whole book; seek = open at the right page.
s: These are three ways SQL Server can read data, and they differ hugely in cost.

A table scan reads every row of a heap, which is a table without a clustered index. An index scan reads all, or a large range, of an index, either the clustered index, which is effectively the whole table, or a non-clustered one. Both scale with the size of the table, so they get slower as data grows. An index seek uses the B-tree structure to navigate directly to the matching rows, reading only a few pages to find them. That scales with the number of matching rows, not the table size.

Seeks aren't always better, though. If a query needs a large percentage of the table, a scan can genuinely be cheaper than thousands of seeks plus lookups, and the optimizer chooses that on purpose. The problem is an unexpected scan for a selective query, usually caused by a missing index, a non-SARGable predicate, or a data type mismatch.

In our slow shipment list, the plan showed a clustered index scan for a query that needed a few hundred rows. Fixing the predicate and adding the right index turned it into a seek, and reads dropped from [about 400,000 to 2,000]. I can explain how to spot that in a plan.
cards.k: table scan, index scan, index seek, sql server, performance, index, indexes, clustered, non-clustered, composite index, filtered index

cards.q: What is query cardinality, and what are statistics?
cards.h: Wrong guess of crowd size, wrong size of venue.
s: Cardinality is the number of rows the optimizer expects at each step of a query plan. Statistics are what it uses to make those estimates.

Statistics are objects that describe how values are distributed in a column or index, mainly through a histogram of up to 200 steps, plus density information. When the optimizer sees a filter like StudyId equals 42, it uses the histogram to estimate how many rows will match. That estimate drives every decision: which index to use, which join type, and how much memory to grant. If the estimate is badly wrong, the plan can be terrible, for example a nested loop over a million rows, or a sort that spills to tempdb.

Statistics go stale when data changes a lot, for example after a big data load. SQL Server updates them automatically after enough changes, but on large tables that threshold can be reached late. Then I update them manually, or schedule maintenance.

The symptom to look for is a big gap between estimated and actual rows in the actual plan. In our IRT system, after a large data import, [one query became slow until we updated statistics], which is why we now update stats after big imports. I can explain how this relates to parameter sniffing.
cards.k: cardinality, statistics, query optimizer, sql server

cards.q: UNION vs UNION ALL?
cards.h: ALL = keep everything.
s: Both combine the results of two or more queries into one result set, with the same columns. The difference is how they treat duplicates.

UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result. To do that, SQL Server has to compare all rows, which means an extra sort or hash operation, and that costs CPU and memory, and can spill to tempdb on large results. UNION ALL simply appends the results and keeps every row, including duplicates. It's faster, because there's no deduplication step, and it can stream results without waiting for all of them.

So my default is UNION ALL. I only use UNION when I actually need distinct rows, and the inputs can genuinely overlap. Very often the two queries can't produce the same row anyway, for example combining "shipments from depot A" with "shipments from depot B", and then UNION is just wasted work.

It's one of those small things I look for in code reviews of SQL, because people often write UNION out of habit. On a large reporting query, switching to UNION ALL removed an expensive sort from the plan. I can explain how to read that in the execution plan.
cards.k: union, union all, sql

cards.q: EXISTS vs IN?
cards.h: NOT IN + NULL = surprise empty result.
s: EXISTS and IN both check whether a value has a match in another set, and modern SQL Server often produces the same plan for both. But there are differences worth knowing.

EXISTS checks whether a subquery returns any row, and stops at the first match, so it's naturally efficient for existence checks. It's also correlated, meaning it can compare several columns. IN compares a value against a list of values, or the result of a subquery. For a short fixed list, like status IN Pending and Shipped, IN is the clearest. For subqueries, the optimizer usually converts both into the same semi-join.

The important difference is with negation and NULLs. NOT IN returns no rows at all if the subquery returns even one NULL, because comparing with NULL is unknown. That's a classic, silent bug. NOT EXISTS doesn't have that problem. So I always prefer NOT EXISTS for "find rows with no match".

For example, "sites with no shipments" in our system is written with NOT EXISTS against the shipments table, which is correct and uses the foreign key index efficiently. In EF Core, a negated Any translates to exactly that. I can show an example of the NOT IN bug.
cards.k: exists, in, not exists, not in, sql

cards.q: CTE vs temporary table?
cards.h: CTE = sticky note; temp table = scratch notebook.
s: Both hold an intermediate result inside a larger query, but they behave very differently.

A CTE, defined with WITH, is a named query that exists only for the single statement that follows it. It's not stored anywhere; the optimizer simply expands it into the main query, like a view. So it's mainly about readability, breaking a complex query into named steps. It's also the only way to write recursive queries, like walking a depot hierarchy. But if you reference a CTE twice, it may be computed twice. A temporary table, with a hash prefix, is actually materialised in tempdb. It can have indexes, it gets its own statistics, and it can be reused across several statements in the same session or procedure.

So my rule: CTE for readability and recursion in a single query. Temp table when the intermediate result is large, reused multiple times, or when the optimizer is making bad estimates on a complex query, because materialising it with real statistics often gives a much better plan.

In our IRT reporting, a heavy monthly report became much faster when I moved a large intermediate step from a CTE into an indexed temp table. Table variables are another option, for small sets. I can explain the difference.
cards.k: cte, temporary table, temp table, sql

cards.q: ROW_NUMBER() vs RANK() vs DENSE_RANK()?
cards.h: Number, Rank with gaps, Dense without gaps.
s: All three are window functions that number rows within a partition, based on an ORDER BY. The difference is how they handle ties, rows with the same ordering value.

ROW_NUMBER gives every row a unique sequential number, 1, 2, 3, 4, even if values tie. The order among tied rows is arbitrary, unless you add a tie-breaker column. RANK gives tied rows the same rank, and then leaves a gap. So if two rows tie for second place, you get 1, 2, 2, 4. DENSE_RANK also gives ties the same rank, but without gaps: 1, 2, 2, 3.

The use cases follow from that. ROW_NUMBER is for picking exactly one row per group, like the latest status per shipment, or for deduplication, or paging. RANK is for competition-style rankings, where gaps make sense. DENSE_RANK is for questions like "the top 3 distinct values", for example the sites with the three highest dispensing counts, including ties.
In our IRT database, I use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by shipment, ordered by status date descending, to get each shipment's current status from the history table. I can write that query out.
cards.k: row_number, rank, dense_rank, window functions, sql

cards.q: How do you find duplicate records?
cards.h: GROUP BY + HAVING > 1.
s: There are two common ways to find duplicates in SQL, and the second also helps you clean them up.

The first is GROUP BY with HAVING. For example, select KitNumber and COUNT star from Kits, group by KitNumber, having COUNT star greater than 1. That lists every value that appears more than once, and how many times. If duplicates are defined by several columns, I group by all of them.

The second uses ROW_NUMBER. Over PARTITION BY KitNumber ORDER BY Id, each row in a group of duplicates gets a number, 1, 2, 3. Rows with number 1 are the ones to keep, usually the oldest, and rows with a number greater than 1 are the extras. Wrapped in a CTE, I can review them, and if appropriate, delete or merge them.
Then, most importantly, I prevent it from happening again with a unique constraint, and fix the code path that allowed it.

In a regulated system, I wouldn't just delete duplicates. We'd investigate the root cause, document it, and apply a reviewed data fix with an audit trail. I've done that for a duplicate import issue, which is also why our CSV import now uses a file hash. I can walk through that.
cards.k: duplicate records, group by, having, row_number, sql

cards.q: How do you find the second-highest or nth-highest salary?
cards.h: DENSE_RANK = N, ties handled.
s: There are a few ways to find the nth-highest value, and the main thing to get right is how ties are handled.

The cleanest general approach uses DENSE_RANK. Rank the salaries with DENSE_RANK over ORDER BY Salary descending, in a CTE, and then select the rows where the rank equals N. Because DENSE_RANK gives equal salaries the same rank, with no gaps, "second highest" really means the second distinct salary, and it returns every employee who earns it. Another approach is SELECT DISTINCT Salary ORDER BY Salary descending, then OFFSET N minus 1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROW ONLY. And for just the second highest, a classic answer is SELECT MAX Salary WHERE Salary is less than the overall MAX.
The trap is using ROW_NUMBER or TOP without DISTINCT. If two people share the highest salary, "second row" gives you the highest salary again, which is wrong.
I also mention what happens if there's no Nth value, for example fewer than N distinct salaries: these queries return nothing, or null with MAX, and the caller should handle that.
In my day-to-day work, the same pattern answers questions like "the second most recent shipment per site". I can write the full query if you like.
cards.k: nth highest salary, second highest, dense_rank, sql

cards.q: How do you get the top N records per group?
cards.h: Partition, number, filter.
s: "Top N per group" is one of the most common SQL patterns, for example the three most recent shipments for each site.

The standard solution uses ROW_NUMBER in a CTE. Select from Shipments, adding ROW_NUMBER OVER PARTITION BY SiteId ORDER BY ShipDate descending, as rn. PARTITION BY restarts the numbering for each site, and ORDER BY decides which rows come first. Then, in the outer query, select where rn is less than or equal to 3. If ties should be included, I use RANK or DENSE_RANK instead. An alternative is CROSS APPLY: for each site, apply a subquery that selects TOP 3 shipments for that site ordered by date. With a good index on SiteId and ShipDate, CROSS APPLY can be very efficient when there are few groups and many rows per group, because it seeks per group.
Either way, an index on the partition column and the order column, like SiteId and ShipDate, is what makes it fast.

In EF Core, the same thing can be written with GroupBy and Take inside a Select, and recent versions translate it into a ROW_NUMBER query. In our IRT dashboards, we use this pattern to show each site's latest shipments. I can write it out.
cards.k: top n per group, row_number, partition by, cross apply, sql

cards.q: What are dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads?
cards.h: Dirty = unsaved, non-repeatable = changed, phantom = new.
s: These are three concurrency problems that can happen when transactions run at the same time, and isolation levels exist to prevent them.

A dirty read is reading data that another transaction has changed but not yet committed. If that transaction rolls back, you've read data that never really existed. A non-repeatable read is when you read the same row twice in one transaction and get different values, because another transaction updated and committed it in between. A phantom read is when you run the same range query twice, like all pending shipments for a site, and the second time new rows appear, because another transaction inserted them.

Isolation levels map to these. Read Uncommitted allows all three. Read Committed, SQL Server's default, prevents dirty reads. Repeatable Read also prevents non-repeatable reads. Serializable prevents phantoms too. Snapshot isolation gives a consistent view of the data as of the start of the transaction, without blocking writers.

In practice, I pick the level per use case. For example, when allocating kits to a site, a phantom could mean promising the same stock twice, so that short transaction uses stricter isolation. I can explain how snapshot isolation works.
cards.k: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, isolation levels

cards.q: What is ACID?
cards.h: All, Correct, Alone, Durable.
s: ACID is the set of four guarantees that a reliable database transaction provides.

Atomicity means all or nothing. If a transaction has five steps and the fourth fails, the first three are rolled back, so you never end up halfway. Consistency means a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, so all rules, like constraints, foreign keys and checks, still hold after it commits. Isolation means concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other, and each behaves as if it were running alone, to the degree set by the isolation level. Durability means once a transaction is committed, it stays committed, even if the server crashes a second later, because SQL Server writes changes to the transaction log on disk before confirming the commit.
These guarantees are why relational databases are the backbone of systems where correctness really matters.

In clinical trials, that's critical. When a subject is randomised, recording the assignment and allocating the kit must happen together or not at all. With a single ACID transaction, we never get a subject randomised without a kit. Across services, where we can't have one transaction, we use outbox and sagas instead. I can explain those.
cards.k: acid, atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability, transactions

cards.q: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?
cards.h: Optimistic = check on save; pessimistic = lock before edit.
s: These are two strategies for handling two users or processes trying to change the same data at the same time.

Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare. It doesn't lock anything while the user works. Instead, each row has a version, like a SQL Server rowversion column. When saving, the update includes WHERE version equals the original version. If someone else changed the row in the meantime, no row is updated, and the application detects the conflict and handles it, by retrying, merging, or returning 409 to the user. In EF Core, that's a concurrency token and DbUpdateConcurrencyException. It's scalable, because no locks are held.

Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely, so it locks the rows up front, for example with an UPDLOCK hint inside a transaction, and others must wait. It guarantees no conflicts, but reduces concurrency, and long locks cause blocking and deadlocks.

So my rule: optimistic by default, pessimistic only for short, high-contention critical sections. In our IRT system, editing shipments and sites is optimistic. But allocating the last available drug kits at a depot uses a short pessimistic lock, because two sites must never get the same kit. I can explain that design.
cards.k: optimistic locking, pessimistic locking, concurrency, rowversion

cards.q: How do you optimize database performance?
cards.h: Measure, fix the worst, then scale.
s: My approach to database performance is always to measure first, fix the biggest problems, and then measure again.

First, find what's actually slow. Query Store shows the most expensive queries by CPU, duration and reads, wait statistics show what the server is waiting on, and application metrics show which endpoints suffer. Second, fix the top queries. That usually means proper indexes, SARGable predicates, avoiding SELECT star, removing N+1 patterns from the application, and checking execution plans. Third, the schema and maintenance: correct data types, sensible normalisation, up-to-date statistics, and index maintenance. Fourth, reduce load: cache reference data in the application or Redis, use read replicas for reporting, and archive or partition old data. And keep transactions short, to reduce blocking and deadlocks.
Only after that do I consider scaling up the server, because hardware hides problems rather than fixing them.

My best example is our shipment list, which went from [about 9 seconds to under 300 ms], and logical reads from [about 400,000 to 2,000], with a predicate rewrite, a covering index and paging, no hardware changes at all. I can walk through that.
cards.k: database performance, optimization, query store, indexes, tuning

cards.q: How do you design indexes?
cards.h: Index for the questions you actually ask.
s: I design indexes from real query patterns, not by guessing, and I always weigh the read benefit against the write cost.

The clustered index should usually be narrow, unique, static and ever-increasing, like an integer identity, because every non-clustered index carries the clustered key, and random keys cause page splits. Then non-clustered indexes. I index foreign key columns, since SQL Server doesn't do it automatically, and the columns used in frequent filters and joins. For composite indexes, I put equality columns first and range columns last, and add INCLUDE columns for what the query selects, so it's covered without key lookups. For hot subsets, like only pending records, a filtered index can be much smaller.

Then I verify. I check the execution plan to confirm the index is actually used, and over time I look at the index usage DMVs to find indexes that are never read but are constantly updated, and remove unused or duplicate ones.

The covering index from our shipment list fix is a good example: StudyId and Status for equality, ShipmentDate for the range, plus the displayed columns. We also tested its write impact in validation. I can explain how I'd find missing indexes.
cards.k: index design, composite index, covering index, sql server

cards.q: What are microservices?
cards.h: Small teams, small services, own data.
s: Microservices is an architectural style where an application is built as a set of small, independently deployable services. Each service owns one business capability and its own data, and they communicate over APIs or messages.

The key word is independent. Each service can be developed, deployed, scaled and even written in a different technology, without coordinating a big release with everyone else. A service owns its database, so no other service reaches into its tables; it shares data only through its API or events. That gives teams autonomy, and a failure in one service can be isolated instead of taking down everything.

But it's a trade-off. You exchange the simplicity of one process for the complexity of a distributed system: network failures, eventual consistency, distributed tracing, and a lot more DevOps work. So it pays off for large systems and multiple teams, not for every project.

In my work, our IRT platform is built as microservices, for example randomisation, supply, shipments and notifications, as ASP.NET Core services on AWS ECS, communicating via REST and RabbitMQ. I coordinate releases across [about 5] scrum teams. I can explain how we drew the service boundaries.
cards.k: microservices, architecture, distributed systems, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of microservices?
cards.h: Freedom costs operations.
s: Microservices bring real benefits, but every benefit comes with a cost.

The advantages: independent deployment, so one team can release without waiting for others. Independent scaling, so only the busy service gets more instances. Fault isolation, so a failure in notifications doesn't stop randomisation. Team autonomy, with clear ownership of each service. And freedom to choose the best technology per service.

The disadvantages: everything becomes a network call, which adds latency and new failure modes, so you need timeouts, retries and circuit breakers. Data is distributed, so you lose simple transactions and must handle eventual consistency, with patterns like outbox and sagas. Testing and debugging across services is harder, so you need contract tests, correlation ids and distributed tracing. And there's much more DevOps work: a pipeline per service, container orchestration, monitoring and alerting for many moving parts.

My summary is that microservices trade code complexity for operational complexity. It's worth it when you have several teams and parts of the system that genuinely change and scale differently. In our IRT platform, correlation ids and the outbox pattern were exactly the kind of investments this required. I can explain when I'd avoid them.
cards.k: microservices advantages, disadvantages, trade-offs, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: When would you NOT use microservices?
cards.h: Don't build a fleet for one passenger.
s: I wouldn't use microservices when the costs clearly outweigh the benefits, which is more often than people think.

Some clear signals. A small team, because one team managing ten services spends more time on infrastructure than features. An early-stage product, where the domain isn't well understood yet, because wrong service boundaries are very expensive to fix later, and you end up with a distributed monolith, where every change touches several services. Low scale, where there's no need to scale parts independently. Low DevOps maturity, without solid CI/CD, monitoring and on-call, because microservices depend on all of that. And a domain that needs strong transactional consistency across most of its data, where splitting the data creates more problems than it solves.

In those cases, I'd start with a modular monolith: one deployable application, but with clear internal module boundaries, separate schemas or at least separate DbContexts per module, and communication through interfaces or in-process events. If a module later needs independent scaling or a separate team, it can be extracted into a service with much less risk.
I'd rather earn microservices than start with them. I can describe how I'd extract a module from a monolith.
cards.k: when not to use microservices, monolith, modular monolith, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: How do you identify service boundaries, and what is a bounded context?
cards.h: One language per context, one service per context.
s: Service boundaries are the hardest part of microservices, and I use Domain-Driven Design, specifically bounded contexts, to find them.

A bounded context is an area of the business where one model and one language stay consistent. The same word can mean different things in different contexts. For example, in clinical trials, a "kit" in the supply context is stock with a lot number and expiry date, while in the dispensing context, it's something assigned to a subject at a visit. Each bounded context is a natural candidate for a service, with its own model and its own data.

To find them, I look at business capabilities, like randomisation, supply management, shipments, consent and notifications. Then I check some signals: Does each area own its own data? Do they change at different rates, or belong to different teams? And how chatty would they be? If two candidate services constantly need synchronous calls to each other to do anything, the boundary is probably wrong, and they belong together.

In our IRT platform, randomisation, supply and shipments are separate contexts that communicate mainly through events, which keeps them loosely coupled. I can explain how event storming helps discover these boundaries.
cards.k: service boundaries, bounded context, ddd, domain driven design, microservices, microservice, service boundary, distributed

cards.q: How should microservices communicate?
cards.h: Ask with REST, announce with events.
s: Microservices communicate in two main ways, and choosing between them depends on whether the caller needs an immediate answer.

Synchronous communication, with REST or gRPC, is request and response. The caller waits for the result. It's simple and intuitive, and it's the right choice when the caller genuinely needs the answer now, like the UI loading a study, or checking whether a subject is eligible. gRPC is useful for high-performance internal calls. The downside is temporal coupling: if the callee is slow or down, the caller is too.

Asynchronous communication uses messages through a broker, like RabbitMQ or Kafka. Commands ask another service to do something, and events announce that something happened, like "shipment dispatched". The producer doesn't wait, and doesn't even need to know who's listening. That decouples services, absorbs traffic spikes and survives temporary outages, but it brings eventual consistency and harder tracing.

Whatever the style, every contract, API or message, is versioned and kept backward compatible. In our IRT platform, the UI and partners use REST, and workflows between services use RabbitMQ events, with an outbox for reliability. I can explain when we chose Kafka instead.
cards.k: microservices communication, rest, grpc, messaging, async, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: REST vs messaging; synchronous vs asynchronous communication?
cards.h: Phone call vs letter.
s: The core difference is whether the caller waits.

With synchronous communication, like REST or gRPC, the caller sends a request and waits for the response. It's simple to build and debug, and the caller gets an immediate, definite result. But it creates temporal coupling: both services must be up at the same time. If the callee is slow, the caller is slow too, and long chains of synchronous calls multiply latency and failure risk.

With asynchronous messaging, through queues or event streams, the sender publishes a message and moves on. The receiver processes it when it can. That decouples services: if the receiver is down, messages wait safely in the queue. It absorbs load spikes, and new consumers can subscribe without changing the producer. The costs are eventual consistency, because the result isn't immediate, more complex error handling with retries, dead-letter queues and idempotency, and harder end-to-end tracing.

My rule is: use synchronous when the user or caller needs the answer now, and asynchronous for everything that can happen in the background. In our platform, creating a shipment is a REST call, but notifying the vendor and updating inventory happen through RabbitMQ events. I can explain how we trace those flows.
cards.k: rest vs messaging, synchronous, asynchronous, communication, messaging, message broker, kafka, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: What is service discovery?
cards.h: A live phone book for services.
s: Service discovery is how services find each other's current network address, when instances are constantly starting, stopping and moving.

In a cloud or container environment, you can't hard-code IP addresses. Containers are replaced on every deployment, scaled up and down automatically, and restarted on failure, and each time they may get a new IP. Service discovery solves this with a registry that tracks healthy instances, and a stable name that callers use.

There are two common approaches. Server-side discovery through a load balancer: callers use a stable DNS name for the load balancer, which knows the healthy targets. In AWS, that's an internal Application Load Balancer in front of ECS services. And DNS-based discovery built into the platform: in Kubernetes, a Service gives a stable DNS name, and in ECS, Service Connect or Cloud Map registers tasks automatically. There's also client-side discovery, where the client asks a registry and picks an instance itself, which was common with tools like Consul or Eureka.

In our setup, services find each other through stable DNS names in configuration, backed by internal load balancers and ECS service registration, with health checks removing unhealthy instances. I can explain how health checks feed into it.
cards.k: service discovery, dns, cloud map, service connect, kubernetes

cards.q: Why shouldn't you retry everything?
cards.h: Retry the hiccup, not the refusal.
s: Retries are useful, but retrying everything can turn a small problem into a big one.

There are three main dangers. First, non-idempotent operations. If a POST to create a shipment timed out, it may have actually succeeded. Retrying it blindly can create a duplicate. So I only retry operations that are idempotent, or made idempotent with an idempotency key. Second, permanent errors. A 400 validation error, a 401 or a 404 won't succeed the second time, so retrying just wastes time and resources and delays the real error. Third, retry storms. If a service is struggling and every client retries aggressively, the load multiplies, and the struggling service can never recover. With several layers each retrying three times, one request can become dozens.

So I retry only transient errors, like timeouts, 503s, 429s and network failures. I use exponential backoff with jitter, so clients don't retry in sync, a small maximum number of attempts, and a circuit breaker to stop retrying a service that's clearly down. And I retry at one layer only, not at every level.
That's how our vendor API calls are configured with the standard resilience handler. I can explain how jitter helps.
cards.k: retries, retry storm, idempotency, backoff, resilience

cards.q: What is bulkhead isolation?
cards.h: One flooded room doesn't sink the ship.
s: Bulkhead isolation is a resilience pattern that stops one failing dependency from taking down everything else. The name comes from ships, which are divided into watertight compartments, so a leak in one doesn't sink the whole ship.

In software, the problem is shared resources. If a service calls three dependencies, and one becomes very slow, requests to it pile up and hold threads, connections or memory. Eventually the whole service runs out, and even requests that don't need the slow dependency start failing. A bulkhead gives each dependency its own limited pool of resources: a maximum number of concurrent calls, a separate connection pool, or a separate queue. When one dependency's pool is full, extra calls to it fail fast, or queue briefly, but other dependencies keep working normally.
In .NET, Polly's concurrency limiter, or the rate limiter strategy, implements this per HttpClient. At the infrastructure level, running separate worker services per queue is also a bulkhead.

In our platform, slow vendor SFTP transfers run in their own worker service with their own limits, so a slow vendor never affects randomisation or the main API. I can explain how it combines with circuit breakers.
cards.k: bulkhead, isolation, resilience, concurrency limiter

cards.q: What is distributed tracing?
cards.h: Breadcrumbs across services.
s: Distributed tracing is the ability to follow a single request as it travels through multiple services, and see where time is spent and where errors happen.

Each incoming request gets a trace id. Every service that handles part of it records a span, a timed unit of work, like "handle HTTP request", "query database" or "publish message", with the trace id and a parent span id. The trace context is passed along between services in headers, using the W3C traceparent standard, and in message headers for queues. The spans are sent to a tracing backend, like AWS X-Ray, Jaeger or Grafana Tempo, which reassembles them into a timeline, a waterfall view showing every hop and how long it took.

In .NET, OpenTelemetry is the standard way to do this. ASP.NET Core, HttpClient and many libraries already create spans automatically through Activity, so you mostly add the exporter and a few custom spans.

Before full tracing, we solved the most painful part with our correlation-id middleware in [2024], which links logs across our [4] services. Tracing adds timing on top of that, so you can see, for example, that a slow request was waiting on one database query in one service. I can explain how logs and traces connect.
cards.k: distributed tracing, opentelemetry, trace id, spans, observability

cards.q: What is eventual consistency?
cards.h: Consistent soon, not instantly.
s: Eventual consistency means that when data changes in one service, other services will see the change, but not instantly. After a short delay, everything becomes consistent.

In a microservices system, each service owns its data, and they share changes through events. When the shipment service marks a shipment as dispatched, it publishes an event, and the inventory and notification services update their own data when they process it, maybe a few hundred milliseconds later. During that window, different services can show slightly different states. We accept that in exchange for availability and loose coupling, because the alternative, distributed transactions across services, is slow and fragile.

The important part is designing for it. Use clear intermediate states, like Pending or Processing, so users understand that something is in progress. Make consumers idempotent, because events can arrive twice. Handle out-of-order events, for example with version numbers. And monitor for messages that fail, so nothing stays inconsistent forever.

In our IRT platform, the UI shows a shipment as "Requested" until the vendor confirms it, rather than pretending it's instant. And dead-letter queue alarms make sure stuck events are investigated. I can explain where we still need strong consistency.
cards.k: eventual consistency, distributed systems, events

cards.q: How do you handle failures between services?
cards.h: Expect failure, design the recovery.
s: Failures between services are normal in a distributed system, so I design for them at several levels.

For synchronous calls: a timeout on every call, so nothing hangs forever. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, only for transient errors and idempotent operations. A circuit breaker, so we stop calling a service that's clearly down and fail fast instead. And a fallback where it makes sense, like serving cached reference data.

For workflows that don't need an immediate answer, I prefer asynchronous messaging with durable queues. If the consumer is down, messages wait. Failed messages are retried a limited number of times and then moved to a dead-letter queue, so they're not lost and don't block the queue. Consumers are idempotent, so redelivered messages are safe. For multi-step business processes across services, a saga coordinates the steps, and compensating actions undo earlier steps if a later one fails.
And all of this needs monitoring: alerts on error rates, circuit breaker state, queue depth and dead-letter queues.
A real example: during our RabbitMQ incident in [mid-2024], publisher confirms and outbox retries meant that [about 1,200] updates were delayed, but none were lost. I can walk through that story.
cards.k: failure handling, resilience, timeout, retry, circuit breaker, dlq

cards.q: How do you version microservices?
cards.h: Add, don't break.
s: Versioning microservices is about letting each service evolve without breaking the others, because they're deployed independently.

For APIs, I version in the URL or a header, like /api/v2, and stay backward compatible within a version. Additive changes, like new optional fields or new endpoints, are fine. Removing or renaming fields, or changing their meaning, is breaking, and needs a new version. The old version stays available, is marked deprecated, and is removed only after consumers have moved, which we confirm in the logs. For messages and events, the same rules apply: additive changes only, a schema version field in the message, and consumers that tolerate unknown fields. For a breaking change, we publish a new event type or version, sometimes both in parallel during the transition.
Consumers should also be tolerant readers: ignore fields they don't understand, and don't fail on them.

The deployable artifacts are versioned too: container images use semantic versions and the git commit, so we always know exactly what's running. In our pipelines, we compare OpenAPI documents between versions to catch accidental breaking changes. I can explain consumer-driven contract tests, which help here too.
cards.k: microservices versioning, api versioning, backward compatibility, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: How do you deploy microservices?
cards.h: Own pipeline, own pace.
s: The key principle is that every microservice can be built, tested and deployed independently.

Each service has its own CI/CD pipeline. It builds the code, runs unit and integration tests, runs quality and security scans like a SonarQube gate and container image scanning, builds a Docker image tagged with the version and commit, and pushes it to a registry like Amazon ECR. Infrastructure is defined as code, with Terraform or CloudFormation, so environments are reproducible. Then the pipeline deploys to the orchestrator, ECS or Kubernetes, environment by environment.

For the deployment itself, I use rolling updates by default: new tasks start, pass health checks, and only then are old tasks drained and stopped, so there's no downtime. For riskier changes, blue-green or canary deployments let us shift traffic gradually and switch back instantly. Automated rollback triggers if health checks or alarms fail. Database changes are backward compatible, so old and new versions can run side by side during the rollout.

In our regulated environment, deployments to validated environments go through approval gates, with release evidence attached. I coordinate those releases across [about 5] scrum teams. I can explain how we handle a rollback.
cards.k: microservices deployment, ci/cd, ecs, rolling deployment, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: How do you monitor microservices?
cards.h: Metrics, logs, traces, alerts.
s: Monitoring microservices means being able to answer, quickly, "is anything broken, where, and why" across many services.

I think of three pillars. Metrics: for each service, the golden signals, which are latency, traffic, errors and saturation, plus business metrics like shipments processed. For message-driven services, queue depth, consumer lag and dead-letter queue counts are essential. Logs: structured JSON logs from every service, centralised in one place, with a correlation id so one search shows a request across services.
