Traces: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, to see the path and timing of a request through every hop.

On top of that, dashboards in Grafana or CloudWatch per service and per business flow, and alerts based on service level objectives, like "p95 latency above 500 ms for 5 minutes", or "any message in a dead-letter queue". Alerts must be actionable, or people start ignoring them.

In our platform, CloudWatch and Grafana dashboards show each service's health, and our correlation-id work from [2024] means support can trace a failed request across [4] services in [a few minutes] instead of [about an hour]. I can explain how we tune alerts to avoid noise.
cards.k: microservices monitoring, observability, metrics, logs, tracing, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: How do you secure service-to-service communication?
cards.h: Zero trust: every call shows ID.
s: I secure service-to-service communication on the principle of zero trust: a request isn't trusted just because it comes from inside our network.

There are several layers. Network: services run in private subnets inside a VPC, with security groups allowing only the expected traffic, so most services aren't reachable from the internet at all. Encryption: TLS between services, and mutual TLS where policy requires, so both sides prove their identity. Identity: each service has its own identity, either OAuth client-credentials tokens from the identity provider, with specific scopes, or IAM roles when calling AWS services. The receiving service validates the token and its scopes on every call, just as it would for a user. Least privilege: each service gets only the permissions it needs. And secrets, like client secrets or keys, live in AWS Secrets Manager, never in code or images, and are rotated.
The point is that if one service is compromised, the attacker shouldn't automatically be able to call everything else.

In our platform, internal services call each other with client-credential tokens and scopes, and use IAM roles for AWS resources, with no long-lived keys. I can explain how token caching works for service calls.
cards.k: service-to-service security, mtls, client credentials, iam, zero trust

cards.q: How do you prevent cascading failures?
cards.h: Firebreaks between services.
s: A cascading failure is when one slow or failing service causes its callers to fail, and then their callers, until the whole system is down. Preventing it is about containing failure.

The main techniques work together. Timeouts on every call, so a slow dependency can't hold threads forever. Circuit breakers, so after repeated failures we stop calling and fail fast, giving the dependency time to recover. Bulkheads, so each dependency has its own limited resources and can't exhaust the whole service. Rate limiting and load shedding, so when overloaded, a service rejects some requests quickly rather than slowing down for everyone. Asynchronous queues, which absorb spikes and decouple services. Caching and graceful degradation, so non-essential features can be switched off while core features keep working. And careful retries with backoff and jitter, because aggressive retries are often what turns a slowdown into an outage.
Architecturally, the biggest factor is avoiding long chains of synchronous calls, because each hop multiplies the risk.

In our IRT platform, vendor integrations run asynchronously in separate workers. So when a vendor's system was slow, only vendor transfers were delayed. Randomisation and the main UI weren't affected. I can explain how we tested that.
cards.k: cascading failure, circuit breaker, timeout, bulkhead, resilience

cards.q: How do you test microservices?
cards.h: Unit, integration, contract, a little E2E.
s: Testing microservices needs several layers, because a lot of the risk is in how services interact, not just inside each one.

Unit tests cover the business logic of each service, quickly and in isolation. Integration tests check each service with its real dependencies, like a real SQL Server and RabbitMQ in containers with Testcontainers, so queries, serialisation and messaging configuration are tested. Contract tests check the agreements between services. With consumer-driven contracts, using a tool like Pact, each consumer defines what it expects from a provider, and the provider's pipeline verifies it still meets those expectations. That catches breaking changes before deployment, without needing every service running together. A small number of end-to-end tests then cover the critical business journeys across the whole system.
For resilience, load tests and chaos tests, like killing an instance or adding latency, verify that timeouts, retries and circuit breakers really work.

In our IRT work, integration tests with WebApplicationFactory and real databases caught the most bugs per effort, and Playwright and Cucumber tests cover critical flows like randomisation for validation evidence. I can explain how contract tests fit into the pipeline.
cards.k: microservices testing, contract testing, integration tests, test, testing, unit test, integration test, xunit, moq, mock, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: How do you manage configuration across services?
cards.h: One source of config truth per environment.
s: Configuration across many services needs to be consistent, secure and traceable, without rebuilding images for each environment.

The principle is "build once, configure per environment". The same container image runs everywhere, and only configuration changes. Non-secret settings come from environment variables and a central store, like AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, organised by path, like /irt/production/shipments. Secrets, like database passwords, API keys and certificates, live in AWS Secrets Manager, with encryption, access controlled by IAM, and automatic rotation. They're never in code, images or appsettings files committed to git. The values for each environment are managed through infrastructure as code, so changes are reviewed and versioned. Each service loads its configuration at startup, binds it to typed Options classes, and validates it with ValidateOnStart, so a missing or invalid setting fails the deployment immediately.
For settings that must change without a redeploy, like feature flags, a dynamic source with IOptionsMonitor or a feature flag service works well.
In our services, Secrets Manager and Parameter Store feed ASP.NET Core configuration, and per-vendor SFTP settings are named options. I can explain how we rotate secrets without downtime.
cards.k: configuration management, parameter store, secrets manager, options pattern

cards.q: How do you handle centralized logging?
cards.h: All logs, one place, one format.
s: Centralised logging means all services send their logs to one place, in a consistent format, so you can search across the whole system instead of logging into individual servers or containers.

Each service writes structured JSON logs, with message templates, not free text. Every log line carries common fields: service name, environment, version, and most importantly a correlation id, plus business identifiers like ShipmentId where relevant. Containers write logs to standard output, and the platform ships them to the central store, like CloudWatch Logs, OpenSearch, or Grafana Loki. Then one query can show everything that happened for one request, across every service. Log levels are controlled in configuration, so we can increase detail temporarily without redeploying.

Two rules are critical. Retention policies, so we keep logs as long as needed for support and compliance, but not forever. And never logging secrets or personal or clinical data, which in our domain is a regulatory issue.

In our platform, logs go to CloudWatch, and since our correlation-id rollout in [2024], a saved Logs Insights query by correlation id shows a request's full journey across [4] services. That cut support triage from [about an hour to a few minutes]. I can show a sample query.
cards.k: centralized logging, cloudwatch, structured logging, correlation id, logging, ilogger, serilog, observability, tracing

cards.q: How would you design a scalable microservices architecture?
cards.h: Gateway, stateless services, own data, events, eyes everywhere.
s: I'd design it in layers, with scalability and resilience built into each one.

At the edge, an API gateway or load balancer handles routing, TLS, authentication and rate limiting. Behind it, stateless services, so any instance can handle any request, running in containers on ECS or Kubernetes with autoscaling on CPU, requests or queue depth. For data, each service owns its database, so they scale and change independently. A Redis cache takes repeated reads off the database, read replicas serve reporting, and very high-volume, simple access patterns can use DynamoDB.

Between services, I prefer asynchronous events through Kafka or RabbitMQ for workflows. That absorbs traffic spikes and decouples services. The outbox pattern makes publishing reliable, and consumers are idempotent so retries are safe. Synchronous calls are kept for cases that need an immediate answer, with timeouts, retries and circuit breakers.
Across everything: observability with metrics, logs and tracing, CI/CD per service with infrastructure as code, and security with service identities and secrets management.
That's broadly how our IRT platform on AWS works: ASP.NET Core services on ECS behind an ALB, SQL Server on RDS, ElastiCache, and RabbitMQ with an outbox. I can draw it on a whiteboard.
cards.k: scalable architecture, microservices design, system design, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: Why did you choose REST here?
cards.h: Need the answer now? REST.
s: I chose REST where the caller needs an immediate, definite answer, as part of a request and response interaction.

Typical cases are the UI and partner systems. When a site user opens a study, randomises a subject, or requests a shipment, they need to know the result right now: did it succeed, and what was assigned? That's a natural request-response interaction, and REST over HTTP is the simplest way to model it. It's also universally understood. Front-end developers, external partners and testers all know it, tools like Swagger and Postman make it easy to explore and test, and responses can be cached where appropriate. Errors map cleanly to HTTP status codes and ProblemDetails, and it works through every proxy and firewall.

I didn't choose REST for everything, though. For things that can happen in the background, like updating inventory after a shipment, notifying vendors or sending emails, we use messaging, because the caller shouldn't wait for or depend on those services.
So the decision is really about coupling and timing: REST for "I need the answer now", events for "something happened, whoever cares can react". I can explain why we used Kafka in some cases.
cards.k: why rest, api choice, design decision

cards.q: Why Kafka instead of REST?
cards.h: Many listeners, replayable history? Kafka.
s: I'd choose Kafka over REST when the communication is really "something happened" rather than "please give me an answer".

With REST, the producer calls each consumer directly, waits for each one, and needs to know who they are. If a consumer is down, the producer must handle it. With Kafka, the producer publishes an event to a topic once, and doesn't know or care who consumes it. Several consumers can read the same events independently, each at its own pace. Kafka also retains events for a configured period, so a consumer that was down catches up from where it left off, a new consumer can replay history, and you can reprocess events after fixing a bug. And it handles very high throughput.

So Kafka fits when producers shouldn't wait for consumers, multiple services need the same events, replay and retention matter, or volume is high. REST stays the right choice when the caller needs an immediate answer.

For example, shipment status events are needed by inventory, notifications, reporting and audit. Publishing them once to a topic, instead of the shipment service calling four other APIs, removed coupling and made adding a new consumer a non-event for the producer. I can compare Kafka with RabbitMQ too.
cards.k: kafka vs rest, event streaming, design decision, kafka, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, messaging, message broker, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: What happens if Kafka is unavailable?
cards.h: Outbox keeps the letters until the post office reopens.
s: Producers buffer and retry for a while, but if Kafka stays down, the app must not lose events. That's why we use the outbox pattern: events are saved in the database with the business change, and published when Kafka is back. Consumers simply pause and continue from their last committed offset when Kafka recovers.
cards.k: kafka unavailable, outbox, resilience, failure handling, kafka, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, event streaming, messaging, message broker, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: How do you guarantee exactly-once processing?
cards.h: At-least-once + idempotency = effectively once.
s: True exactly-once across systems is very hard. Kafka has transactions and idempotent producers for exactly-once inside Kafka. But when the consumer writes to a database or sends an email, I use at-least-once delivery with an idempotent consumer: a processed-messages table with a unique message id, so duplicates are skipped. That gives an exactly-once effect.
cards.k: exactly-once, idempotent consumer, kafka transactions, deduplication

cards.q: Explain your AWS architecture.
cards.h: Gateway, containers, data, events, eyes, code-defined.
s: Our services run as Docker containers on ECS Fargate in private subnets across two availability zones, behind an Application Load Balancer, with API Gateway and SSO in front. Data is in SQL Server on RDS with Multi-AZ, plus DynamoDB for some cases and ElastiCache Redis for caching. Secrets are in Secrets Manager, and we monitor with CloudWatch and Grafana. Deployments go through Azure DevOps.

cards.q: Why did you use AWS?
cards.h: Managed, compliant, global.
s: AWS was the company standard, and its managed services fit a small team: ECS Fargate means no servers to patch, RDS handles database backups and failover, and ElastiCache, Secrets Manager and CloudWatch cover caching, secrets and monitoring. That let us focus on building the product.

cards.q: ECS vs EKS?
cards.h: ECS = AWS's own; EKS = Kubernetes on AWS.
s: ECS is AWS's own container service. It's simpler, tightly integrated with AWS, and has no control plane cost. EKS is managed Kubernetes. It's more powerful and portable, with a huge ecosystem, but more complex to run. For a team focused on AWS, ECS is often enough, and that's what we use.

cards.q: What is Fargate?
cards.h: Containers without servers to babysit.
s: Fargate is the serverless way to run containers on ECS or EKS. I just define the CPU and memory for a task, and AWS runs it without me managing any EC2 servers or patching. I pay per second for what the task uses. All our ECS services run on Fargate.
cards.k: fargate, serverless containers, ecs, aws, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: API Gateway vs Application Load Balancer?
cards.h: Gateway = smart receptionist; ALB = traffic cop.
s: API Gateway is a managed API front door with features like authentication, throttling, request validation, usage plans and API keys, and it's great with Lambda. An ALB is a load balancer that routes HTTP traffic by path or host to containers or servers, and is cheaper at high volumes. Often we use API Gateway for public APIs, and an ALB in front of ECS services.
cards.k: api gateway, alb, application load balancer, comparison, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: What is Lambda?
cards.h: Code that wakes up on events.
s: Lambda is AWS's serverless compute. I upload a function, and AWS runs it in response to events, like an HTTP request, a file in S3, or a message in a queue, scaling automatically. I pay only for the time it runs. It's best for short, event-driven tasks. We used one for [shipment notifications].

cards.q: What is Lambda concurrency?
cards.h: How many copies run at once.
s: Concurrency is the number of Lambda instances running at the same time, and each one handles one request at a time. Accounts have a regional limit. Reserved concurrency guarantees and also caps the number for one function, which protects downstream things like databases. Provisioned concurrency keeps instances warm to avoid cold starts.
cards.k: lambda concurrency, reserved concurrency, provisioned concurrency, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: What is a Lambda timeout?
cards.h: Know when to give up.
s: A Lambda timeout is the maximum time a function can run, from 3 seconds by default up to 15 minutes. If it runs longer, it's stopped. I set it a bit above the normal run time, put timeouts on downstream calls, and remember that API Gateway has its own, shorter timeout. For long jobs, I use a different service, like ECS.
cards.k: lambda timeout, aws lambda, limits, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: What is DynamoDB?
cards.h: Lockers by key, any scale.
s: DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database. It gives very fast, predictable performance at any scale, with no servers to manage. I design it around access patterns, using partition and sort keys. It's great for simple, high-volume lookups, but not for complex joins or ad-hoc queries.
cards.k: dynamodb, nosql, key-value, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: What is a GSI, and what is an LSI?
cards.h: Global = new drawer system; local = new order inside the same drawer.
s: A GSI, global secondary index, lets me query by a completely different partition key, and I can add it any time. It's eventually consistent. An LSI, local secondary index, keeps the same partition key with a different sort key, must be created with the table, and can be strongly consistent. I use GSIs for most extra access patterns.
cards.k: gsi, lsi, secondary index, dynamodb

cards.q: What is RDS, and RDS vs an EC2-hosted database?
cards.h: RDS = database as a service.
s: RDS is AWS's managed relational database service for engines like SQL Server and PostgreSQL. AWS handles backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover and monitoring. Running a database on EC2 gives full control of the operating system and settings, but then we do all that work ourselves. For most cases, RDS is the better choice, and we use it for SQL Server.
cards.k: rds, ec2 database, managed database, aws

cards.q: Redis vs database?
cards.h: Redis = desk drawer; database = filing archive.
s: Redis keeps data in memory, so it's extremely fast, often under a millisecond, but it's best for temporary data like caches, sessions and counters. A database stores data durably and supports complex queries and transactions, but is slower. So the database is the source of truth, and Redis speeds up hot reads. Our logout denylist uses Redis with an expiry.
cards.k: redis, database, cache, elasticache, comparison, caching, memory cache, hybridcache, output caching

cards.q: How do you secure S3?
cards.h: Private, encrypted, logged, time-limited.
s: I keep buckets private with Block Public Access, and grant access through IAM roles and bucket policies with least privilege. Data is encrypted at rest with KMS and in transit with HTTPS only. I use presigned URLs for temporary access, turn on versioning for important data, and log access with CloudTrail.
cards.k: s3 security, bucket policy, encryption, block public access

cards.q: What is IAM, and IAM role vs user?
cards.h: User = permanent badge; role = visitor pass.
s: IAM is AWS's identity and access management: it controls who can do what on which resources. A user is a long-term identity, a person or app with permanent credentials. A role is an identity that's assumed temporarily, with short-lived credentials. I prefer roles everywhere, like ECS task roles, because there are no long-lived keys to leak.
cards.k: iam, iam role, iam user, aws security

cards.q: CloudWatch Logs vs Metrics?
cards.h: Logs tell stories; metrics draw graphs.
s: CloudWatch Logs stores the detailed text or JSON log events from our services, which I search with Logs Insights to see what exactly happened. CloudWatch Metrics are numbers over time, like CPU, request count or errors, which are cheap to keep and great for dashboards and alarms. I can also turn log patterns into metrics with metric filters.
cards.k: cloudwatch logs, cloudwatch metrics, monitoring, aws

cards.q: What are CloudWatch alarms?
cards.h: A smoke detector on a metric.
s: A CloudWatch alarm watches a metric and changes state when it crosses a threshold for a set time, like error rate above two percent for five minutes. It can send a notification through SNS to email or chat, or trigger actions like autoscaling. We have alarms on errors, latency and queue depth for our services.
cards.k: cloudwatch alarms, alerting, sns, monitoring

cards.q: How do you troubleshoot an AWS production issue?
cards.h: Scope, signals, logs, changes, fix.
s: I start with the dashboards to see what's affected and since when, and check if it matches a recent deployment or a change. Then I look at CloudWatch Logs Insights and traces with the correlation id, and check the health of dependencies like RDS or the message broker. I mitigate first, often with a rollback, then fix the root cause.
cards.k: aws troubleshooting, production issue, cloudwatch, incident, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam

cards.q: How do you design disaster recovery?
cards.h: RTO = how fast back; RPO = how much lost.
s: First I agree two numbers with the business: RPO, how much data we can lose, and RTO, how fast we must recover. Then I pick a strategy: backup and restore for relaxed targets, pilot light or warm standby for faster recovery, or active-active across regions for near zero. Infrastructure as code helps rebuild quickly, and we regularly test the recovery.
cards.k: disaster recovery, rpo, rto, backup, multi-region

cards.q: What is autoscaling?
cards.h: Thermostat for capacity.
s: Autoscaling adds or removes capacity automatically based on demand. In ECS, I use target tracking, for example keep average CPU around 60 percent or a set number of requests per task. It scales out quickly when load rises and scales in slowly to avoid flapping. The service must be stateless and shut down gracefully.
cards.k: autoscaling, target tracking, ecs, scaling

cards.q: Security Group vs NACL?
cards.h: SG = door guard who remembers you; NACL = gate that checks both ways.
s: A security group is a firewall on each resource, like an ECS task or a database. It's stateful, so return traffic is allowed automatically, and it has only allow rules. A NACL is a firewall on the whole subnet. It's stateless, so I need rules both ways, and it supports deny rules. We mostly rely on security groups.
cards.k: security group, nacl, network acl, aws networking, security, owasp, xss, csrf, sql injection, cors, cookie

cards.q: What is a NAT Gateway?
cards.h: One-way door to the internet.
s: A NAT Gateway lets resources in private subnets reach the internet for outbound calls, like downloading packages or calling external APIs, while nothing from the internet can connect in. It's charged per hour and per gigabyte, so for AWS services like S3, I use VPC endpoints instead to save cost.
cards.k: nat gateway, private subnet, vpc, aws networking

cards.q: How do containers access AWS services securely?
cards.h: Roles, not keys.
s: Each ECS task gets an IAM task role. The AWS SDK inside the container automatically picks up temporary credentials for that role, so there are no keys in code or config. The role allows only what that service needs, like reading one secret or one bucket. Traffic to AWS services can go through VPC endpoints.
cards.k: ecs task role, iam role, container security, aws credentials, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store?
cards.h: Secrets Manager rotates; Parameter Store stores.
s: Secrets Manager is built for secrets: it supports automatic rotation, for example of database passwords, and cross-account sharing, but costs per secret. Parameter Store is great for configuration and can store encrypted values too, with a free standard tier, but no built-in rotation. We use Secrets Manager for database credentials and Parameter Store for configuration.
cards.k: secrets manager, parameter store, secrets, configuration

cards.q: How do you reduce AWS cost?
cards.h: Right-size, schedule, commit, clean up.
s: First I find where the money goes using Cost Explorer and tags. Then I right-size over-sized resources, use Savings Plans for steady workloads, scale down non-production environments at night, and move to Graviton where possible. I also clean up unused resources and old snapshots, and use VPC endpoints to cut NAT costs.
cards.k: aws cost, cost optimization, savings plans, rightsizing, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch

cards.q: What happens if Terraform state is lost?
cards.h: No state, no memory: Terraform thinks the world is empty.
s: If the state file is lost, Terraform no longer knows which real resources it manages, so the next apply would try to create everything again and fail or duplicate things. The resources themselves still exist. To recover, I'd import them back into state, or restore a previous version from the versioned S3 bucket. That's why we keep state remote, versioned and locked.
cards.k: terraform state, lost state, terraform import, recovery, terraform, cloudformation, iac, infrastructure as code

cards.q: What are Terraform modules?
cards.h: Modules = functions for infrastructure.
s: A Terraform module is a reusable package of infrastructure code with inputs and outputs, like a function. For example, one module creates an ECS service with its load balancer rules, alarms and IAM role. Each service just calls the module with its own values. This keeps environments consistent and avoids copy-paste.
cards.k: terraform modules, reuse, infrastructure as code, terraform, cloudformation, iac

cards.q: How do you manage and structure environments in Terraform?
cards.h: Same modules, different values, separate state.
s: I keep the same modules for every environment, and change only the input values, like instance sizes, using a separate variables file per environment. Each environment has its own state file, often in a separate AWS account, so a mistake in dev can never touch production. Changes are promoted from dev to test to production through the pipeline.
cards.k: terraform environments, workspaces, tfvars, structure, terraform, cloudformation, iac, infrastructure as code

cards.q: How do you manage secrets in Terraform?
cards.h: Secrets live in a vault, not in code or state you share.
s: I never put secrets in Terraform code or variable files in Git. Terraform creates the secret in Secrets Manager, but the value is set separately or generated and rotated there. Services read secrets at runtime. Also, the state file can contain sensitive values, so it's encrypted in S3 with restricted access.
cards.k: terraform secrets, secrets manager, sensitive values, state encryption, terraform, cloudformation, iac, infrastructure as code

cards.q: How do you safely deploy infrastructure changes?
cards.h: Plan, review, approve, apply, watch.
s: All changes go through a pull request, where the pipeline runs terraform plan and reviewers check exactly what will change, especially anything being destroyed or replaced. We apply to dev first, then test, then production, with approval for production. For risky resources, we use lifecycle settings to prevent accidental deletion.
cards.k: infrastructure deployment, terraform plan, safe changes, approvals

cards.q: What is Docker?
cards.h: Ship the whole kitchen, not just the recipe.
s: Docker is a tool for packaging an application with everything it needs, its runtime, libraries and settings, into an image, and running it as a container. The container runs the same way on my laptop, in testing and in production. Containers share the host's kernel, so they're much lighter and faster to start than virtual machines.
cards.k: docker, containers, images, containerization, virtual machine, vm, docker vs vm, containers vs virtual machines, container, dockerfile, image

cards.q: What is a Docker layer?
cards.h: Layers are a stack of transparent sheets.
s: Each instruction in a Dockerfile, like COPY or RUN, creates a layer, and an image is a stack of these read-only layers. Docker caches layers, so if nothing changed in a step, it reuses it. That's why I copy the project file and restore packages before copying the rest of the code, so code changes don't trigger a full restore every time.
cards.k: docker layer, layer caching, dockerfile, build cache, docker, container, image

cards.q: COPY vs ADD?
cards.h: COPY is plain; ADD has surprises.
s: Both copy files into the image. COPY just copies local files, which is clear and predictable. ADD can also download from a URL and automatically extract tar files, which can cause surprises. So I always use COPY, unless I specifically need ADD's extraction.
cards.k: copy, add, dockerfile

cards.q: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?
cards.h: ENTRYPOINT = the program; CMD = default arguments.
s: ENTRYPOINT defines the main command the container always runs, like dotnet MyApi.dll. CMD gives default arguments, or a default command, which can be easily overridden when starting the container. I use the exec form, with square brackets, so the app runs as the main process and receives the stop signal for graceful shutdown.
cards.k: cmd, entrypoint, dockerfile

cards.q: How do you reduce image size?
cards.h: Build in the workshop, ship only the product.
s: I use multi-stage builds, so the final image has only the runtime and the published app, not the SDK. I start from small base images, like the ASP.NET runtime or chiseled images, add a dockerignore file, and combine commands to avoid extra layers. Smaller images are faster to pull and have fewer vulnerabilities.
cards.k: image size, multi-stage build, chiseled image, dockerignore

cards.q: What is Docker Compose?
cards.h: One file, whole local stack.
s: Docker Compose lets me define and run several containers together with one YAML file, like an API, a SQL Server and RabbitMQ, with their networks, ports and environment variables. One command starts the whole set. I use it for local development and testing, not for production.
cards.k: docker compose, local development, multi-container, docker, container, dockerfile, image

cards.q: Container networking and volumes?
cards.h: Networks connect, volumes remember.
s: Containers on the same Docker network can reach each other by container name, and I publish ports to reach them from outside. Volumes store data outside the container's filesystem, so it survives when the container is removed, like a database's data folder. Containers themselves should be stateless and easy to replace.
cards.k: container networking, volumes, docker network, persistence

cards.q: How do you secure and scan Docker images?
cards.h: Small, non-root, scanned, signed.
s: I start from small, official, regularly updated base images, run as a non-root user, and never put secrets in the image. In the pipeline, I scan images for vulnerabilities, using tools like Trivy or ECR scanning, and fail the build on critical issues. I also pin versions and rebuild regularly to pick up security patches.
cards.k: image security, vulnerability scanning, non-root, trivy, ecr, docker, container, dockerfile, image

cards.q: How do you troubleshoot a container?
cards.h: Logs, inspect, exec, limits.
s: First I check the logs with docker logs, and use docker inspect to see the exit code and whether it was killed for out of memory. If it's running, I can exec into it to look around. Then I check environment variables, configuration, and connectivity to dependencies. On ECS, I check the stopped task reason and CloudWatch logs.
cards.k: container troubleshooting, docker logs, docker inspect, debugging

cards.q: What happens when a container crashes?
cards.h: Process dies, orchestrator revives.
s: The container process exits, with an exit code that explains why, for example 137 means it was killed, often for running out of memory. Depending on the restart policy, Docker may restart it. On ECS, the service scheduler starts a new task to replace it, and on Kubernetes, the pod is restarted. Repeated crashes show up as events and alerts.
cards.k: container crash, exit code, oom, restart policy

cards.q: How do you configure environment variables and pass secrets to containers?
cards.h: Config by env, secrets by vault at runtime.
s: Normal configuration goes in as environment variables, which .NET reads automatically through its configuration system. Secrets don't go in the image or plain variables in code. On ECS, the task definition references Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and the values are injected securely when the container starts.
cards.k: environment variables, secrets, containers, configuration

cards.q: What is Kubernetes?
cards.h: A manager that keeps your containers alive and in place.
s: Kubernetes is an open-source platform for running containers across a cluster of machines. I describe the desired state, like run three copies of this image, and Kubernetes keeps it that way: it schedules containers, restarts failed ones, scales them, does rolling updates and handles service discovery and load balancing.
cards.k: kubernetes, k8s, container orchestration, pod, deployment, service, helm

cards.q: ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LoadBalancer?
cards.h: Inside, through the node, or through a cloud LB.
s: ClusterIP gives a service an internal IP that only works inside the cluster, and it's the default. NodePort opens a port on every node so the service can be reached from outside on that port. LoadBalancer asks the cloud provider to create a real load balancer in front of the service. In practice, we use ClusterIP with an Ingress for HTTP traffic.
cards.k: clusterip, nodeport, loadbalancer, kubernetes services

cards.q: What is a ReplicaSet?
cards.h: ReplicaSet = headcount keeper.
s: A ReplicaSet makes sure a set number of identical pods are always running, and replaces any that die. I almost never create ReplicaSets directly. A Deployment manages them for me, creating a new ReplicaSet for each new version during a rolling update, which also makes rollback easy.
cards.k: replicaset, deployment, kubernetes, pods

cards.q: What is a rolling deployment, and what is a rollback?
cards.h: Replace one by one; undo if it hurts.
s: A rolling deployment replaces old instances with new ones a few at a time, checking health as it goes, so there's no downtime. A rollback means going back to the previous version if something is wrong. In Kubernetes I use kubectl rollout undo, and in ECS the deployment circuit breaker can roll back automatically.
cards.k: rolling deployment, rollback, kubernetes, ecs

cards.q: What happens if a Pod crashes?
cards.h: Kubernetes revives, then reschedules.
s: If a container in a pod crashes, the kubelet restarts it based on the restart policy, with increasing delays, which shows as CrashLoopBackOff if it keeps failing. If the whole pod or node is lost, the Deployment creates a new pod elsewhere. To debug, I use kubectl describe and kubectl logs with the previous flag.
cards.k: pod crash, crashloopbackoff, kubernetes, restart

cards.q: How does Kubernetes perform service discovery?
cards.h: Stable name in front of moving pods.
s: Each Kubernetes Service gets a stable DNS name from CoreDNS, like orders dot default dot svc. Pods call that name, and Kubernetes routes the traffic to the healthy pods behind the service, which it tracks through labels. So pods can come and go, but the name stays the same.
cards.k: service discovery, kubernetes dns, coredns, services, kubernetes, k8s, pod, deployment, service, helm

cards.q: How do you secure Kubernetes?
cards.h: Who can do what, who can talk to whom, what can run.
s: I use RBAC with least privilege for people and service accounts, network policies to allow only needed traffic between pods, and pod security standards so containers run as non-root without extra privileges. Secrets are encrypted or come from an external vault, and images are scanned. And I keep the cluster updated.
cards.k: kubernetes security, rbac, network policies, pod security, kubernetes, k8s, pod, deployment, service, helm

cards.q: How do you deploy a .NET application to Kubernetes?
cards.h: Image, manifest, probes, pipeline.
s: I build a Docker image of the .NET app in the pipeline and push it to a registry. Then I deploy it with a Deployment YAML or a Helm chart, setting replicas, resources, environment variables from ConfigMaps and Secrets, and readiness and liveness probes mapped to the app's health checks. A Service and Ingress expose it. The app handles SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.
cards.k: deploy .net to kubernetes, helm, deployment yaml, docker, kubernetes, k8s, pod, deployment, service

cards.q: How do you run unit tests in CI?
cards.h: Every PR, every test, red stops the line.
s: In Azure DevOps, the pipeline runs dotnet test after the build on every pull request and merge. It collects test results and code coverage and publishes them to the pipeline. If any test fails, the build fails and the pull request can't be merged. Integration tests use containers for real dependencies.
cards.k: unit tests in ci, dotnet test, pipeline, code coverage

cards.q: What is SonarQube?
cards.h: A strict code reviewer that never sleeps.
s: SonarQube is a static code analysis tool. It scans the code for bugs, security vulnerabilities, code smells, duplication and test coverage. It runs in our pipeline, and a quality gate decides if new code is good enough to merge. It helps keep code quality from slowly getting worse.
cards.k: sonarqube, static analysis, code quality, quality gate

cards.q: How do you prevent bad code from reaching production?
cards.h: Many gates, each catching something.
s: I use several gates. Branch protection needs reviewed pull requests and passing builds. The pipeline runs tests, the SonarQube quality gate and security scans. Then the build goes through test environments, FV and UAT, with approvals before production. And after release, monitoring and quick rollback catch anything that slipped through.
cards.k: quality gates, code review, branch protection, approvals, ci/cd

cards.q: What is an artifact, and how do you version it?
cards.h: Build once, promote the same box.
s: An artifact is the output of a build that gets deployed, like a zip of the published app or a Docker image. I version it with a unique version, usually semantic version plus build number, and tag the Git commit. Then the same artifact is promoted through every environment, never rebuilt, so what we tested is exactly what we release.
cards.k: artifact, versioning, build once, semantic versioning

cards.q: How do you build Docker images in a pipeline?
cards.h: Build, scan, tag, push.
s: The pipeline builds the image using the Dockerfile, tags it with the build version and commit, scans it for vulnerabilities, and pushes it to the registry, like ECR. Docker layer caching makes builds faster. The deployment stages then use that exact image tag.

cards.q: How do you deploy to AWS from Azure DevOps?
cards.h: Azure DevOps drives, an IAM role opens the AWS door.
s: Azure DevOps connects to AWS through a service connection, ideally using short-lived credentials with OIDC instead of stored keys. The pipeline pushes the image to ECR, then updates the ECS task definition with the new image and updates the service, which does a rolling deployment. Infrastructure changes go through Terraform or CloudFormation steps.
cards.k: azure devops aws, ecs deployment, service connection, ci/cd, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, iam, cloudwatch, pipeline, azure devops, build, release, deployment

cards.q: How do you manage environment variables and secrets in CI/CD?
cards.h: Variables per environment, secrets from a vault, masked.
s: Non-secret settings go in pipeline variables or variable groups per environment. Secrets go in secret variables or linked from a vault, and they're masked in logs. Even better, the app reads secrets at runtime from Secrets Manager, so the pipeline doesn't need to handle them at all. Nothing sensitive is committed to Git.

cards.q: How do you implement deployment approvals?
cards.h: No production without a named yes.
s: In Azure DevOps, I set approvals and checks on environments or release stages, so production deployment waits until named approvers say yes. Approvals are recorded with who and when, which is important for our GxP audit. Our MCP release tools never bypass these: the agent can only check if an approval is pending.
cards.k: deployment approvals, azure devops, environments, gates

cards.q: What is Kafka, and what are broker, topic, partition, offset, producer and consumer?
cards.h: A post office of append-only logbooks.
s: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. A broker is a Kafka server. A topic is a named stream of events, split into partitions for parallelism. An offset is the position of a message in a partition. A producer writes events to topics, and a consumer reads them, keeping track of its offset so it can continue where it left off.
cards.k: kafka, broker, topic, partition, offset, producer, consumer, consumer group, event streaming, messaging, message broker, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: How does Kafka achieve scalability and fault tolerance?
cards.h: Split for speed, copy for safety.
s: Kafka scales by splitting topics into partitions spread across brokers, so many producers and consumers can work in parallel. For fault tolerance, each partition is copied to several brokers. If a broker fails, a copy takes over as leader. With acks set to all and min in-sync replicas, no acknowledged data is lost.
cards.k: kafka scalability, fault tolerance, partitions, replication, kafka, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, event streaming, messaging, message broker, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: What are replication factor and leader/follower?
cards.h: One leader writes, followers keep copies.
s: Replication factor is how many copies of each partition exist, usually three in production. One copy is the leader, which handles all reads and writes, and the others are followers that copy its data. If the leader's broker fails, one of the in-sync followers is elected as the new leader, so the partition stays available.
cards.k: replication factor, leader, follower, isr, kafka

cards.q: What is partition ordering, and can Kafka guarantee message ordering?
cards.h: Same key, same lane, same order.
s: Kafka guarantees order only within a single partition, not across the whole topic. So to keep related events in order, I give them the same key, like the shipment id, and they all go to the same partition. That's how our shipment status events stay in the right order for each shipment.
cards.k: kafka ordering, partition key, message ordering, kafka, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, event streaming, messaging, message broker, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: What are retention and log compaction?
cards.h: Retention = keep for a while; compaction = keep the latest per key.
s: Retention is how long Kafka keeps messages, by time or size, whether or not they've been read, which allows replay. Log compaction is a different mode where Kafka keeps at least the latest message for each key and removes older ones. It's useful for topics that hold the current state, like the latest status per shipment.
cards.k: retention, log compaction, kafka

cards.q: What happens if a consumer crashes?
cards.h: Someone else picks up your logbook at your last bookmark.
s: If a consumer crashes, the group coordinator notices and rebalances, giving its partitions to the other consumers in the group. They continue from the last committed offset. Because I commit offsets only after processing, a few messages might be processed again, so my consumers are idempotent.
cards.k: consumer crash, rebalance, committed offset, kafka

cards.q: What is consumer lag, and how do you troubleshoot it?
cards.h: Lag = the unread pile.
s: Consumer lag is how far behind a consumer group is, the difference between the latest offset and the committed offset. Growing lag means consumers can't keep up. I check if processing got slower, for example a slow database, if a poison message is stuck, or if traffic spiked. Then I fix the slow step or add consumers, up to the partition count.
cards.k: consumer lag, kafka monitoring, troubleshooting

cards.q: How do you scale consumers, and what if there are more consumers than partitions?
cards.h: One partition, one consumer per group.
s: I scale by adding consumers to the same group, and Kafka spreads the partitions between them. But each partition goes to only one consumer in a group, so if there are more consumers than partitions, the extra ones sit idle. To scale further, I add partitions, or process messages in parallel inside each consumer while keeping order per key.
cards.k: scaling consumers, consumer group, partitions, kafka

cards.q: How do you design Kafka topics?
cards.h: Name, schema, key, partitions, retention.
s: I usually create one topic per event type or business entity, with clear names, like shipment status changed. I choose a key that keeps related events in order, like shipment id, and enough partitions for future consumer parallelism. I define retention and use a schema for the event with versioning.
cards.k: kafka topic design, partitions, keys, schema, kafka, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, event streaming, messaging, message broker, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: How do you handle poison messages, retries and dead-letter topics?
cards.h: Retry a little, park it, move on, fix later.
s: A poison message is one that keeps failing. I retry temporary errors a few times, sometimes through retry topics with delays. If it still fails, I send it to a dead-letter topic with the error details, so the main flow continues. We alert on the dead-letter topic, fix the cause, and replay the messages.
cards.k: poison messages, retries, dead letter topic, dlq, kafka, rabbitmq, queue, exchange, amqp, dead letter

cards.q: How do you secure and monitor Kafka?
cards.h: Lock the topics, watch the lag.
s: For security, I use TLS for encryption, authentication with SASL or IAM on Amazon MSK, and ACLs so each service can only read or write its own topics. For monitoring, the key things are consumer lag, under-replicated partitions, broker health, and request latency, with alerts on lag.
cards.k: kafka security, kafka monitoring, tls, acl, consumer lag, kafka, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, event streaming, messaging, message broker, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: What is RabbitMQ, and what are queues and bindings?
cards.h: Exchange = sorting office, binding = address rule, queue = mailbox.
s: RabbitMQ is a message broker. Producers send messages to an exchange, and the exchange routes them to queues based on bindings, which are rules linking an exchange to a queue with a routing key. Consumers read from queues. Once a message is acknowledged, it's removed. We use it for task-style work like notifications.
cards.k: rabbitmq, queues, bindings, exchange, message broker, queue, amqp, dead letter, dlq, messaging, kafka, event driven

cards.q: What is acknowledgement, and publisher confirm vs consumer acknowledgement?
cards.h: Confirm = broker got it; ack = consumer handled it.
s: Acknowledgements confirm a message was handled. Publisher confirms are from the broker to the producer: RabbitMQ confirms it has safely stored the message, so the producer knows it wasn't lost. Consumer acknowledgements are from the consumer to the broker, saying I've processed it, now remove it. I use manual consumer acks after the work is committed.
cards.k: acknowledgement, publisher confirms, consumer ack, rabbitmq

cards.q: What are message durability and persistent messaging?
cards.h: Durable box + persistent letter.
s: For messages to survive a broker restart, I need both a durable queue and persistent messages. A durable queue's definition survives the restart, and a persistent message is written to disk. If either is missing, messages can be lost. Today, quorum queues are the recommended durable, replicated queue type.
cards.k: durability, persistent messages, durable queue, quorum queues, rabbitmq, messaging, message broker, kafka, event driven

cards.q: What happens if RabbitMQ goes down?
cards.h: Outbox holds mail while the post office is closed.
s: Publishers can't send, and consumers lose their connection. That's why we use the outbox pattern, so events wait in the database and are sent when RabbitMQ is back. Clients reconnect automatically, and unacknowledged messages are delivered again. During our [mid-2024] outage, we replayed about [1,200] missed updates safely.
cards.k: rabbitmq down, outage, outbox, reconnect, rabbitmq, queue, exchange, amqp, dead letter, dlq, messaging, message broker, kafka, event driven

cards.q: How do you implement retries in RabbitMQ?
cards.h: Wait queue, try again, then DLQ.
s: For temporary errors, I don't requeue immediately, because that creates a tight loop. Instead, I send the message to a retry queue with a delay, using a message TTL that dead-letters it back to the main queue, and count the attempts in a header. After a few attempts, it goes to a parking or dead-letter queue for investigation.
cards.k: rabbitmq retries, retry queue, ttl, dead letter exchange, rabbitmq, queue, exchange, amqp, dead letter, dlq, messaging, message broker, kafka, event driven

cards.q: How do you prevent message loss?
cards.h: Confirm, persist, ack late, never drop.
s: I protect every step. The producer saves events in an outbox and uses publisher confirms. The broker uses durable quorum queues with persistent messages. The consumer acknowledges manually only after committing its work, and failed messages go to a dead-letter queue. Confirms cost us about [5 percent] throughput, which is well worth it.
cards.k: message loss, reliability, publisher confirms, outbox, manual ack

cards.q: How do you scale and monitor RabbitMQ?
cards.h: Add consumers; watch depth and unacked.
s: I scale consumers by running more instances on the same queue, the competing consumers pattern, and tune the prefetch count. I monitor queue depth, unacknowledged messages, consumer count, memory and disk alarms, using the management UI or Prometheus with Grafana, and alert when queues keep growing.
cards.k: rabbitmq scaling, monitoring, prefetch, competing consumers, rabbitmq, queue, exchange, amqp, dead letter, dlq, messaging, message broker, kafka, event driven

cards.q: How do you identify whether an issue is application, database or infrastructure related?
cards.h: Follow the request down the stack.
s: I look at where the time and errors are. If database waits or slow queries spike at the same time, it points to the database. If only one service has errors, especially after a deploy, it's likely the application. If many unrelated services fail together, it points to infrastructure or a shared dependency, like the network or broker. Traces make this quick.
cards.k: troubleshooting, root cause, application vs database vs infrastructure

cards.q: How do you trace a request across microservices?
cards.h: One id, every hop.
s: Every request gets a correlation id at the edge, which our middleware adds to every log line and passes in headers and message metadata to the next service. With OpenTelemetry, we also get trace ids and spans. So I search one id in CloudWatch, or open the trace, and see the whole journey across services.
cards.k: request tracing, correlation id, distributed tracing, opentelemetry, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: What logs do you check first?
cards.h: Errors first, then the edges, then dependencies.
s: First, the error logs of the failing service around the time the issue started, filtered by correlation id if I have one. Then I check the deployment history for recent changes. After that, the logs of its dependencies, like the database or message broker, and infrastructure events, like containers restarting or running out of memory.
cards.k: logs, troubleshooting, first steps, incident

cards.q: How do you distinguish symptoms from root cause?
cards.h: Symptom = fever; root cause = infection.
s: A symptom is what we see, like high CPU or slow responses. The root cause is why it happens, like a missing index causing table scans. I keep asking why until fixing that one thing would stop the problem. Then I prove it, by reproducing it, or showing that the fix removes the symptom.
cards.k: symptoms vs root cause, root cause analysis, 5 whys

cards.q: How do you handle production incidents and prevent recurrence?
cards.h: Stop the bleeding, find the cause, vaccinate.
s: First I reduce the impact, often by rolling back, and keep people updated. Then I find the root cause with logs, metrics and traces. Afterwards we do a blameless review with a timeline and actions with owners, like an alert, a test, or a design fix. For example, after our RabbitMQ outage, we added publisher confirms and memory alerts.
cards.k: incident management, post-mortem, prevention, production incident

cards.q: Tell me about the reverse-tabnabbing issue and how you fixed it.
cards.h: Open a new tab, but don't hand it your remote control.
s: In [2024], a security review found that external links in our UI used target blank without noopener. That lets the opened page change our original tab, for example to a fake login page. I fixed about [40] links across React and Angular by adding rel noopener noreferrer, and turned on an ESLint rule so the build fails if it comes back. It passed retest with no regressions.
cards.k: reverse tabnabbing, security fix, noopener, story

cards.q: What is mocking, and mock vs stub vs fake?
cards.h: Stub answers, mock checks, fake works.
s: Mocking means replacing a real dependency with a test double. A stub just returns fixed answers. A mock also checks that certain calls were made, like verifying an email was sent once. A fake is a simple working version, like an in-memory repository. I prefer fakes and stubs, and use mocks only when the call itself is what matters.
cards.k: mocking, mock, stub, fake, test doubles

cards.q: How do you test a service with dependencies?
cards.h: Mock at the boundary, test the logic.
s: For unit tests, I inject fakes or mocks for the dependencies, so I test only the service's logic. For integration tests, I use real dependencies where possible, like SQL Server or RabbitMQ in Docker with Testcontainers, and replace only external systems, like vendor APIs, with fakes.
cards.k: testing dependencies, unit test, integration test, testcontainers, test, testing, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: How do you test controllers?
cards.h: Test controllers through HTTP.
s: I prefer testing controllers through HTTP, using WebApplicationFactory, which runs the real pipeline with routing, model binding, validation, filters and authentication. Then I check status codes and responses. Unit testing controller methods directly misses most of that. Business logic is tested separately in the services.
cards.k: controller testing, webapplicationfactory, integration test, test, testing, unit test, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: How do you test EF Core code?
cards.h: Test against the real engine.
s: I test EF Core code against a real database, usually SQL Server in a Docker container with Testcontainers, because the in-memory provider doesn't behave like a real relational database, for example with constraints and transactions. Each test starts with known data. For pure business logic, I keep it outside the queries and unit test it.
cards.k: ef core testing, testcontainers, in-memory provider, database tests, ef core, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq to entities, test, testing, unit test, integration test, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: Playwright vs Cucumber?
cards.h: Cucumber writes the story; Playwright acts it out.
s: Playwright is a browser automation tool for end-to-end tests: it drives real browsers, clicks and checks pages, with auto-waiting. Cucumber is a BDD framework where tests are written in plain Given, When, Then language. They work together: Cucumber describes the scenario in business language, and Playwright does the actual steps in the browser.
cards.k: playwright, cucumber, bdd, e2e testing

cards.q: What is a flaky test, and how do you handle it?
cards.h: Flaky = untrusted; fix it or it trains people to ignore red.
s: A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change. Common causes are timing and fixed sleeps, shared data between tests, dependence on test order, real time and dates, or network calls. I find the cause and fix it, and only quarantine the test briefly, because flaky tests make people ignore real failures.
cards.k: flaky test, test reliability, intermittent failure, test, testing, unit test, integration test, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: What is test coverage, and is 100 percent coverage desirable?
cards.h: Coverage measures visits, not checks.
s: Test coverage shows the percentage of code run by tests. It's useful to find untested code, but high coverage doesn't mean good tests, because tests without proper assertions also count. 100 percent is usually not worth the cost. I aim for high coverage on business rules and risky code, like our 80 percent gate on new code.
cards.k: test coverage, code coverage, 100 percent coverage, test, testing, unit test, integration test, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: How do you design good unit tests, and what is Arrange-Act-Assert?
cards.h: Arrange, Act, Assert.
s: A good unit test checks one behaviour, has a clear name that says what's expected, and is fast, independent and repeatable. Arrange-Act-Assert is the structure: arrange the data and dependencies, act by calling the method once, and assert the result. I test behaviour, not internal details, so refactoring doesn't break tests.
cards.k: unit test design, arrange act assert, aaa, best practices

cards.q: How do you test asynchronous code and exception handling?
cards.h: Await in tests; assert the throw.
s: I write the test method as async Task and await the code, never use async void or .Result. For exceptions, I use await Assert.ThrowsAsync with the expected exception type and check the message if it matters. For timeouts and delays, I use a fake time provider, so tests don't actually wait.

cards.q: How do you test Kafka and RabbitMQ integrations?
cards.h: Real broker in a container, assert the effect.
s: For unit tests, I test the message handler logic separately from the broker. For integration tests, I run real Kafka or RabbitMQ in Docker with Testcontainers, publish a test message, and check the consumer processed it, including retries, dead-lettering and duplicate handling. I also use contract tests for message formats.
cards.k: kafka testing, rabbitmq testing, testcontainers, messaging tests, kafka, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, event streaming, rabbitmq, queue, exchange, amqp, dead letter, dlq, messaging, message broker, event driven, test, testing, unit test, integration test, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: What is React?
cards.h: UI = f(state).
s: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components. I describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React updates the page efficiently when the state changes. It's maintained by Meta and has a huge ecosystem. I build reusable React components with TypeScript for our IRT screens.
cards.k: react, frontend, ui library, components, hooks, component, props, state, redux

cards.q: Component vs element?
cards.h: Component = cookie cutter; element = the cookie.
s: A component is a function that takes props and returns what should be shown. An element is the plain object that a component returns, describing one piece of UI, which is what JSX creates. So a component is like a blueprint, and elements are what it produces each time it renders.
cards.k: component, element, jsx, react

cards.q: Functional vs class components?
cards.h: Functions + hooks won.
s: Class components are the older way, with this.state and lifecycle methods like componentDidMount. Functional components are just functions, and with hooks like useState and useEffect, they can do everything classes did, with less code and easier reuse. Today I write only functional components. Error boundaries are the main thing that still needs a class.
cards.k: functional components, class components, hooks, react

cards.q: What are props, what is state, and props vs state?
cards.h: Props = arguments; state = memory.
s: Props are inputs passed into a component from its parent, and the component can't change them. State is data the component owns and can change, using useState, which causes it to re-render. So props flow down from the parent, and state lives inside the component. When two components need the same state, I lift it up to their common parent.
cards.k: props, state, props vs state, react

cards.q: What is the dependency array, and what if it is empty?
cards.h: [] = once; [x] = when x changes; none = every time.
s: The dependency array in useEffect tells React when to run the effect again. With values in it, the effect runs whenever one of them changes. If it's empty, the effect runs only once, after the first render, which is good for initial data loading. If there's no array at all, it runs after every render. Missing a dependency causes stale-data bugs.
cards.k: dependency array, useeffect, react hooks

cards.q: useMemo, useCallback, and the difference?
cards.h: useMemo remembers the answer; useCallback remembers the function.
s: useMemo remembers the result of a calculation and recalculates it only when its dependencies change. useCallback remembers a function itself, so the same function object is passed on each render, which matters when passing it to memoized child components. So useMemo is for values, useCallback is for functions. I use them only where profiling shows a benefit.
cards.k: usememo, usecallback, memoization, react performance

cards.q: What is useRef?
cards.h: A pocket that survives renders silently.
s: useRef gives me a box that keeps a value across renders without causing a re-render when it changes. I use it mainly to access a DOM element directly, like focusing an input, and to store things like a timer id or the previous value of a prop.
cards.k: useref, react hooks, dom reference

cards.q: What is the Context API, and Context vs Redux?
cards.h: Context = broadcast; Redux = central bank with ledger.
s: The Context API shares values, like the logged-in user or theme, with any component in the tree without passing props through every level. Redux, with Redux Toolkit, is a full state management library with a central store, actions, devtools and middleware. Context is fine for simple, rarely changing data, and Redux suits large, frequently updated shared state.
cards.k: context api, redux, state management, prop drilling, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http, react, hooks, component, props, state

cards.q: How do you manage API calls and loading/error states?
cards.h: Loading, error, empty, data: four states, always.
s: I use a library like React Query, or RTK Query, which handles fetching, caching, loading and error states, retries and refetching for me. Each screen shows a loading indicator, a clear error message with a retry, and an empty state. All API calls go through one client that adds the auth token and handles common errors.
cards.k: api calls, loading state, error handling, react query, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Controlled vs uncontrolled components?
cards.h: Controlled = React holds the pen.
s: In a controlled component, React state holds the input's value and updates it on every change, so React is the single source of truth. In an uncontrolled component, the browser keeps the value and I read it when needed with a ref. Controlled is simpler for validation, and libraries like React Hook Form use uncontrolled inputs for better performance.
cards.k: controlled components, uncontrolled components, forms, react

cards.q: What causes unnecessary re-rendering?
cards.h: New references look like new data.
s: Unnecessary re-renders happen when a parent re-renders and all its children follow, when new objects or functions are created on every render and passed as props, or when a context value changes. I first profile with React DevTools, then fix it by moving state closer to where it's used, and using memo, useMemo and useCallback where it actually helps.
cards.k: re-rendering, react performance, memo

cards.q: How do you handle authentication and protect routes in React?
cards.h: The UI hides doors; the API locks them.
s: The user logs in through our SSO identity provider, and the app keeps the session, ideally in secure cookies. Protected routes check if the user is logged in and has the right role, and redirect to login otherwise. But that only hides screens. The real protection is on the API, which validates the token and permissions on every request.
cards.k: react authentication, protected routes, route guards, sso, react, hooks, component, props, state, redux

cards.q: How do you manage forms?
cards.h: Library for state, schema for rules.
s: I use React Hook Form with a schema library like Zod for validation, which keeps forms fast and the rules in one place, and the same schema gives the TypeScript types. I show errors next to each field, disable submit while saving, and show server-side validation errors too, since the API validates again.
cards.k: forms, react hook form, zod, validation

cards.q: How do you structure a large React application?
cards.h: Group by feature, share the basics.
s: I organise by feature rather than by file type, so each feature, like shipments or imports, has its components, hooks and API calls together. Shared UI components and utilities live in a common folder. I use TypeScript everywhere, a clear routing structure, lazy loading for big screens, and consistent patterns for data fetching and state.
cards.k: react project structure, feature folders, architecture, react, hooks, component, props, state, redux

cards.q: Why React over Angular?
cards.h: React = toolkit; Angular = complete workshop.
s: React is a flexible library focused on the UI, with a huge ecosystem, and you choose your own tools for routing and state. Angular is a complete framework with strong conventions built in. Both are good choices. We use React for new screens because of the team's experience, flexibility and the ecosystem.
cards.k: react vs angular, frontend framework, comparison, react, hooks, component, props, state, redux

cards.q: JavaScript var vs let vs const?
cards.h: const by default, let if it changes, var never.
s: var is function-scoped and can be used before it's declared, which leads to bugs. let and const are block-scoped, so they only exist inside their curly braces. const means the variable can't be reassigned, though an object it points to can still be changed. I use const by default, let when I need to reassign, and never var.
cards.k: var, let, const, javascript, scope, js, typescript, ts

cards.q: What is hoisting?
cards.h: Declarations float up; values do not.
s: Hoisting means JavaScript processes declarations before running the code, so they're known at the top of their scope. Function declarations are fully hoisted, so I can call them before they appear. var is hoisted but set to undefined. let and const are hoisted too, but using them before the declaration throws an error, which is called the temporal dead zone.
cards.k: hoisting, javascript, temporal dead zone, var

cards.q: What is a closure in JavaScript?
cards.h: A function with a backpack of variables.
s: A closure is when a function remembers the variables from where it was created, even after that outer function has finished. It's used for private data and factory functions. In React, every render's functions capture that render's state, which is why you can get a stale value in a timer if you're not careful.
cards.k: closure, javascript, scope, stale closure, js, typescript, ts

cards.q: What is a Promise, and Promise vs async/await?
cards.h: Promise = IOU; await = wait for the IOU.
s: A Promise represents a value that will be available in the future, and it can be pending, fulfilled or rejected. I can chain then and catch on it. async and await are just a cleaner way to write the same thing, so asynchronous code reads like normal step-by-step code with try-catch. For parallel calls, I use Promise.all.
cards.k: promise, async await, javascript, asynchronous, async, await, task, valuetask, configureawait

cards.q: What is callback hell?
cards.h: The pyramid of doom.
s: Callback hell is when asynchronous steps are nested inside each other's callbacks, again and again, so the code moves to the right like a pyramid and becomes hard to read and handle errors. The fix is using Promises and async-await, and breaking logic into small named functions.
cards.k: callback hell, callbacks, promises, javascript

cards.q: Optional chaining and nullish coalescing?
cards.h: ?. = safe step; ?? = default only for nothing.
s: Optional chaining, the question mark dot, safely reads a nested property and returns undefined instead of throwing if something in the chain is null. Nullish coalescing, the double question mark, gives a default value only when the left side is null or undefined. Unlike the OR operator, it keeps valid values like zero or an empty string.
cards.k: optional chaining, nullish coalescing, javascript, typescript

cards.q: any vs unknown?
cards.h: any = no seatbelt; unknown = check before you drive.
s: any turns off type checking completely, so TypeScript lets you do anything with it, and bugs slip through. unknown also accepts any value, but forces me to check its type before using it. So unknown is the safe choice for things like parsed JSON or caught errors, and I avoid any.
cards.k: any, unknown, typescript, type safety

cards.q: What are generics in TypeScript?
cards.h: Generics = type placeholders.
s: Generics let me write a function or type that works with many types while keeping type safety. For example, an apiGet function that takes a type parameter T and returns a Promise of T, so each call gets the right response type. It's the same idea as generics in C#.
cards.k: typescript generics, generics, type safety, javascript, js, typescript, ts

cards.q: Union types, intersection types and type narrowing?
cards.h: Union = either; intersection = both; narrowing = find out which.
s: A union type means a value can be one of several types, like string or number, or a fixed set of values like the shipment status. An intersection type combines several types into one with all their properties. Type narrowing is when TypeScript figures out the exact type after a check, like typeof, or a status field in a discriminated union.
cards.k: union types, intersection types, type narrowing, typescript

cards.q: What is strict mode?
cards.h: Strict = the compiler as a pessimist.
s: In JavaScript, use strict turns on stricter rules, like throwing errors for undeclared variables, and ES modules are strict automatically. In TypeScript, the strict setting turns on all the strict checks, like strict null checks and no implicit any. I always turn on strict mode in TypeScript projects, because it catches many bugs early.
cards.k: strict mode, use strict, typescript strict

cards.q: Synchronous vs asynchronous Node.js?
cards.h: Never block the single waiter.
s: Node runs JavaScript on a single main thread. Synchronous code blocks that thread until it finishes, so a slow synchronous operation blocks every other request. Asynchronous code, like file or network calls with callbacks, Promises or async-await, lets Node handle other work while waiting. So in Node, I keep all input and output asynchronous.

cards.q: What is Express, and what is middleware in Express?
cards.h: Express middleware = ASP.NET Core middleware in JavaScript.
s: Express is the most popular minimal web framework for Node, for building APIs and web apps. Middleware in Express are functions that receive the request, the response and a next function. They run in order, can change the request or response, end it, or call next. Error middleware has an extra error parameter. It's the same idea as ASP.NET Core middleware.
cards.k: express, express middleware, node.js, middleware, pipeline, request delegate, request pipeline

cards.q: How do you handle errors in Node.js?
cards.h: Catch, centralise, log, never ignore.
s: I use try-catch around awaited code, and send all errors to one central error middleware that logs them and returns a clean response. Express 5 passes errors from async handlers to that middleware automatically. I also handle unhandled rejections at the process level, log them, and restart cleanly instead of running in a broken state.
cards.k: node.js error handling, express, try catch, unhandled rejection

cards.q: How do you secure Node.js APIs?
cards.h: Same rules as .NET, different packages.
s: I validate every input with a schema library like Zod, check JWTs and permissions, and add security headers with Helmet. I add rate limiting, use parameterized queries, keep secrets in a secret store, and run npm audit or similar in the pipeline to catch vulnerable packages.
cards.k: node.js security, express security, helmet, validation

cards.q: Node.js vs .NET for backend development?
cards.h: .NET for the core, Node for the glue.
s: Node is great for input-output heavy services and lets the team use one language with the front end. .NET has stronger typing, higher raw performance for heavy work, and very mature tooling for large business systems. We use .NET for our core domain services, and Node for small tools where it fits better.

cards.h: Python = the team's Swiss army knife.

Pydantic made checking vendor file formats quick and easy to read, so I built a [vendor file pre-validation service] with FastAPI that returns exact errors before our .NET import runs. cards.h: Routers, schemas, services, Depends.
