cards.q: How do you implement authentication in FastAPI?
cards.h: A Depends that checks the badge.
s: In FastAPI, I add a dependency that reads the Bearer token from the header and validates the JWT from our identity provider: signature, issuer, audience and expiry. Endpoints that need a logged-in user declare that dependency, and I add role checks on top. FastAPI's OAuth2 helpers also show this in the docs page.
cards.k: fastapi authentication, jwt, oauth2, depends

cards.q: What is SFTP, and SFTP vs FTP vs FTPS?
cards.h: SFTP = SSH; FTPS = FTP + TLS; FTP = postcard.
s: SFTP is secure file transfer over SSH, usually on port 22, with everything encrypted in one connection. FTP is the old protocol that sends data and even passwords in plain text. FTPS is FTP with TLS encryption added, but it uses separate data connections, which can be hard with firewalls. For vendor file exchange, we use SFTP.
cards.k: sftp, ftp, ftps, file transfer, comparison, vendor file

cards.q: How does SFTP authentication work, and password vs private-key authentication?
cards.h: Check the server's face, then show your key.
s: SFTP can log in with a password or with a key pair. With keys, the vendor's server has our public key, and we prove we hold the private key, so no secret is sent over the network. Key authentication is more secure and better for automation. We also check the server's host key fingerprint to avoid connecting to a fake server.
cards.k: sftp authentication, private key, password, host key, sftp, ftp, file transfer, vendor file

cards.q: How did you switch between providers?
cards.h: Change the setting, not the code.
s: All three libraries implement our ISftpClient interface. A factory reads which library to use for each vendor from configuration, for example DepotA uses Rebex, and returns that implementation. So switching a vendor to another library is just a configuration change, with no code deployment.
cards.k: provider switching, factory, configuration, sftp

cards.q: How did you handle connection failures and retries?
cards.h: Retry the network, not the wrong password.
s: Our base class wraps every operation with Polly: [3] retries with exponential backoff and jitter for temporary errors like timeouts, using a fresh connection each time. Login and host key failures are not retried, because they won't fix themselves. After the last attempt, the job is marked failed and an alert goes to support, and the next scheduled run tries again.
cards.k: sftp retries, polly, connection failures, resilience

cards.q: How did you validate file integrity and handle partial transfers?
cards.h: Upload as .part, rename when whole.
s: After uploading, I compare the remote file size with the local one, and check a SHA-256 checksum where the vendor supports it. To avoid partial files, I upload with a temporary name and rename it when complete, so the vendor never picks up half a file. When downloading, I only read complete files and verify them before processing.
cards.k: file integrity, checksum, partial transfer, sftp

cards.q: How did you handle duplicate files?
cards.h: Remember every file you have eaten.
s: Files have predictable names with vendor, type, timestamp and sequence. We keep a processed-files table keyed by name and hash, so the same file is never imported twice, even if it's sent again. Processed files are moved to an archive folder on the server.
cards.k: duplicate files, deduplication, file hash, sftp

cards.q: How did you secure SFTP credentials?
cards.h: Keys in the vault, fingerprints pinned.
s: Private keys and passwords are stored in [AWS Secrets Manager] and read at runtime using the service's IAM role, never kept in config files or the code repository. Host key fingerprints are pinned in configuration. Keys are rotated with vendors on a schedule, through change control, and access is logged.
cards.k: sftp credentials, secrets manager, key rotation, security, sftp, ftp, file transfer, vendor file

cards.q: What problems did you face with SFTP?
cards.h: Algorithms, folders, timeouts.
s: Vendor servers differ, so I faced a few problems. A depot vendor disabled old algorithms, which broke ComponentPro and led us to Rebex. Another vendor moved their pickup folder without telling our team, so we added post-upload checks and alerts. And large files timed out on slow links, which I fixed with longer timeouts and resumable uploads.
cards.k: sftp problems, challenges, vendors, story, sftp, ftp, file transfer, vendor file

cards.q: How would you test an SFTP integration?
cards.h: Mock for logic, real server in a container for the wire.
s: For unit tests, I use a fake ISftpClient to test our logic. For integration tests, I run a real SFTP server in a Docker container in CI and test uploads, downloads, large files, timeouts, wrong keys and reconnects. Every provider runs the same contract tests. Then we test against each vendor's test server before going live.
cards.k: sftp testing, integration test, testcontainers, contract tests, test, testing, unit test, xunit, moq, mock, sftp, ftp, file transfer, vendor file

cards.q: WCF vs Web API?
cards.h: WCF = envelope with forms; Web API = simple JSON note.
s: WCF is the older .NET Framework technology for SOAP services, supporting many protocols and the WS-star standards, with a lot of configuration. Web API is the modern way to build HTTP REST APIs with JSON, simpler and lighter. WCF server isn't supported in modern .NET, so new services use ASP.NET Core Web API, or gRPC.

cards.q: What is SOAP?
cards.h: XML in an envelope with a strict contract.
s: SOAP is a protocol where messages are XML envelopes with a header and body, and the service is described in a WSDL contract, so clients can generate strongly typed proxies. It supports standards for security and transactions. It's verbose but still common in older enterprise and healthcare systems.
cards.k: soap, xml, wsdl, web services, wcf, service contract

cards.q: What are service contracts, operation contracts and data contracts?
cards.h: Service = the shop; operation = the counter; data = the parcel.
s: In WCF, a service contract is the interface marked with the ServiceContract attribute, which defines the service. Operation contracts are the methods in it, marked with OperationContract, that clients can call. Data contracts are the classes sent back and forth, marked with DataContract and DataMember. Together they produce the WSDL.
cards.k: service contract, operation contract, data contract, wcf

cards.q: What is dependency injection in .NET Framework?
cards.h: Framework: bring your own container.
s: .NET Framework had no built-in dependency injection container like .NET Core does. Teams used third-party containers like Unity, Autofac or Ninject, and plugged them into ASP.NET MVC or Web API. WCF needed extra custom code to inject dependencies into services. In modern .NET, DI is built in everywhere.
cards.k: dependency injection, .net framework, unity, autofac, di, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes

cards.q: Why migrate from WCF, and what challenges occur?
cards.h: Leave the old house, but keep the old address forwarding.
s: We migrate from WCF because WCF server isn't supported in modern .NET, it ties us to old Windows hosting, and REST or gRPC are easier to build, test and integrate with. The challenges are clients that still need SOAP, WS-Security features, and making sure behaviour stays exactly the same, so we migrate one service at a time with thorough testing.
cards.k: wcf migration, modernization, challenges, wcf, soap, service contract

cards.q: What does IRT mean?
cards.h: IRT decides who gets which kit, and makes sure it is there.
s: IRT stands for Interactive Response Technology. It's the system clinical trials use to randomly assign patients to treatment groups and manage the drug supply, kit dispensing and shipments to sites. It was earlier called IVRS or IWRS, voice and web response systems, and is also known as RTSM.
cards.k: irt, interactive response technology, rtsm, clinical trials

cards.q: What is GxP, and why is it important?
cards.h: GxP = prove it is right, and prove nobody changed it.
s: GxP means Good Practice regulations, like Good Clinical Practice and Good Manufacturing Practice, where the x stands for the area. They make sure products are safe and data is reliable. For software, rules like FDA 21 CFR Part 11 cover electronic records and signatures. It's important because errors can affect patient safety and trial results.
cards.k: gxp, regulated, compliance, 21 cfr part 11, good practice, validation, audit trail, change control

cards.q: How does GxP affect software development?
cards.h: Every change has a ticket, a test and a signature.
s: In GxP, every requirement must be documented, tested and traced, changes go through formal change control, releases are validated with evidence, and every data change has an audit trail. So we write more documentation and testing evidence, and we can't just deploy whenever we like. It makes us very careful about quality.
cards.k: gxp software development, validation, change control, gxp, audit trail, 21 cfr part 11, regulated

cards.q: What are validation, traceability and auditability?
cards.h: Proves it works, shows why, records who.
s: Validation is proving that the software does what it's supposed to, with documented testing. Traceability means every requirement is linked to the tests that verify it, and to the code change. Auditability means every action is recorded, who did what, when and why, so it can be reviewed later by auditors.
cards.k: validation, traceability, auditability, gxp

cards.q: What is change control?
cards.h: No change without paperwork and approval.
s: Change control is the formal process for any change to a validated system. Each change has a request, an impact and risk assessment, approvals, testing evidence, and a record of when it was released. Even emergency fixes must be documented afterwards. Our releases always reference an approved change request.
cards.k: change control, change request, gxp, compliance, validation, audit trail, 21 cfr part 11, regulated

cards.q: What are UAT, FV and TechOps?
cards.h: FV proves, TechOps installs, UAT accepts.
s: FV is formal validation, where the validation team runs scripted tests against the requirements and records evidence. TechOps is the operations team that installs and checks releases in controlled environments. UAT is user acceptance testing, where business users confirm the release meets their needs before it goes to production.
cards.k: uat, fv, techops, environments, validation

cards.q: How do you ensure production changes are controlled?
cards.h: Approved artifact, approved person, approved window.
s: Every production change needs an approved change request. It goes through gated pipelines, with the same validated artifact promoted through FV and UAT, and production deployment needs named approvers. Only a few people have production access. Even our MCP deployment tools keep these approvals and log every action.
cards.k: controlled changes, production changes, change control, approvals

cards.q: How do you maintain software quality in a regulated environment?
cards.h: Quality is built in, then proven.
s: I combine engineering practices with regulatory ones. On the engineering side, code reviews, automated tests, the SonarQube gate and security scans in CI. On the regulatory side, documented requirements, traceability to tests, formal validation and change control. Automated tests make validation faster and more reliable.
cards.k: software quality, regulated environment, gxp, testing

cards.q: How do you handle security in clinical-trial software?
cards.h: Protect patients, protect the blind.
s: We use role-based access so people see only their studies, and we protect blinding so treatment information is visible only to those allowed. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest, every change has an audit trail, and we do security testing for OWASP issues. Fixes like the reverse tabnabbing one on [about 40] links came from that testing.
cards.k: clinical trial security, blinding, access control, audit trail, security, owasp, xss, csrf, sql injection, cors, cookie

cards.q: How does shipment tracking integrate with external systems?
cards.h: Order out, status back, events inside.
s: IRT creates shipment orders and sends them to depot and courier vendors through SFTP files or APIs. Vendors send back status updates, like dispatched, in transit and delivered. Our integration services validate, deduplicate and process them safely, publish events to update shipments and notify sites, and alert on failures. A reconciliation report catches anything missed.
cards.k: shipment tracking, integration, vendors, sftp, events

cards.q: What external integrations does your system have?
cards.h: Depots, couriers, EDC, identity, notifications.
s: Our system integrates with depots and couriers through SFTP files and APIs, with EDC systems for clinical data, with our identity provider for single sign-on, and with notification services for emails. Each integration has monitoring, alerts and reconciliation, so we know quickly when something goes wrong.
cards.k: external integrations, vendors, edc, sso, sftp

cards.q: How do you ensure data integrity?
cards.h: ALCOA: who, readable, when, original, right.
s: I protect data integrity at every layer. The database has constraints, transactions and foreign keys. The application validates input at each boundary and uses idempotency keys so retries don't duplicate data. Every change is recorded in an audit trail, and reconciliation reports confirm nothing was lost or altered between systems.
cards.k: data integrity, constraints, transactions, audit trail, alcoa

cards.q: Why was MCP created, and what problem does it solve?
cards.h: MCP = USB-C for AI tools.
s: Before MCP, every AI app had to build its own custom integration for every tool or data source, which doesn't scale. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 that standardises how AI apps discover and call tools. So one MCP server works with many AI apps. In December 2025 it was donated to the Linux Foundation, and it now has broad industry support.
cards.k: mcp, model context protocol, why mcp, ai integration, tool, agent, agentic

cards.q: How does MCP work: server, client, tool?
cards.h: Host - client - server - tool.
s: An MCP host, like Cursor or Claude, contains an MCP client, which connects to an MCP server. First they agree on capabilities, then the client asks the server for its list of tools, each with a name, description and input schema. When the AI decides to use a tool, the client sends a call with the arguments, and the server runs it and returns the result. Ours runs locally over standard input and output.
cards.k: mcp architecture, mcp server, mcp client, tools, stdio, mcp, model context protocol, tool, agent, agentic

cards.q: MCP vs REST API, and why use MCP instead of calling APIs directly?
cards.h: REST for programmers, MCP for agents.
s: A REST API is designed for programs written by developers. MCP is designed for AI agents: tools come with descriptions the model can read, discovery is automatic, and the same server works in any MCP app. Instead of giving the AI every raw endpoint, I expose a smaller set of task-focused tools, like deploy release to UAT, with safety checks built in. Behind the scenes, my server still calls the Azure DevOps REST APIs.
cards.k: mcp vs rest, api, ai agents, tool design, rest, web api, endpoint, http, mcp, model context protocol, tool, agent, agentic

cards.q: How does an agent discover tools and decide which to call?
cards.h: The menu is the description.
s: The client calls the server's list-tools method and gets each tool's name, description and input schema. The host passes these to the model as available functions. The model reads the user's request and the descriptions, and picks the best tool and arguments. That's why clear names and descriptions matter so much, and with about 77 tools, I made sure they don't overlap.
cards.k: tool discovery, tool selection, mcp, agent

cards.q: How are tool parameters defined and responses returned?
cards.h: Schema in, structured content out.
s: Each tool's parameters are defined with a JSON schema: names, types, which are required, and allowed values. In the C# SDK, I just write a method with attributes and descriptions, and the schema is generated automatically. The server returns results as content, and I keep them short and structured: a summary, ids, status and next steps, so the AI can use them reliably.
cards.k: tool parameters, json schema, mcp, tool response

cards.q: How do you handle tool errors?
cards.h: Errors the model can act on.
s: I return tool errors as clear results the AI can understand, not crashes, with what went wrong and what to do next, like this release is waiting for approval, please ask the approver. I never put secrets or internal details in error messages. The full error is logged on the server side with a correlation id, so I can investigate.
cards.k: tool errors, error handling, mcp

cards.q: How do you prevent unauthorized deployments and dangerous operations?
cards.h: Your token, your rights, and production still needs a human yes.
s: The server uses each user's own Azure DevOps token, so the agent can never do more than that person is allowed to. Most tools are read-only. Write tools need explicit confirmation, and environment names are checked against an allow-list. Production approvals stay with named humans in Azure DevOps, and there are no destructive tools at all.
cards.k: unauthorized deployments, security, approvals, mcp safety

cards.q: How do you validate tool inputs and AI-generated parameters?
cards.h: Never trust the model's arguments; check them like user input.
s: I never trust what the model sends just because it matches the schema. The server validates every input in code: the environment must be on the allow-list, the version must have the right format, and the release or build must actually exist. If something is wrong, it rejects it with a clear message listing the valid values.
cards.k: input validation, ai parameters, mcp, validation, ai, llm, rag, openai, claude, copilot, prompt

cards.q: How do you implement authentication and authorization?
cards.h: Who you are = your PAT; what you can do = Azure DevOps + allow-lists.
s: Our server runs locally on each engineer's machine, and authenticates to Azure DevOps with that person's own personal access token from their credential store. So authorization is Azure DevOps permissions, plus extra rules in the server, like the environment allow-list. For a shared HTTP version, the MCP spec uses OAuth, which is what I'd use.
cards.k: mcp authentication, authorization, pat, oauth

cards.q: How do you audit AI tool usage?
cards.h: Who asked, which tool, what happened.
s: Every tool call is logged as structured data: who called it, which tool, the parameters with secrets removed, the result and how long it took, with a correlation id. And Azure DevOps keeps its own history of every build, release and approval, which remains the official record. That's important for GxP traceability.
cards.k: audit, ai usage, logging, traceability, mcp, ai, llm, rag, openai, claude, copilot, prompt

cards.q: How do you handle secrets in the MCP server?
cards.h: Secrets in env, never in output.
s: Secrets never go into prompts, tool outputs, logs or config files in Git. Each user's personal access token is stored in their operating system's credential store or an environment variable, with the smallest scope needed, only build and release, and an expiry date. Tools never return credentials, even if asked.
cards.k: secrets, mcp security, pat, credentials, mcp, model context protocol, tool, agent, agentic

cards.q: What technology did you use, and why?
cards.h: Our language, our SDK, one-command install.
s: I used C# and .NET with the official C# MCP SDK, calling the Azure DevOps Server REST APIs, and packaged it as a .NET global tool. The team already knew .NET, our deployment code is .NET, and the SDK gives dependency injection, logging and configuration out of the box. Installing it is one command.
cards.k: mcp technology, c# mcp sdk, .net, design decision

cards.q: Explain the ~77 tools and how they are categorized.
cards.h: Build, Release, Deploy, Diagnose.
s: The about 77 tools are grouped by job. Builds, about 15, like queue a build, check status and get logs. Releases, about 20, like create a release and check pending approvals. Deployments and nodes, about 25, like deploy to an environment and check each node. And diagnostics, about 17, like health checks, versions per node and log summaries. Read-only tools came first, and write tools are clearly named and need confirmation.
cards.k: 77 tools, tool categories, mcp, tool groups

cards.q: How does MCP interact with Azure DevOps, and how does it trigger builds and releases?
cards.h: Agent asks, MCP translates, Azure DevOps executes.
s: The server calls the on-premise Azure DevOps Server REST APIs with the user's token. For a build, it queues the build definition for a branch and returns the build id, which a status tool polls. For a release, it creates a release from the release definition and artifact version, then starts the deployment to an environment. Pending approvals stay with humans.
cards.k: azure devops, builds, releases, rest api, mcp, ci/cd, pipeline, build, release, deployment, model context protocol, tool, agent, agentic

cards.q: How does MCP perform multi-node deployments?
cards.h: One command, many nodes, one status table.
s: A deploy tool starts the release stage for an environment, and that stage runs our Ansible, Python and Shell install scripts across [4 to 6] nodes. Status tools poll each node's steps and return a table showing pending, running, succeeded or failed per node. At the end, a version check confirms every node runs the same version.
cards.k: multi-node deployment, nodes, mcp, ansible, model context protocol, tool, agent, agentic

cards.q: How did you handle deployment failures and rollback?
cards.h: Fail on one node, retry one node; rollback = redeploy previous.
s: When something fails, the status tool shows which node and step failed with the key log lines summarised. The agent suggests options, and after the user confirms, a retry-node tool reruns only that node. For rollback, we redeploy the previous approved release through the same tools, and our database scripts are backward compatible, so the old version works on the new schema.
cards.k: deployment failure, rollback, retry node, mcp

cards.q: How did you reduce people from 6 to 1, and why was that possible?
cards.h: Repeatable steps became tools; judgment stayed human.
s: Before, one person from each area, like release, database, application nodes, UI, monitoring and verification, joined a long call to run and check their own steps by hand. Now the tools run each step, poll status and verify versions across nodes, so one engineer drives the deployment, and others join only if something fails. It was possible because the steps were repeatable.
cards.k: 6 people to 1, automation, impact, mcp

cards.q: What was automated, and what remained manual?
cards.h: Machines run steps; humans approve and decide.
s: We automated queuing builds, creating releases, starting deployments, polling each node, checking versions across nodes, summarising logs and smoke checks. What stays manual is approvals for controlled environments, change requests, FV and UAT validation, and decisions when something fails. Keeping those clear human steps is why it was accepted in our GxP environment.
cards.k: automated vs manual, human in the loop, mcp, gxp

cards.q: What was the biggest security challenge?
cards.h: Agent power = user power, never more.
s: The biggest challenge was giving an AI agent the power to deploy, without giving it more power than the person using it. I solved it with each user's own token instead of a shared account, allow-listed environments, confirmation on write tools, no destructive tools at all, the existing Azure DevOps approvals, and an audit log of every call.
cards.k: security challenge, mcp security, least privilege, security, owasp, xss, csrf, sql injection, cors, cookie

cards.q: What would you improve in your MCP implementation?
cards.h: Fewer tools, stronger tests, central audit.

I'd make all outputs structured, move to a shared HTTP version with OAuth and central audit logs, add automated tests that check the AI picks the right tool, and build dashboards on usage and failures.
cards.k: improvements, mcp, future work, model context protocol, tool, agent, agentic

cards.q: How would you prevent prompt injection and tool misuse?
cards.h: Data is not instructions; writes need a human.
s: I treat everything the AI reads, like logs and tool outputs, as data, not instructions. Write actions need user confirmation, and environments are allow-listed. cards.q: How do you handle human approval for production actions?

cards.q: How would you secure an AI deployment agent and prevent accidental production deploys?
cards.h: Production behind a separate key and a human.
s: I'd give the agent only the user's own permissions, keep production tools separate with explicit confirmation, and validate the environment against an allow-list, never guessing it. Production approvals stay with humans in Azure DevOps. A dry-run mode shows what would happen first. And every action is logged.
cards.k: ai deployment agent security, production safety, approvals, ai, llm, rag, openai, claude, copilot, prompt

cards.q: How would you implement approval workflows?
cards.h: Agent requests, human approves, system enforces.
s: I'd use the platform's existing approval gates, like Azure DevOps release approvals, rather than building a separate system. The agent can only request a deployment and check approval status, never approve. Each approval records the approver, the time and the change request reference.
cards.k: approval workflows, approvals, azure devops

cards.q: How would you maintain an audit trail?
cards.h: Every action, who, why, result, forever.
s: I'd log every tool call as structured data: the user, tool, parameters with secrets removed, result, duration and a correlation id, in a central, append-only store. The platform, like Azure DevOps, remains the official record of builds, releases and approvals. Together they show exactly what the agent did and who asked.
cards.k: audit trail, ai agent, logging, gxp, validation, change control, 21 cfr part 11, regulated

cards.q: How would you handle failed agent actions?
cards.h: Stop, explain, let the human choose.
s: Tools return clear, structured errors with suggested next steps, so the agent reports the problem instead of guessing. Only safe steps, like status checks or retrying a single node, are retried, and never a blind redeploy of everything. The user decides what to do next, and the failure is logged.
cards.k: failed agent actions, error handling, retries

cards.q: How would you design an agent for multiple environments?
cards.h: Name the environment, every time.
s: The environment is always an explicit parameter, checked against an allow-list, never guessed by the AI. Each environment has its own settings, and the rules get stricter as we move toward production, with more confirmations and human approvals for controlled environments.
cards.k: multiple environments, agent design, environments

cards.q: How would you implement RBAC for AI agents and prevent privilege escalation?
cards.h: The agent wears the user's badge, never a master key.
s: The agent acts with the user's own identity and permissions, never a shared super-user account. Tools are grouped by risk and checked against the user's role. And no tool can change permissions or approvals, so the agent can't be used to escalate privileges.
cards.k: rbac, ai agents, privilege escalation, permissions, ai, llm, rag, openai, claude, copilot, prompt

cards.q: How would you handle secrets for an AI agent?
cards.h: The model never sees the key.
s: Secrets stay in the operating system's credential store or a vault, never in prompts, tool outputs or logs. I use short-lived, least-privilege tokens with expiry and rotation. The agent never sees the secret value, only the server uses it to call the API.
cards.k: secrets, ai agent, credentials, vault, ai, llm, rag, openai, claude, copilot, prompt

cards.q: How would you evaluate whether an AI action is safe?
cards.h: Risk tier decides: auto, confirm or approve.
s: I classify tools by risk: read-only, write, and destructive. Read tools run freely, write tools need confirmation, and destructive actions need human approval or aren't offered at all. Before running anything, deterministic checks validate the environment, version and that the target exists.
cards.k: ai safety, action safety, risk classification, ai, llm, rag, openai, claude, copilot, prompt

cards.q: How would you design a multi-agent architecture?
cards.h: Specialists, one coordinator, shared notes, human gate.
s: I'd use a few specialised agents, like a planner, a coder and a reviewer, each with only the tools it needs, and a coordinator that passes work between them. I'd add limits on steps and cost, and clear stopping conditions. Our [AutoGen experiment] used a coder and a reviewer agent to draft unit tests.
cards.k: multi-agent architecture, design, autogen

cards.q: What is OAuth 2.0, and OAuth vs OpenID Connect?
cards.h: OAuth = valet key; OIDC = ID card.
s: OAuth 2.0 is about authorization: it lets an app get an access token to call an API on the user's behalf, without the user's password. OpenID Connect is built on top and adds authentication: an ID token that tells the app who the user is. For browser apps, I use the authorization code flow with PKCE.
cards.k: oauth, openid connect, oidc, authorization, authentication, auth, login, sso

cards.q: What is SSO, and how does it work?
cards.h: One key ring, many doors.
s: SSO, single sign-on, lets a user log in once and access many applications. The app redirects the user to the identity provider, the user signs in there, and the provider sends back a token that the app trusts. Other apps trust the same provider, so no new login is needed. Our SSO cookie fix came from storing too many claims in that cookie.
cards.k: sso, single sign-on, identity provider, oidc, saml, auth, authentication, authorization, login, oauth

cards.q: What is SQL injection?
cards.h: Never let data become code.
s: SQL injection is when user input is put directly into a SQL query, so an attacker can change the query, for example to read or delete data. I prevent it by always using parameterized queries. EF Core and Dapper do this by default, and with raw SQL I use interpolated or explicit parameters, never string concatenation.
cards.k: sql injection, security, parameterized queries, owasp, sql, sql server, query, index, t-sql, database, xss, csrf, cors, cookie

cards.q: What is secure cookie configuration: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite?
cards.h: HttpOnly hides it, Secure encrypts the trip, SameSite keeps it home.
s: HttpOnly stops JavaScript from reading the cookie, which protects it from XSS. Secure means it's only sent over HTTPS. SameSite controls whether the cookie is sent with requests from other sites: Lax or Strict help prevent CSRF, and None requires Secure. For auth cookies, I set all three properly.
cards.k: secure cookies, httponly, secure, samesite, cookie security

cards.q: How do you secure APIs and microservices?
cards.h: Authenticate, authorise, validate, limit, log.
s: I authenticate every request, at the gateway and in each service, and authorize with policies and per-record checks. Traffic is encrypted with TLS, inputs are validated, and rate limiting protects against abuse. Services talk using their own identities with least privilege, and secrets are in a vault.
cards.k: api security, microservices security, zero trust, microservices, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: How do you secure AWS resources?
cards.h: Least privilege, private by default, encrypted, watched.
s: I use IAM roles with least privilege, keep services and databases in private subnets with tight security groups, and encrypt data at rest with KMS and in transit with TLS. CloudTrail and GuardDuty monitor activity, and all infrastructure changes go through code and review.
cards.k: aws security, iam, encryption, cloudtrail, guardduty, aws, ecs, fargate, lambda, s3, rds, dynamodb, cloudwatch

cards.q: How do you perform dependency vulnerability scanning?
cards.h: Scan every build, patch every sprint.
s: The pipeline scans dependencies on every build, using tools like dotnet list package vulnerable, npm audit, or Dependabot, and fails the build on serious issues. I also scan container images. We update packages regularly, and central package management made it easy to update the same package across all projects.
cards.k: dependency scanning, vulnerabilities, npm audit, dependabot

cards.q: How do you handle security vulnerabilities found in production?
cards.h: Contain, fix, verify, prevent.
s: First I assess how serious and exploitable it is. Then I reduce the risk quickly, for example with a configuration change or a WAF rule, and release a proper fix through an emergency change, still documented. Afterwards I find the root cause and add a test or scan rule so it doesn't come back.
cards.k: security vulnerability, production, incident response, security, owasp, xss, csrf, sql injection, cors, cookie

cards.q: Design a scalable REST API or a high-volume API.
cards.h: Stateless, cached, paged, async, limited.
s: I'd keep the API stateless behind a load balancer so I can add instances, with autoscaling. I'd add caching for hot reads, pagination for lists, async processing for heavy work, and rate limits. For the database, indexes first, then read replicas, and partitioning if needed. And I'd monitor p95 latency and errors.
cards.k: scalable api, high volume, system design, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Design a URL shortener.
cards.h: Encode an id, cache the hot ones, redirect fast.
s: The service takes a long URL and returns a short code, like a base62 version of a unique id, and stores the mapping in a database. When someone opens the short link, it looks up the code and redirects, using a cache like Redis for popular links. I'd add expiry, abuse protection, and click analytics if needed.
cards.k: url shortener, system design, base62, redis

cards.q: Design a notification service.
cards.h: Event in, preferences, template, channel workers.
s: Other services publish a notification request to a queue. Workers for each channel, like email, SMS and push, pick it up, apply templates and the user's preferences, and send through providers. Failed sends are retried with backoff and then go to a dead-letter queue. An idempotency key prevents duplicate messages.
cards.k: notification service, system design, queues, email, sms

cards.q: Design an order management system.
cards.h: Saga over services, state machine per order.
s: I'd model the order as a state machine with clear allowed transitions, like created, paid, shipped and delivered. Placing an order reserves stock and takes payment through a saga, with compensating actions if a step fails. Events are published through an outbox, and APIs use idempotency keys so retries don't create duplicate orders.
cards.k: order management, system design, saga, state machine

cards.q: Design a file upload service.
cards.h: Presigned upload, scan on arrival.
s: The client asks the API for a presigned S3 URL and uploads directly to S3, so large files don't go through our servers. An S3 event then triggers processing, like virus scanning and extracting metadata. I'd use multipart upload for big files, size limits, and store file details in a database with access control.
cards.k: file upload service, system design, s3, presigned url

cards.q: Design a distributed job-processing system.
cards.h: Enqueue, work, retry, dead-letter, report.
s: Jobs go into a queue, and a pool of workers picks them up. Each job is idempotent, so retries are safe, failed jobs are retried with backoff and then sent to a dead-letter queue. I track each job's status in a database so users can see progress, and scale the workers based on the queue length.
cards.k: job processing, distributed jobs, workers, queues, system design

cards.q: Design a payment system.
cards.h: Idempotent, double-entry, reconciled.
s: Every payment request carries an idempotency key, so a retry never charges twice. I'd keep a ledger with double-entry records and reconcile it with the payment provider daily. Card data is never stored by us, we use a PCI-compliant provider with tokens. Payment status updates come through provider webhooks.
cards.k: payment system, system design, idempotency, ledger

cards.q: Design a messaging (chat) system.
cards.h: Sockets in, persist, fan out.
s: Clients connect with WebSockets, using SignalR in .NET, for live messages. Messages are stored per conversation with an ordering id, and delivered to online users instantly, while offline users get a push notification and fetch messages later. To scale across servers, I'd use a backplane like Redis.
cards.k: chat system, messaging, system design, websockets, signalr, message broker, kafka, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: Design an event-driven microservices system.
cards.h: Outbox, broker, idempotent consumers.
s: Services publish events when something important happens, and other services react to them. Events are versioned contracts with schemas, published reliably through an outbox, and consumers are idempotent. For simple flows, services react on their own, and for longer business processes, an orchestrator saga gives better visibility.
cards.k: event-driven, microservices, system design, events, outbox, messaging, message broker, kafka, rabbitmq, event driven, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: Design a scalable authentication system.
cards.h: Central IdP, stateless tokens, fast local validation.
s: I wouldn't build my own, I'd use a proven identity provider with OpenID Connect. Apps use short-lived access tokens with refresh token rotation, and MFA for users. For logout or revocation, a denylist of token ids in Redis works, like our fix with [15-minute] tokens and about [1 millisecond] checks.
cards.k: authentication system, system design, oidc, tokens

cards.q: Design a distributed caching system.
cards.h: Hash ring, TTL, invalidate, avoid stampedes.
s: I'd use cache-aside with expiry times, spread keys across nodes with consistent hashing, and invalidate entries when data changes. To avoid a stampede, where many requests rebuild the same entry at once, I'd use request coalescing, which HybridCache in .NET does for us. Redis cluster is the usual choice.
cards.k: distributed cache, caching, redis, system design

cards.q: Design your IQVIA-style clinical-trial platform at a high level.
cards.h: Setup, Randomize, Supply, Ship, Audit.
s: Users and vendors come in through a gateway with SSO. Behind it are services for study setup, randomization, supply, shipments and subjects, each with its own SQL Server database and audit tables. Kafka and RabbitMQ carry events and work queues, vendor integrations use SFTP and APIs, everything runs on ECS across availability zones, and GxP controls like validation and audit trails apply throughout.
cards.k: clinical trial platform, irt design, system design, architecture

cards.q: How would you scale the architecture, and handle database scaling?
cards.h: Scale out the services, tune then split the data.
s: I'd scale services horizontally since they're stateless, cache reference data, and move heavy work to queues. For the database, first tune queries and indexes, then add read replicas for reporting, and finally partition data, for example by study, if one database can't keep up.
cards.k: scaling, database scaling, read replicas, partitioning

cards.q: Where would you use caching, Kafka, RabbitMQ and synchronous APIs?
cards.h: Cache what's read, Kafka what's streamed, Rabbit what's queued, REST what's asked.
s: I'd use caching for reference data and permissions, in Redis. Kafka for shipment status events that many services consume and we may need to replay. RabbitMQ for task-style work like notifications and reports, with retries per message. And synchronous APIs for user-facing reads and commands that need an immediate answer, like randomizing a patient.
cards.k: caching, kafka, rabbitmq, synchronous apis, design choices, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, event streaming, queue, exchange, amqp, dead letter, dlq, messaging, message broker, event driven

cards.q: How would you handle failures?
cards.h: Expect failure everywhere.
s: I'd use timeouts on every call, retries with backoff for temporary errors, circuit breakers, dead-letter queues and the outbox pattern so nothing is lost. Each failure is visible through alerts, with runbooks so the on-call person knows what to do.
cards.k: failure handling, resilience, outbox, dlq

cards.q: How would you monitor and secure the system?
cards.h: Watch everything; trust nothing.
s: To monitor, I'd use metrics, logs and traces with correlation ids, and alerts based on service level objectives. To secure it, SSO for users, role-based access, encryption everywhere, audit trails for all regulated data, and least-privilege IAM roles for the services.
cards.k: monitoring, security, observability, system design

cards.q: Did you process the CSV import synchronously or asynchronously?
cards.h: Small capped file: answer now; big file: job and poll.
s: I processed it synchronously within the request, because files are limited to [5 MB, about 10,000 rows], and parsing is streamed, so validation finishes in [a few seconds] and users see the preview right away. All the file and database work is async, so no threads are blocked. For much bigger files, I'd move it to a background job that returns 202 with a status endpoint.
cards.k: csv import, synchronous, asynchronous, background job, 202

cards.q: How did you secure uploaded files?
cards.h: Who, how big, what type, never executed.
s: Only authorised users with the right role for that study can upload. I check the size limit, the CSV extension, and that the content really is text CSV. Files are processed in memory or temporary storage, never executed or served back. When we export the error report, I protect against CSV injection, and every upload is audited with who uploaded what.
cards.k: file upload security, csv injection, validation, audit

cards.q: How did you optimize large CSV processing?
cards.h: Stream, preload lookups, batch writes.
s: I read the file as a stream with CsvHelper instead of loading it all into memory. Validation runs in stages and stops early if the headers are wrong. Lookups, like existing sites, countries and depots, are loaded once into dictionaries, instead of a database call per row. Then rows are inserted in batches inside one transaction.
cards.k: csv performance, streaming, csvhelper, batching, optimization

cards.q: How did you test the import?
cards.h: Every rule, the whole save, the real UI.
s: I wrote unit tests for each validation rule, like missing fields, wrong types, duplicates in the file or database, and invalid countries or depots. Integration tests saved a file into a test database and checked that a failure rolls everything back. Playwright tests covered upload, preview, error download and confirm. I also tested a file at the maximum size.
cards.k: csv import testing, unit tests, integration tests, playwright, test, testing, unit test, integration test, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: How did you handle concurrent imports?
cards.h: One study, one import at a time.
s: Only one import per study can run at a time, enforced by a lock row checked inside the transaction, so a second user gets a clear "import in progress" message. A file hash stops the same file being imported twice. And a [limit of 2 imports per user] at a time protects the server.
cards.k: concurrent imports, locking, concurrency, file hash

cards.q: What happens if the import fails halfway through?
cards.h: All or nothing means halfway = nothing.
s: Nothing is saved. All rows are written in one transaction, so if anything fails, like a database error or timeout, everything is rolled back. The user sees a clear error and can simply try again, and the audit log records the failed attempt. The study is never left half set up.
cards.k: import failure, transaction, rollback, atomicity

cards.q: How would you redesign it for millions of records?
cards.h: S3, worker, staging table, bulk copy, merge.
s: For millions of rows, I'd upload directly to S3 with a presigned URL. A background worker would stream and validate the file in chunks, load rows into a staging table with SqlBulkCopy, validate them with set-based SQL, and then merge them into the live tables in controlled batches, with progress reporting and an error file. A file hash and job id keep it idempotent.
cards.k: large scale import, millions of records, sqlbulkcopy, staging table, s3

cards.q: How did you test the study transfer safety guard?
cards.h: Each rule pass and fail, plus the race.
s: I wrote unit tests for each of the five checks, both passing and failing, like a live study with randomized patients or a missing change request. Integration tests covered the transaction and the lock, including two transfers at once. Tests confirmed every attempt is audited, and the FV scripts cover each blocking scenario.
cards.k: testing, study transfer, safety guard, unit tests, test, unit test, integration test, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: How did you audit blocked transfers?
cards.h: Blocked attempts are evidence, not noise.
s: Every attempt, allowed or blocked, writes an audit record with the user, the source and target study and environment, the change request reference, which check failed and why, and the time. The audit is written separately, so it's saved even when the transfer is blocked. Validators and support can report on blocked attempts.
cards.k: audit, blocked transfers, audit trail, gxp

cards.q: What is release integration?
cards.h: Many teams in, one tagged release out.
s: Release integration means bringing together every team's changes for a release, the application, APIs, database scripts and UI, merging them into the release branch, resolving conflicts, tagging one version, and producing a consistent set of artifacts to install and validate. I'm the release integrator for our team, coordinating with about [5] teams.
cards.k: release integration, release management, merging, tagging

cards.q: How do you validate releases and promote from UAT to production?
cards.h: Same artifact, proven in UAT, approved for production.
s: We validate with automated tests, smoke tests after install, version checks on every node, FV scripts with evidence, and UAT sign-off. To promote to production, we take the exact same tagged artifacts that passed UAT, under an approved change request, deploy them through the controlled pipeline, and verify afterwards.
cards.k: release validation, uat to production, promotion, change request

cards.q: How do you coordinate application, API, database and UI releases?
cards.h: DB first, then API, then app, then UI.
s: We use one release version and one checklist. The deployment order is backward-compatible database scripts first, then APIs, then application services, then the UI. Incomplete features stay behind feature flags, and I do a daily status check with each team in the days before the release.
cards.k: release coordination, deployment order, feature flags, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Why use Python and Shell automation?
cards.h: Scripts make every node identical.
s: Our nodes run Linux-based install steps, where Shell is natural. Python handles the logic, like reading manifests, comparing versions and calling APIs. Together with Ansible, they make installs repeatable and identical on every node, which removed a lot of manual steps and mistakes.
cards.k: python, shell, ansible, automation, scripting

cards.q: How do you perform multi-node deployments and ensure all nodes run the same version?
cards.h: Same playbook everywhere, then compare versions.
s: Ansible playbooks with Python and Shell scripts run the install steps across [4 to 6] nodes in order, and stop if something fails. Each node reports its installed version, through a version file and a health endpoint, and a check compares them with the release tag. Any mismatch fails the verification.
cards.k: multi-node deployment, version check, ansible, consistency

cards.q: How do you verify a deployment?
cards.h: Version, health, smoke, logs, sign-off.
s: I check the version on every node, make sure the health endpoints are green, and run smoke tests of key flows, like login, randomizing in a test study, and the shipment list. Then I check logs and dashboards for any new errors, and sign off in the release record.
cards.k: deployment verification, smoke tests, health checks

cards.q: What is Agile, and Scrum vs Kanban?
cards.h: Scrum = timeboxes; Kanban = flow.
s: Agile means delivering in small pieces, getting feedback often and adapting. Scrum uses fixed-length sprints with roles like product owner and scrum master, and events like planning, review and retrospective. Kanban uses a continuous flow with limits on work in progress and no sprints, which suits support and operations work. Our team uses Scrum with [two-week] sprints.
cards.k: agile, scrum, kanban, methodology

cards.q: What happens during sprint planning, and what is a retrospective?
cards.h: Plan what to do; reflect on how we did it.
s: In sprint planning, the team picks the top priority, refined stories that fit our capacity, agrees a sprint goal, and breaks stories into tasks. The retrospective happens at the end of the sprint, where we talk about what went well and what didn't, and agree one or two improvements to try next sprint.
cards.k: sprint planning, retrospective, scrum, agile

cards.q: How do you handle changing requirements?
cards.h: Welcome the change, trade the scope.
s: First I understand why it's changing and how important it is, by talking with the product owner and BA. Then I estimate the impact and we agree what moves out of the sprint, and we update the acceptance criteria and traceability, which matters in GxP. I also write code that's easy to change, with clean boundaries and tests.
cards.k: changing requirements, scope change, agile

cards.q: How do you conduct code reviews, and handle disagreement during review?
cards.h: Review the code, respect the coder.
s: I review for correctness, security, readability, tests and design, and I keep comments about the code, not the person, explaining why and marking what's a must-fix versus a suggestion. If we disagree, I bring data, like documentation or our team standards. If comments keep going back and forth, I have a quick call, and if needed, we agree a team rule with the lead.
cards.k: code review, disagreement, pull requests, feedback

cards.q: Tell me about a technical decision you influenced.
cards.h: Prototype, demo, address fears, measure.
s: Release deployments needed about 6 people and 6 hours. I proposed automating them with an MCP server, built a read-only prototype in [two weeks], and demoed it to my lead and the release manager. I addressed their safety concerns, like using each person's own token and keeping approvals, and measured before and after. The team adopted it: 6 hours to 2, and 6 people to 1.
cards.k: technical decision, influence, mcp, story

cards.q: How do you handle production pressure?
cards.h: Calm, mitigate, communicate, then fix properly.
s: I stay calm and structured. First I reduce the impact, then I update people regularly, and split the work clearly if several people are helping. I avoid risky changes under pressure, and do the proper root cause work afterwards. Checklists and runbooks help a lot to avoid panic.
cards.k: production pressure, stress, incidents, calm

cards.q: How do you communicate technical problems to non-technical stakeholders?
cards.h: Impact, action, next update.
s: I start with the impact: who is affected and how badly. Then what we're doing about it and when the next update will come, in plain language with simple comparisons and no jargon. If they need to decide something, I give two or three options with the trade-offs and my recommendation.
cards.k: communication, non-technical stakeholders, stakeholder management

cards.q: What is Spring Boot?
cards.h: Spring Boot = ASP.NET Core for Java.
s: Spring Boot is a framework on top of Spring for building Java services quickly. It gives auto-configuration, an embedded web server like Tomcat, starter dependencies, and production features like health and metrics with Actuator. It's basically the Java counterpart of ASP.NET Core.
cards.k: spring boot, java, framework

cards.q: Dependency injection and the IoC container in Spring; @Autowired?
cards.h: Same DI idea, different annotations.
s: Spring's IoC container, the ApplicationContext, creates objects called beans and injects their dependencies, just like the .NET service provider. Constructor injection is the preferred way. The Autowired annotation marks where to inject, and if a class has only one constructor, it's not even needed.
cards.k: spring dependency injection, ioc container, autowired, beans, di, dependency injection, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes

cards.q: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository?
cards.h: Same bean, different labels; Repository also translates errors.
s: All three register a class as a Spring bean through component scanning. Component is the generic one. Service marks business logic, and it's mostly for readability. Repository marks data access classes and also translates database exceptions into Spring's standard data access exceptions.
cards.k: component, service, repository, spring annotations

cards.q: How do you build a Spring Boot REST controller?
cards.h: @RestController = [ApiController].
s: I create a class with the RestController annotation and a base path with RequestMapping, like api slash shipments. Methods use GetMapping and PostMapping. Parameters come from PathVariable, RequestParam, or RequestBody with Valid for validation. I return ResponseEntity to control the status code, just like returning results in ASP.NET Core.
cards.k: spring rest controller, restcontroller, getmapping, java api

cards.q: Spring Boot configuration and profiles?
cards.h: Profiles = appsettings.{Environment}.json.
s: Spring Boot reads configuration from application.yml or properties files, environment variables, and typed ConfigurationProperties classes, which are like the .NET options pattern. Profiles, like dev, uat and prod, load their own application-profile.yml file, and are chosen with spring.profiles.active, similar to ASP.NET Core environments.
cards.k: spring configuration, profiles, application.yml

cards.q: Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, and JPA vs EF Core?
cards.h: JPA = spec, Hibernate = engine, Spring Data = shortcuts.
s: JPA is the Java standard for persistence, Hibernate is the most common implementation, and Spring Data JPA adds repository interfaces that generate queries from method names. Compared with EF Core, the ideas are very similar, entities, change tracking and lazy loading. But migrations use Flyway or Liquibase, and queries use JPQL instead of LINQ.
cards.k: spring data jpa, hibernate, jpa vs ef core, orm, ef core, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: Spring Boot exception handling and security?
cards.h: ControllerAdvice = global handler; Spring Security = auth middleware.
s: For exceptions, I use a RestControllerAdvice class with ExceptionHandler methods that return ProblemDetail responses, which is like exception middleware in .NET. For security, Spring Security has a filter chain, the OAuth2 resource server validates JWTs, and method security with PreAuthorize checks roles.
cards.k: spring exception handling, spring security, controlleradvice, exception, error handling, problemdetails, exception handling, security, owasp, xss, csrf, sql injection, cors, cookie

cards.q: Java vs C#?
cards.h: Cousins: same family, different habits.
s: Java and C# are very similar: both are statically typed, object-oriented and garbage collected. C# got some features earlier, like LINQ, async-await, properties, records and pattern matching, and has real value types and generics at runtime. Java has a huge ecosystem, many JVM vendors, and virtual threads since Java 21.
cards.k: java vs c#, comparison, languages

cards.q: Why choose Spring Boot over .NET, or .NET over Spring Boot?
cards.h: Choose the platform your team and systems already speak.
s: I'd choose Spring Boot if the organisation's platform, libraries and people are already Java. I'd choose .NET if the team and code base are .NET, for its performance, LINQ and EF Core productivity, and great tooling. Both are excellent, so team skills and existing systems should decide, not personal preference.
cards.k: spring boot vs .net, technology choice

cards.q: Why this role?

cards.q: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core?
cards.h: Russian dolls: each layer wraps the next, in on the way in, out on the way back.
s: Middleware is a component that sits in the ASP.NET Core request pipeline. Every HTTP request passes through a chain of middleware, and each one gets the HttpContext and a reference to the next one in the chain.

Each middleware can do three things. It can do some work before the request goes further, like reading headers. It can call next, to pass the request to the next middleware. And after next returns, it can do work on the way back, like adding a response header or logging the duration. It can also decide not to call next and end the request early, which is called short-circuiting. The pipeline is built in Program.cs with app.Use calls, and it runs in exactly the order you register them, which is why the order matters so much.
A lot of the framework is just middleware: exception handling, HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and finally the endpoints.
In my project, I wrote a correlation-id middleware, so every request carries one id across our [4] services, and one log search shows the whole journey. I can walk you through how I wrote that one.
cards.k: middleware, request pipeline, request delegate, use, next, http pipeline, pipeline

cards.q: What is custom middleware, and how do you write one?
cards.h: Before, next, after.
s: Custom middleware is my own component in the ASP.NET Core request pipeline. I write one when I need logic that should run for every request, or a group of requests, and that isn't specific to one controller, like correlation ids, request timing, audit logging or adding security headers.

There are three ways to write it. The most common is convention-based: a class whose constructor takes the next RequestDelegate, with a public InvokeAsync method that takes HttpContext. Inside InvokeAsync, I do my work, then await next of context, then do any work on the way back. The second way is implementing the IMiddleware interface, which is created from DI per request, so it's better when I need scoped services. And for something tiny, I can write it inline with app.Use and a lambda. I register the class with app.UseMiddleware, usually wrapped in an extension method like app.UseCorrelationId, and I place it carefully, because order matters.

My real example is our correlation-id middleware. It reads the X-Correlation-ID header, or creates a new id, adds it to the response headers and to the logging scope, and then calls next. So every log line for that request carries the id across our [4] services.
One pitfall to watch is injecting scoped services like DbContext into the constructor. I can explain why if you like.
cards.k: custom middleware, invokeasync, requestdelegate, usemiddleware, httpcontext, middleware, pipeline, request delegate, request pipeline

cards.q: Convention-based vs factory-based (IMiddleware) middleware, and the scoped-service pitfall?
cards.h: Constructor = once forever; InvokeAsync parameters = per request.
s: There are two ways to write a middleware class, and the difference is really about lifetime.

Convention-based middleware is a class with a constructor taking RequestDelegate next, and an InvokeAsync method. ASP.NET Core creates it once, when the pipeline is built, so it's effectively a singleton for the life of the app. Factory-based middleware implements the IMiddleware interface. I register it in the DI container, as scoped or transient, and the framework resolves a new instance from the request scope on every request.

That leads to the classic pitfall. If you inject a scoped service, like DbContext, into the constructor of convention-based middleware, it's captured once and reused for every request forever. That's a captive dependency: it's not thread-safe and it serves stale data. In development, scope validation throws an exception at startup to catch it.

There are two fixes. For convention-based middleware, take scoped services as extra parameters of InvokeAsync, which are resolved per request. Or use IMiddleware, where constructor injection of scoped services is fine. Our audit middleware needed the DbContext, so we made it IMiddleware and registered it as scoped. I can show both versions in code.
cards.k: imiddleware, convention-based middleware, factory-based middleware, scoped service, captive dependency, custom middleware, middleware factory, middleware, pipeline, request delegate, request pipeline

It reads the X-Correlation-ID header, or creates a new id if there isn't one, returns it in the response header, and opens a logging scope, so every log line in that request automatically carries the id. To pass it on, I added an HttpClient DelegatingHandler that copies the id to outgoing calls, and our RabbitMQ publisher puts it in the message headers, so consumers continue the same scope. For the audit side, an IMiddleware component records who changed what with the same id. I rolled it out service by service, with a short wiki page and a saved Logs Insights query.

cards.q: What are the MVC filter types and their order, and how do you write a custom action filter?
cards.h: Auth, Resource, Action, Exception, Result: ARAER.
s: Filters are like middleware, but they run inside MVC, around controller actions, so they know which action is running and can see its arguments and results.

They run in a fixed order. First authorization filters, which can block the request. Then resource filters, which run before model binding and can short-circuit, which is useful for caching. Then model binding happens. Then action filters, before and after the action itself. If anything throws, exception filters handle it. Then result filters run around the execution of the result, like serialising the response.

To write a custom action filter, I implement IAsyncActionFilter, or inherit ActionFilterAttribute. In OnActionExecutionAsync, I do work before, call await next, and then inspect the executed context afterwards. I can register it globally in AddControllers options, as an attribute on a controller or action, or with ServiceFilter or TypeFilter when it needs dependencies from DI.

The rule I follow: middleware for concerns that apply to every request, like correlation ids, and filters for MVC-aware concerns. For example, we have an audit action filter that records which study an action changed, reading the action arguments. I can compare filters and middleware in more detail.
cards.k: filters, action filter, authorization filter, resource filter, exception filter, result filter, iasyncactionfilter, filter

cards.q: IOptions vs IOptionsSnapshot vs IOptionsMonitor?
cards.h: Options = photo, Snapshot = photo per request, Monitor = live video.
s: All three give your code access to strongly-typed configuration, but they differ in lifetime and in how they handle configuration changes.

IOptions is a singleton. The values are read once, the first time they're needed, and never change while the app runs. It's the simplest, and it's fine for settings that only change with a deployment. IOptionsSnapshot is scoped. The values are recomputed for each request, so if appsettings changes on disk, the next request sees the new values. It also supports named options. But because it's scoped, you can't inject it into a singleton. IOptionsMonitor is a singleton that always gives the latest values through CurrentValue, supports named options, and has an OnChange callback, so it works in singletons and background services.
I also add ValidateDataAnnotations and ValidateOnStart, so bad configuration fails at startup, not on the first request.

In our vendor exchange, each vendor's SFTP settings are named options, and our background poller is a singleton, so it uses IOptionsMonitor, reading CurrentValue at the start of each run. That way, we can change a vendor's polling settings without a restart. I can explain how this works with AWS configuration sources.
cards.k: ioptions, ioptionssnapshot, ioptionsmonitor, options pattern, configuration reload, configuration, appsettings

cards.q: What are hosted services and BackgroundService?
cards.h: The host's own employees: start with the app, stop with the app.
s: Hosted services are how you run background work inside an ASP.NET Core or worker app, managed by the same host as the web server.

The base interface is IHostedService, with StartAsync and StopAsync. The host calls StartAsync when the app starts, and StopAsync during graceful shutdown. BackgroundService is a helpful base class on top of it. You just override ExecuteAsync, which usually contains a loop that runs until the stopping token is cancelled. You register it with AddHostedService, and it's registered as a singleton.

Two things are important. First, because it's a singleton, it must not inject scoped services, like DbContext, directly. Instead, it injects IServiceScopeFactory and creates a scope per unit of work. Second, it must respect the stopping token, so shutdown is clean, and it should catch and log exceptions inside the loop, because since .NET 6, an unhandled exception in a BackgroundService stops the whole host by default.

In our system, the SFTP poller and the RabbitMQ consumers are BackgroundServices. Each poll or each message runs in its own scope with a fresh DbContext. I can explain how we used PeriodicTimer for the polling loop.

cards.q: What is ILogger<T> and structured logging?
cards.h: Template + named holes = searchable fields.
s: ILogger of T is the built-in logging abstraction in .NET. I inject it into a class, and T sets the log category, which is the class's full name. That category lets you filter logs in configuration, for example showing debug logs for one namespace only.

Structured logging means logging with message templates and named placeholders, instead of building strings. For example, "Shipment {ShipmentId} moved to {Status}". The values are captured as separate fields, not just text, so in the log system you can search and filter by ShipmentId, or count failures by Status. It's also more efficient, because the string isn't formatted if that log level is disabled. Providers decide where logs go, like the console, Serilog, or CloudWatch, and logging scopes add context, like a correlation id, to every log line inside them.
A common mistake is string interpolation in log calls, which loses the structure. For hot paths, the LoggerMessage source generator avoids allocations.

In our services, logs are written as JSON to CloudWatch. Because every line has a CorrelationId and fields like ShipmentId, one Logs Insights query finds everything about a failed shipment. I can show a typical query.

cards.q: What is rate limiting, and how do you implement it in ASP.NET Core?
cards.h: Bouncer with a clicker: N per window, then 429.
s: Rate limiting limits how many requests a client, or an endpoint, can make within a period. When the limit is exceeded, the API returns 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with a Retry-After header. It protects the service from abuse, accidental loops in a client, and one noisy consumer starving everyone else.

Since ASP.NET Core 7, there's built-in rate limiting middleware. In Program.cs I call AddRateLimiter and define policies. There are four algorithms: fixed window, like 100 requests per minute; sliding window, which smooths the edges between windows; token bucket, which allows short bursts; and a concurrency limiter, which limits how many requests run at the same time. Policies can be partitioned, so each user, IP address or API key gets its own limit. Then I add UseRateLimiter to the pipeline, and apply policies per endpoint with RequireRateLimiting or the EnableRateLimiting attribute.
In a multi-instance setup, these limits are per instance, so for global limits we also use API Gateway or WAF limits.
For our CSV import, we used a concurrency-style limit, so each user can run only [2] imports at a time. I can explain how token bucket works.
cards.k: rate limiting, throttling, 429, token bucket, fixed window, sliding window, addratelimiter

cards.q: What is a minimal API?
cards.h: A route and a lambda: the whole controller in one line.
s: A minimal API is a lightweight way to build HTTP APIs in ASP.NET Core without controllers. You map routes directly to handlers, using MapGet, MapPost and so on, with a lambda or method.

The handler's parameters are bound automatically: route values, query strings, the body, and services from DI, all just as parameters. You return results using TypedResults, like TypedResults.Ok or TypedResults.NotFound, which also documents the response types in OpenAPI. For structure, MapGroup creates route groups that share a prefix, authorization and filters, and endpoint filters give you filter-like logic. Since .NET 10, there's built-in validation, which used to be a gap compared with controllers.

The benefits are less ceremony, faster startup, and slightly better performance. It's also more friendly with native AOT. For larger APIs, I organise endpoints into extension methods per feature, so Program.cs stays small.

In our team, older services use controllers, and newer small services, like an internal lookup service, use minimal APIs. Both share the same middleware, DI and authentication. I can compare them with controllers in more detail.

cards.q: What is exception middleware, and IExceptionHandler with ProblemDetails in .NET 8?
cards.h: One net at the top of the pipeline, one standard error shape.
s: Exception middleware is the safety net at the top of the pipeline that catches unhandled exceptions from everything after it, and turns them into a proper error response instead of a crash or a raw stack trace.

In ASP.NET Core, it's UseExceptionHandler. In .NET 8, Microsoft added the IExceptionHandler interface, which makes this much cleaner. I write a handler class with a TryHandleAsync method that maps exception types to status codes. For example, a validation exception becomes 400, a not-found exception becomes 404, and a concurrency exception becomes 409. I register it with AddExceptionHandler, and you can chain several handlers. With AddProblemDetails, every error is returned in the standard ProblemDetails format, with a type, title, status and a trace id.

The important rule is never leak internals. Stack traces and exception messages are only shown in development. In production, the client gets a generic message, plus a trace id, and the full details go to the logs.

In our services, the ProblemDetails response also includes our correlation id, so when a user reports an error, support searches the logs by that id and finds the exact exception. I can show a sample handler.

cards.q: What is IHttpClientFactory, and why not new HttpClient()?
cards.h: Factory = a pool of phone lines, refreshed regularly.
s: IHttpClientFactory is the recommended way to create HttpClient instances in .NET, because using HttpClient naively causes two opposite problems.

If you create and dispose a new HttpClient for every request, each one opens new connections, and closed sockets stay in the TIME_WAIT state for a while. Under load, you can run out of sockets. But if you go the other way and keep one static HttpClient forever, it never picks up DNS changes, which is a problem in cloud environments where IPs change. IHttpClientFactory solves both. It pools the underlying message handlers and rotates them, by default every two minutes, so connections are reused but DNS is refreshed.

It also gives a central place for configuration. I use typed clients, where a class like VendorApiClient gets a preconfigured HttpClient injected, with its base address, timeout and headers. I can add DelegatingHandlers as outgoing middleware, and AddStandardResilienceHandler for retries and circuit breaking.
In our services, our correlation-id DelegatingHandler is attached to every typed client, so the id automatically flows to downstream calls. I can show how that's registered.

cards.q: What are Span<T> and Memory<T>?
cards.h: A window onto memory, not a copy.
s: Span of T is a type that gives you a view over a contiguous block of memory, like part of an array, a string, or stack memory, without copying it. Slicing a span is free, it just points to a different start and length.

That makes it perfect for high-performance parsing. For example, instead of calling Substring, which allocates a new string each time, I can slice a ReadOnlySpan of char and parse numbers directly from it. Span is a ref struct, so it can only live on the stack. That's what makes it safe and fast, but it also means it can't be a field in a class, can't be boxed, and can't be used across an await. Memory of T is the companion type that can live on the heap, so it works in async methods, and you get a span from it when you need to do the work.
Many .NET APIs now accept spans, like int.Parse, so you can avoid allocations entirely.

I used this when optimising our CSV parsing. Reading fields as spans instead of splitting strings reduced allocations a lot, which reduced garbage collection during large imports. I can explain ArrayPool, which works well with it.
cards.k: span, memory, performance, allocations, stackalloc, parsing

cards.q: What is IAsyncEnumerable<T> and async streams?
cards.h: A conveyor belt you can wait on.
s: IAsyncEnumerable of T is an asynchronous sequence. It lets you produce and consume items one at a time, where getting each item may involve async work, like reading from a database, a file or a network stream.

To produce one, you write an async iterator: an async method returning IAsyncEnumerable that uses await and yield return. To consume it, you use await foreach. The big benefit is that items are processed as they arrive, instead of waiting for the whole list to be loaded into memory first. So memory stays flat, and the first results are available sooner. It supports cancellation through the EnumeratorCancellation attribute, or WithCancellation.

It's well integrated. EF Core can stream query results with AsAsyncEnumerable. ASP.NET Core can return IAsyncEnumerable from an action, and System.Text.Json serialises it without buffering everything.

We used it for a large data export endpoint. Instead of loading tens of thousands of rows into a list, we streamed them from EF Core straight into the response, so memory usage stayed constant regardless of the export size. I can explain the difference from IEnumerable with Task.
