cards.q: Response caching vs output caching vs IMemoryCache vs HybridCache?
cards.h: Headers for clients, outputs for endpoints, data for code.
s: These four are all caching, but at different levels.

Response caching is based on HTTP headers. The server sets Cache-Control headers, and browsers and proxies can reuse the response. The response caching middleware can also cache on the server, but it strictly follows HTTP rules. Output caching, added in .NET 7, is a server-side cache of whole responses that the server controls. You define policies, vary by query or header, and evict by tags, for example evicting all "sites" responses when a site changes. IMemoryCache caches data in code, inside one process. It's fast, but each instance has its own copy. IDistributedCache, like Redis, shares it across instances. And HybridCache, in .NET 9, combines both: a fast local cache and a distributed cache, with stampede protection, so many concurrent misses trigger only one database call.
The hard part is always invalidation. I prefer short expiries and explicit eviction when data changes.

In our services, reference data like depots and country rules is cached in memory with expiry, and shared data is in ElastiCache Redis, which is also where our token denylist lives. I can explain cache stampedes.
cards.k: caching, response caching, output caching, imemorycache, hybridcache, redis, distributed cache, cache, elasticache, memory cache

cards.q: How does JWT bearer authentication work in the ASP.NET Core pipeline?
cards.h: Authentication reads the badge; authorization checks the door list.
s: JWT bearer authentication in ASP.NET Core is split between two middleware: authentication, which works out who you are, and authorization, which decides what you can do.

When a request comes in, UseAuthentication runs the default scheme handler, which is JwtBearerHandler. It reads the Authorization header, "Bearer" followed by the token, and validates it. It checks the signature using the identity provider's public keys, which it downloads from the authority's JWKS endpoint and caches. Then it checks the issuer, the audience and the expiry. If it's valid, it builds a ClaimsPrincipal from the token's claims and sets HttpContext.User. Then UseAuthorization reads the endpoint's metadata, like Authorize with a policy, and evaluates it. If there's no valid user, it returns a 401 challenge. If the user is authenticated but fails the policy, it returns 403.
I configure it with AddAuthentication and AddJwtBearer, with the authority and audience, and keep clock skew small.

In our services, we added one extra step in the OnTokenValidated event: checking the token's id against our ElastiCache denylist, so logged-out tokens are rejected immediately. I can explain that design.
cards.k: jwt, bearer authentication, token validation, authentication middleware, claims, 401, 403, token, bearer, access token, refresh token

cards.q: What are keyed services in .NET 8 dependency injection?
cards.h: Same interface, labelled drawers.
s: Keyed services, added in .NET 8, let you register several implementations of the same interface under different keys, and then ask the container for a specific one by its key.

Before .NET 8, if you registered three implementations of an interface, injecting the interface gave you the last one, and to pick a specific one you had to write your own factory, or register a Func of string returning the interface. Now, you register with AddKeyedSingleton, AddKeyedScoped or AddKeyedTransient, giving a key, like "rebex". To consume it, you use the FromKeyedServices attribute on a constructor parameter, or call GetRequiredKeyedService with the key at runtime.
It's a clean fit for the strategy pattern, where configuration decides which implementation to use.

That's exactly our SFTP case. Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro clients are registered as keyed services, using the library name as the key. Each vendor's configuration names its library, and our factory simply resolves GetRequiredKeyedService with that name. That replaced a hand-written switch statement, and adding a new library is just a new registration. I can show the code.
cards.k: keyed services, dependency injection, fromkeyedservices, .net 8, multiple implementations, di, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes, .net 10, net 8, net 10, upgrade

cards.q: What are System.Threading.Channels?
cards.h: An in-process queue with a full-sign.
s: System.Threading.Channels provides high-performance, thread-safe queues for the producer-consumer pattern inside one process.

You create a channel with Channel.CreateBounded or CreateUnbounded. Producers write items with WriteAsync, and consumers read them with ReadAllAsync in an await foreach loop. It's fully async, so no threads are blocked while waiting. A bounded channel has a maximum capacity, which gives you backpressure. When it's full, you choose whether the writer waits, or the channel drops the oldest or newest item. That stops a fast producer from exhausting memory. You can also have multiple readers to process items in parallel.

The typical pattern is pairing it with a BackgroundService. An HTTP request quickly writes a job into the channel and returns 202 Accepted, and the background service reads and processes jobs one by one. Of course, it's in-memory, so for work that must survive a restart, a durable queue like RabbitMQ or SQS is the right choice.
We used a bounded channel for sending non-critical notification emails, so slow email calls never delayed API responses. I can compare it with BlockingCollection.
cards.k: channels, producer consumer, queue, back-pressure, backgroundservice

cards.q: What is TimeProvider and why use it?
cards.h: Inject the clock; tests own the clock.
s: TimeProvider is an abstraction over the clock and timers, added in .NET 8. Instead of calling DateTime.UtcNow directly, I inject TimeProvider and call GetUtcNow.

The problem it solves is testability. Code that reads the real clock directly is hard to test. If a rule says "a token expires after 15 minutes" or "retry after 30 seconds", tests either wait for real time to pass or become flaky. With TimeProvider, production uses TimeProvider.System, and tests use FakeTimeProvider from Microsoft's testing extensions, where I can set the time and call Advance to move it forward instantly. It also covers timers through CreateTimer, and many APIs accept it, like Task.Delay and CancellationTokenSource, so even timeouts can be tested deterministically.
Before .NET 8, every team wrote its own IClock or ISystemClock interface. Now there's one standard.

In our system, rules like "block shipments after the study cut-off date" and our token expiry logic use TimeProvider. The tests set the fake time to just before and just after the cut-off, and run in milliseconds. I can show a short test example.
cards.k: timeprovider, faketimeprovider, testing time, datetime, .net 8

cards.q: How do you add resilience with Polly and .NET 8 resilience handlers?
cards.h: Retry, break, time out, fall back.
s: Resilience means handling the temporary failures that always happen with network calls, like timeouts, brief outages or throttling, so they recover on their own instead of becoming errors for users.

Polly is the standard .NET library for this. In Polly version 8, you build a resilience pipeline from strategies: retry, circuit breaker, timeout, rate limiter, fallback and hedging. In .NET 8, Microsoft added the Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience package on top of Polly. With one line, AddStandardResilienceHandler on an HttpClient, you get sensible defaults: an overall timeout, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, a circuit breaker, and a timeout for each attempt. You can customise each part, or build your own pipeline.

A few rules matter. Only retry transient errors, like 5xx, 408 and 429, never a 400. Make sure retried operations are idempotent. And use the circuit breaker so you stop hammering a service that's clearly down.

We use it for vendor API calls. Before, a short vendor outage meant failed shipments and manual retries. With the standard handler, most of those blips now recover automatically, and the circuit breaker protects the vendor. I can explain how the circuit breaker states work.
cards.k: resilience, polly, retry, circuit breaker, timeout, addstandardresiliencehandler, .net 8, .net 10, net 8, net 10, upgrade

script: Thank you. I'm Pradeep, a backend-focused full-stack engineer with about five and a half years of experience, mainly in C# and .NET.

For the last four years I've been at IQVIA, working on IRT. IRT is a regulated clinical-trial platform that handles patient randomization, drug supply, shipment tracking and eConsent for global trials. Because it's GxP regulated, every change we make has to be tested, traceable and auditable, and that has shaped how I work.

Day to day, I design and build .NET microservices and ASP.NET Core Web APIs with EF Core and SQL Server, and I also build Node.js and Python services and React components. Our services run on AWS, on ECS, Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB and RDS, with Terraform and CloudFormation, Docker, and Azure DevOps pipelines.

The work I'm proudest of is an internal MCP server that I designed and built on my own. It exposes about 77 tools for builds, releases and multi-node deployments to AI agents. That cut our deployment time from 6 hours to 2, and the people needed per deployment from 6 to 1, and I packaged it so my teammates install and use it.

I also own production issues. For example, I root-caused a RabbitMQ outage and fixed it with publisher confirms, and I delivered security fixes for token-based logout, SSO cookie failures and reverse tabnabbing. I've delivered features end to end too, like a CSV bulk import that is live in production and a study-transfer safety guard.
Before IQVIA, I started my career at DXC Technology, building C# and .NET Framework solutions on SharePoint.
Now I'm looking for a senior backend role where I can own the design and delivery of scalable services, and keep using AI tools to help the team move faster. That's why this role interests me.
